title: Late Fee Limits
bodyText:
Maine strictly limits late fees on residential rent.

Rent is not late until it remains unpaid 15 days after the date it is due, so you may not charge a late fee for a payment made within those 15 days, whatever grace period the lease states. **The fee may not be more than 4% of the amount due for one month.**

You may not charge any late fee unless, when you and the tenant entered into the rental agreement, you gave the tenant written notice that a penalty of up to 4% of one month's rent may be charged for late payment. Put that notice in the lease itself, as the library's Maine Late Fee clause does, or give a separate signed notice at signing; a notice given later does not satisfy the law.

The rule applies to fixed-term leases and tenancies at will alike, with no small-landlord exemption. A late fee is not rent under Maine's eviction law, so an unpaid late fee alone does not support a 7-day notice for nonpayment of rent. Charging more than the law allows can be challenged as an unfair trade practice.

title: Rent Payment Methods and Card Surcharges
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that tells you which rent payment methods you must accept. You may require a particular method, such as an online portal, and Maine does not require you to offer a cash or paper-check option.

Two related rules matter. First, Maine's consumer credit law bars a seller in a sales transaction from adding a surcharge for paying by credit or debit card instead of cash or check; a discount for cash is allowed. Maine's statutes do not say whether collecting rent is a "sales transaction", so the safer course is not to add a card surcharge to rent and, if card costs matter, to price the same for everyone and offer a discount for other methods.

Second, any payment-processing or portal fee the tenant must pay under the lease is a cost the tenant pays and belongs in the total price disclosure Maine requires before signing when the tenant pays any recurring fee.

If you accept cash, you must give a receipt (see the rent receipt rules).

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Maine has no statute that specifically regulates setting rents with algorithmic pricing software, or landlords sharing nonpublic rent or occupancy data through a common pricing service. That does not make coordinated pricing safe. Maine's general antitrust law makes every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade illegal, and a person injured by one can sue for three times their damages plus attorney's fees; the Attorney General can also seek civil penalties. Federal antitrust law applies as well. If you use revenue-management or pricing software, set your own rents, avoid tools that pool competitors' nonpublic data to recommend rents, and keep records showing your pricing decisions are your own. Maine also has no statewide rent control, but some cities have local rent ordinances (see the local rent ordinance row).

title: Application and Screening Fees
bodyText: In Maine you may not charge an applicant a fee to submit a rental application, or a fee for you to review or approve one. The only exception: you may require the applicant to pay the actual cost of one background check, one credit check or one other screening process, but only one of these, and not more than one such fee from the same applicant in any 12-month period. Before you charge it, you must tell the applicant that the law requires you to give them a complete copy of the information the check produces, and you must then give them that complete copy. Do not mark up the cost or add an administrative or processing charge. The rule covers every rental dwelling unit; there is no small-landlord or owner-occupied exemption. Maine has no rule on refunding an unused screening fee, no fee cap indexed to inflation, no required pre-application disclosure and no rule on holding fees until earlier applicants are screened. Using different application requirements or fees because of a protected characteristic is fair-housing discrimination. Separately, at signing you may collect only the first full month's rent, the security deposit and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees (see the amounts-due-at-signing rules).

title: No Statutory Order for Applying Payments
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that sets the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment to rent, fees or other charges.

The order still matters. Maine law defines rent as the amount paid on a regular schedule under the lease, and says rent does not include security deposits, utility costs, fees, penalties or charges. Your 7-day termination notice for nonpayment is available only when the tenant is 7 days or more behind in rent, and the notice is void if the tenant pays the full rent due before it expires. If you apply a payment to a late fee or repair charge first, the tenant may look behind in rent when the shortfall is really an unpaid fee, which a court may not treat as rent arrears.

Applying payments to the oldest unpaid rent first, as the lease's payment clause does, keeps these categories separate. Collect unpaid fees and charges separately, for example from the security deposit at move-out or in a small claims action.

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent
bodyText: If you send a former tenant's unpaid rent or charges to a collection agency, Maine's debt collection law applies to the agency, because a residential tenant's debt is a consumer debt. A debt collector may not collect any interest, fee, charge or expense on top of the amount owed unless the agreement that created the debt expressly authorizes it or another law permits it. So if your lease says nothing about collection costs, the agency cannot add a collection fee. The law covers outside agencies and you, if you collect your own debts under a name that suggests a third party is collecting; your own employees collecting in your name are excluded. Do not solve this by adding a broad "collection costs" clause. In Maine, any lease term that requires the tenant to pay your legal fees in enforcing the lease is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice (the only exception is a prevailing-party fee clause for wanton disregard of the lease after a contested hearing). Any charge the tenant will have to pay under the lease must also appear in the total price disclosure when one is required. The library offers no Maine collection-fee clause; if you want one, have Maine counsel review it first.

title: Limit on Money Due at Move-In
bodyText:
When a Maine tenant signs a lease or starts a tenancy at will, you, your agent or a real estate broker may require only three things up front: the rent for the first full month of occupancy, a security deposit no larger than two months' rent, and any mandatory recurring fee that you properly listed in the signed total price disclosure. Nothing else may be required at the start: no last month's rent in advance, no key, move-in, amenity, administrative or lease-preparation fee, and no separate pet deposit outside the security deposit (Maine treats any advance whose main purpose is to secure the lease as part of the security deposit, whatever it is called).

The rule covers fixed-term leases and tenancies at will alike and has no small-landlord exemption. A screening fee for one background or credit check at actual cost is a separate, pre-application matter.

Requiring more than the law allows can be challenged as an unfair trade practice. Use the library's Amounts Due Upfront clause, which lists only the permitted items.

title: Total Price Disclosure Before Signing
bodyText: If your tenant will pay any recurring fee besides rent (a mandatory fee for services or common areas, or an optional fee for an added feature such as parking or storage), Maine requires a written total price disclosure before the lease or tenancy at will begins. It must show at least the total rent, every mandatory recurring fee, every optional recurring fee, utility service costs (or, if you cannot get them, the residential energy efficiency disclosure statement) and any other cost the tenant will pay under the agreement. It must be plain and readily understandable, signed by you and the tenant, and each of you keeps a copy. If you do not receive a signed copy, the lease or tenancy at will is unenforceable, and a fee charged in violation of these rules is an unenforceable term and an unfair trade practice. If the tenant pays no recurring fee at all, the disclosure is not required. Maine has no rule requiring an all-in price in long-term rental advertising (that rule covers only short-term lodging), no rule on where fees appear in the lease, and its automatic-renewal law covers subscriptions and health clubs, not leases. Keep a signed copy of each disclosure with the lease.

title: Optional Recurring Fees and Unprovided Services
bodyText: Maine has no statute that expressly says you may not charge a fee for a service you do not provide, but charging for something the tenant does not receive can be an unfair or deceptive practice under Maine's Unfair Trade Practices Act. Maine does regulate recurring fees directly. An optional recurring fee is a regular charge for an added service or feature that is not essential to habitability, such as a parking space, storage unit or amenity package. You may charge one only if, before the fee starts, you tell the tenant in writing that the tenant may opt in to the service and may stop using it and stop paying the fee at any time without penalty. You may not refuse to rent to, or end the tenancy of, a tenant who opts out. A mandatory recurring fee must relate to services or common areas under the lease. Every recurring fee must appear in the signed total price disclosure before the tenancy begins, and a recurring fee charged in violation of these rules is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice. Coin laundry and other occasional, pay-per-use charges are not recurring fees.

title: Fees Are Not Rent in Maine
bodyText: Maine's eviction statute defines rent: money paid on a predetermined recurring basis to fulfill the lease or tenancy at will agreement. The same definition says rent does not include security deposits, utility service costs, fees, penalties, or charges that reimburse you for reasonable costs or that deter lease violations. So late fees, repair charges, returned-check fees and similar charges are not rent, even if a lease calls them "additional rent", and a tenant who owes only fees is not "in arrears in the payment of rent" for the 7-day nonpayment notice. Mandatory and optional recurring fees are defined separately from rent and must be disclosed in the total price disclosure. Rent and mandatory recurring fee increases both need 45 days' written notice (75 days for rent increases of 10% or more). Do not add a clause making your legal fees "additional rent": in Maine any lease term requiring the tenant to pay your legal fees in enforcing the lease is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice, except a prevailing-party fee clause for wanton disregard of the lease after a contested hearing. Collect unpaid fees from the security deposit or in a separate claim. Subsidized tenancies may have additional federal limits.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Maine has no statute that addresses whether you may pass a city's rental registration, licensing or inspection fee on to your tenants, and no statewide rental registration law. Some Maine cities have local registration ordinances, so check local rules. If you want the tenant to bear such a fee, Maine's general rent and fee rules control how you do it. You cannot collect it at move-in, because only the first full month's rent, the security deposit and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees may be required at the start. A fee charged on a regular schedule under the lease is a recurring fee that must be listed in the signed total price disclosure before the tenancy begins, and a mandatory recurring fee may be raised only after 45 days' written notice. A one-time reimbursement demanded during the tenancy must rest on a lease term the tenant agreed to and must be listed among the costs in the total price disclosure when one is required. The simplest lawful approach is to build the cost into the rent. Property taxes are a separate statute (see the tax escalation row).

title: No Rule on Lease-Type Parity
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to offer the same rent or the same terms to a month-to-month tenant (a tenancy at will under Maine law) as to a tenant on a fixed-term lease, and no limit on how much the rent offered for the two may differ. Several Maine rules do turn on the type of tenancy, so check them when you choose: a tenancy at will ends on 30 days' written notice (or 7 days for listed causes) and has a statutory right to reinstate after a nonpayment notice; a security deposit must be returned within 21 days after a tenancy at will ends, but within the time stated in a written lease, not over 30 days; and a domestic violence victim may end a tenancy at will or a lease shorter than a year on 7 days' notice, but needs 30 days' notice for a lease of a year or more. Rent and mandatory recurring fee increases need 45 days' written notice (75 days for 10% or more) in either case. Different terms must never be based on a protected characteristic.

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that specifically regulates rent concessions such as a free first month, a rent credit or a move-in discount.

If you give one, state it in the lease, as the library's rent concession clause does, and make sure the total rent shown in the total price disclosure (required when the tenant pays any recurring fee) matches what the tenant will actually pay.

Be careful with clauses that take a concession back if the tenant leaves early. In Maine a lease term requiring the tenant to pay a fee, penalty or other charge for the act of ending the tenancy is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice, unless the charge only recovers your reasonable costs of finding a new tenant when the tenant broke the lease's notice terms, collects unpaid rent, or covers reasonable repair costs for damage the tenant caused. A clawback that simply makes the tenant repay the concession for leaving is likely to be treated as a prohibited charge. A concession tied to rent actually owed for the months the tenant occupied, with your duty to mitigate by re-renting, is safer.

title: Local Rent Ordinances
bodyText: Maine has no statewide rent control or rent cap, and no state law stops a city or town from adopting its own rent stabilization or other landlord-tenant ordinance. Maine municipalities have broad home-rule power: an ordinance is presumed valid and, unless a state law expressly denies the power, is preempted only if it would frustrate the purpose of a state law. Maine's old municipal rent control statutes were repealed, and a 2025 law directed a state office to develop a model rent stabilization ordinance for municipalities to use. Some Maine cities, including Portland and South Portland, have adopted local rent ordinances, which may limit increases, require registration or notices, or add tenant protections; this library does not track them. Before setting or raising rent, check the ordinances of the municipality where the property is located. State rules still apply everywhere: 45 days' written notice of any rent or mandatory recurring fee increase (75 days for rent increases totaling 10% or more over 12 months, except in certain deed-restricted or subsidized housing) and no rent increase while the unit violates the warranty of habitability. Municipalities may also adopt stricter heat and mold standards, and may step in to provide heat, utilities or repairs a landlord fails to provide and then place a lien on the property.

title: Collecting Rent for a Substandard Unit
bodyText: Maine has no statute that forbids you from asking for or collecting rent simply because the unit has a defect, but substandard conditions sharply limit what you can recover. If you seek to evict for nonpayment, the tenant may defend by showing a habitability violation you knew about and unreasonably failed to fix promptly, if the tenant did not cause it; the court may then let the tenant end the tenancy or stay and pay only a reduced fair rental value, and you may not charge full rent until the unit is fit again. In a suit for rent, if the tenant gave you written notice of a condition making the unit unfit that the tenant (or someone under the tenant's control) did not cause, was current in rent then, and you unreasonably failed to repair it, the court deducts the difference between the rent and the unit's fair value from notice to repair. You may not raise rent while the unit violates the warranty of habitability unless the tenant caused it. And no action for rent may be maintained for a period when fire or other unavoidable casualty has made the premises unfit; a residential lease cannot override that. Fix reported conditions promptly and document your repair efforts.

title: Rent Increases During a Lease Term
bodyText:
Maine law does not itself give you a right to raise rent in the middle of a fixed-term lease; whether you can depends on the lease.

If the lease contains an increase clause, such as the library's optional Maine mid-term increase clause, every increase still needs written notice: at least 45 days for any increase in rent or a mandatory recurring fee, and at least 75 days for a rent increase of 10% or more, counting all increases in a 12-month period. The 75-day rule does not apply to deed-restricted affordable housing or housing whose rent is restricted as a condition of a government subsidy.

The tenant cannot waive these notice periods, and a landlord who collects an improperly noticed increase must repay it with interest and the tenant's attorney's fees. No increase is allowed while the unit violates the warranty of habitability, unless the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused the problem.

Maine's retaliation presumption applies when you bring an eviction within 6 months after a tenant asserts certain rights, including rights under the rent-increase notice and habitability statutes; Maine has no separate rule treating a rent increase itself as retaliation and no safe harbor tied to the lease wording. Local rent ordinances may add limits.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText:
Before you raise the rent or any mandatory recurring fee on a Maine residential tenancy, you must give the tenant **at least 45 days' written notice**. If a rent increase is 10% or more, or several increases within 12 months add up to 10% or more, the notice must be at least 75 days before the increase that reaches 10%.

The 75-day rule does not apply to housing kept affordable by a recorded deed restriction or to housing whose rent is restricted because the landlord or tenant receives a government housing subsidy. The rule covers residential estates generally, so it applies to month-to-month tenancies at will and to any increase allowed during a fixed-term lease.

A tenant cannot waive it, and a landlord who collects an increase without proper notice must repay it with interest plus the tenant's attorney's fees and costs. You may not raise rent at all while the unit violates the warranty of habitability, unless the tenant caused the problem.

Maine has no separate notice duty for not renewing a lease. During a Governor-declared abnormal market disruption, Maine's anti-profiteering law bars unconscionable prices for necessities; whether rent counts is not settled, so avoid sharp increases during a declared emergency. Check local rent ordinances too.

title: Rent Paid in Installments
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that addresses splitting monthly rent into scheduled installments or says whether a scheduled installment counts as a partial payment. You may agree with the tenant in the lease on an installment schedule, as the library's rent installment clause does.

A few Maine rules then apply to each installment.
- If you accept rent in cash in more than one installment, you must give a separate written receipt for each payment, unless you rent a unit in an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.
- A late fee may be charged only if a payment is not made within 15 days after it is due, is capped at 4% of one month's rent, and requires written notice of the penalty when the agreement was made; state in the lease which payment date the late fee runs from, and charge no more than one late fee for the month.
- Maine's 7-day termination notice for nonpayment requires that the tenant be 7 days or more in arrears in rent, so a clear schedule avoids disputes about whether an installment is late.
- Rent excludes fees and utility costs, so do not mix them into the installment amounts.

title: When a Maine Tenant May Deduct from Rent
Receipts for Cash Rent
bodyText: If a tenant pays rent or a security deposit wholly or partly in cash, Maine requires you or your agent to hand the tenant a written receipt at the time you accept the cash. Each receipt must show the date of payment, the amount, the name of the person for whom the payment is made, the period it covers, whether it is for rent or for the security deposit, and the signature and legibly printed name of the person receiving it. If rent or a deposit is paid in installments, give a separate receipt for each installment; if rent and deposit are paid together, give a separate receipt for each. A rent card kept by the tenant that contains the same information satisfies the rule. The rule does not apply to a unit in a building of five or fewer units where you live in one of them. Maine's statute does not set a penalty or make a missing receipt a defense to eviction, but without a receipt you may be unable to prove what was paid, and a disputed cash payment can sink a nonpayment case. Receipts are not required for checks or electronic payments, though a payment record is good practice.

title: No Rule on Rent Reporting
bodyText: Maine has no statute that requires you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to a credit bureau, no state rent-reporting program, and no rule on whether you may require a tenant to enroll in a rent-reporting service. If you choose to report rent payments, or negative information such as unpaid rent, to a consumer reporting agency, you are furnishing information and federal credit reporting law applies, along with Maine's Fair Credit Reporting Act, which requires users and others subject to it to follow the federal law. Report only accurate, complete information. If a rent-reporting service costs the tenant money on a regular schedule, treat it as an optional recurring fee: the tenant must be told in writing that they may opt in and stop paying at any time without penalty, and it must appear in the total price disclosure. One specific Maine rule: if a tenant bought a surety bond instead of paying a deposit and disputes your claim on it, the surety may not report the claim to a credit reporting agency before getting a judgment against the tenant.

title: Sales Tax on Rent
bodyText: Maine's sales tax applies to the rental of living quarters in a hotel, rooming house, tourist camp or trailer camp, and Maine defines "rooming house" broadly: any house, cottage, condominium unit, vacation home or other place held out to the public where living quarters are supplied for pay to transient or permanent guests or tenants. Ordinary residential tenants are nonetheless outside the tax in practice, because rent charged to an individual who lives continuously at the same place for 28 days or more is exempt if the individual does not keep a primary residence somewhere else, or is living away from home for work or school. Tax collected during the first 28 days from someone who qualifies must be refunded by the landlord, who can then take a credit. Rentals of 28 or more consecutive days that a business rents for its employees are also exempt. So a normal lease of a tenant's home carries no sales tax, but short stays, furnished rentals to people who keep a home elsewhere (other than for work or school), and vacation rentals generally do. If you rent short-term, you may need to register and collect the lodging tax; check with Maine Revenue Services. Some municipalities also regulate short-term rentals.

title: Listing and Adding Fees
bodyText: Maine has no rule that every fee must be written into the lease itself or explained by purpose there, but in practice you must list your charges before the tenancy starts. Whenever the tenant will pay any recurring fee besides rent, the signed total price disclosure must list the rent, every mandatory recurring fee, every optional recurring fee, utility service costs and any other cost the tenant will pay under the agreement; without the signed disclosure the lease is unenforceable, and a recurring fee charged in violation of the disclosure or optional-fee rules is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice. A mandatory recurring fee is one tied to services or common areas, paid on a set schedule. During the tenancy, a mandatory recurring fee may be increased only after 45 days' written notice; treat adding a new mandatory fee the same way, and do not add one during a fixed term unless the lease allows it. Optional fees require written notice before they start that the tenant may opt in and stop at any time without penalty. Late fees are limited separately, and Maine has no statute on charges for accepting partial payments; avoid them, since the tenant may not owe a fee the lease and disclosure do not provide for.

title: Returned Checks and Payments
bodyText:
Maine does not cap the fee a lease may charge for a returned rent check or failed electronic payment, and its bad-check law expressly does not override a written agreement between you and the tenant, so a reasonable returned-payment fee stated in the lease is allowed. If it is a cost the tenant will pay under the lease, list it in the total price disclosure when one is required.

Without relying on the lease, Maine's bad-check law gives you a separate path for a dishonored check: send the tenant the statutory notice, in substantially the form the law prescribes, telling them to pay within 10 days. If they do not pay the check amount plus bank fees and mailing costs within 10 days, you may sue to recover the check amount, court costs, processing charges and interest at 12% a year from dishonor, and if they still have not paid by the hearing the court may award attorney's fees and a civil penalty up to $150. A second intentionally bad check to you within a year can bring added damages.

A returned-payment fee is not rent, so an unpaid fee alone does not support a 7-day nonpayment notice. Maine has no rule on postdated checks or electronic-payment network rules for landlords.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: Maine has no law that delays rent, bars late fees or limits evictions for federal or state employees during a government shutdown. Your ordinary rules apply: rent is late only after 15 days, the late fee is capped at 4% of one month's rent, and a nonpayment termination requires a 7-day notice once the tenant is 7 days or more behind, with the tenant's right to cure before the notice expires and, in a tenancy at will, to reinstate before the writ issues. Maine does help affected workers directly. Under the Government Shutdown Loan Guarantee Program, a Maine resident who must work without pay or is furloughed without pay during a federal or state shutdown lasting more than 7 days may get a state-guaranteed loan from a participating bank or credit union, up to the lesser of $6,000 and one month's after-tax pay (reduced by unemployment benefits), with no interest during a grace period and no credit check. If a tenant tells you they are affected, pointing them to that program and agreeing in writing on a short payment plan is often cheaper than an eviction. Members of the National Guard or Reserves ordered to duty have separate eviction protection.

title: No Subsidy Rule for Habitability Rent Reductions
bodyText: Maine has no special rule for reducing rent on a subsidized unit when part of it becomes uninhabitable, or for how a reduction is split between the tenant's share and the part a housing subsidy pays. The general Maine remedies apply to every tenant. In a habitability case, the court may set the fair value of the unit's use and occupancy from when you got notice of the problem until it is fixed and order a rebate of rent paid above that value; in a nonpayment eviction the tenant may raise the habitability defense and the court may reduce the rent owed; and in a suit for rent the court deducts the difference between the rent and the fair value. The statutes do not say whether the subsidy-paid portion is part of the rent measured, so check your housing assistance contract and the program's rules, which often require abatement of the subsidy payment for units that fail inspection. No rent may be raised while the unit violates the warranty of habitability.

title: No Subsidy Late Fee Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute specifically addressing late fees when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, such as barring a late fee when the housing authority's share arrives late. Maine's general late-fee rule applies to every residential tenant: rent is late only if not paid within 15 days after it is due, the penalty may not exceed 4% of the amount due for one month, and you may charge one only if you gave the tenant written notice at signing that a penalty of up to 4% may be charged. The statute does not say whether "the amount due for one month" means the whole contract rent or only the tenant's share. The safer course is to charge a late fee only on the tenant's own share, calculated on that share, and never because the subsidy payment was late. Your housing assistance contract and program rules may limit late fees further. Maine also bars refusing to rent to, or imposing different terms on, someone because they receive public assistance, including housing subsidies, so late-fee terms should not single out voucher holders.

title: Property Taxes and Rent
bodyText: Maine has a long-standing statute that splits real estate taxes between landlord and tenant when there is no agreement. If a tenant paying rent is taxed for the rented real estate, the tenant may keep half of the tax paid out of the rent. If you, as landlord, are taxed for the real estate, you may recover half of the taxes you paid, together with your rent, in an action against the tenant, unless you and the tenant have agreed otherwise. Whether and how this old rule applies to an ordinary apartment lease is not settled by the statute, and no Maine case law was searched, so do not rely on it to collect property taxes; if you and the tenant intend the rent to cover all real estate taxes, say so in the lease. Maine has no statute regulating clauses that pass tax increases on to a tenant during a lease. If a lease does allow it, the added amount is a rent increase, which needs at least 45 days' written notice (75 days if increases reach 10% within 12 months), cannot take effect while the unit breaches the warranty of habitability, and should be shown in the total price disclosure. Maine has no rule letting you deduct a tax share from the security deposit.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText:
Maine's landlord-tenant statutes do not address interest on money a tenant owes, but the general interest statute makes the lease wording matter.

In small claims court, where most deposit and damage disputes go, you cannot recover interest before judgment unless the interest rate is based on a contract. In any civil case on a contract that has an interest provision, prejudgment interest runs at the contract rate; without one, it runs at the one-year Treasury bill rate plus 3%, but only outside small claims. After judgment, interest runs at the greater of the contract rate or the Treasury bill rate plus 6%. Courts may waive interest for good cause.

So if you want interest on unpaid damages or charges, the lease must say so and state the rate.

Do not apply interest to late rent: Maine caps any penalty for late payment of rent at 4% of one month's rent after a 15-day grace period, and interest on late rent could push the total over that cap. The library's optional Maine interest clause applies interest only to non-rent amounts after an itemized written statement. Bad checks carry their own 12% statutory interest after notice.

title: Move-In Condition Records
bodyText:
Maine does not require a move-in or move-out condition checklist, a joint inspection, or any notice to the tenant about one. Doing one anyway is strongly advised.

When you keep any part of a security deposit, you must give the tenant a written statement itemizing the reasons, and if the tenant sues, you carry the burden of proving that what you kept was not wrongful; wrongful retention costs double the amount withheld plus the tenant's attorney's fees. You also may not keep any part of the deposit for normal wear and tear, which Maine defines as deterioration from intended use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household or guests.

A dated, signed move-in condition record with photos, compared with a move-out record, is the most practical way to show what was damage rather than wear.

If the tenant bought a surety bond instead of paying a deposit, Maine does require a written list of damages: at least 10 days before claiming against the bond, you must mail the tenant notice of the claim, the damages list, your actual costs and how to dispute it. Deposit rules do not apply to a unit in an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units, though records still help.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: Maine has no statute that lets a lease fix in advance what you will charge against the security deposit for cleaning, carpet, painting or repairs, and a flat preset charge is risky. You may keep only what you have actual cause to keep, you must list the reasons in a written itemized statement, and you may never keep any part for normal wear and tear. Maine defines normal wear and tear as deterioration from the intended use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, the household or their guests. That definition also tells you what you can charge: the cost of removing things the tenant left behind, such as trash, and, if the unit was rented in habitable condition, what you must spend to return it to habitable condition, which may include cleaning, unless the need arose from your own actions or events outside the tenant's control. Charge the actual, reasonable cost of the work, keep invoices, and be ready to prove the charge, since you carry the burden in court and wrongful retention costs double damages. A schedule of typical charges may be shared as an estimate, but deduct only actual costs.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a former tenant never cashes or claims a security deposit refund you owe, the money does not become yours. Maine's unclaimed property law expressly covers security deposits and refunds. The refund is presumed abandoned 3 years after you owed it, and you then become a holder with duties: if the amount is $50 or more and you have a valid mailing address, you must mail the tenant notice 60 to 180 days before you file your report, and you must then report it by November 1 (covering the year to the prior July 1) and pay it over to the state's unclaimed property administrator. If you report or pay late, you can owe interest at 18% a year (or 10% over the T-bill rate) and a civil penalty of $200 a day up to $5,000. You may not deduct an escheat or reporting fee. A dormancy charge is allowed only under a valid contract the holder regularly enforces, but deducting such a charge from a security deposit would conflict with Maine's rule that you may keep a deposit only for actual cause, so do not use one. A lease clause saying an unclaimed deposit is forfeited to you is void. Mailing the refund and statement to the tenant's last known address on time still satisfies the deposit return deadline; keep records of the mailing and of any returned or uncashed check.

title: No Right to Pay Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Maine law does not give a tenant a right to pay the security deposit in installments; you may require the full deposit when the tenancy begins. You may agree to accept it in installments, and if you do, and any installment is paid in cash, you must hand the tenant a separate written receipt for each installment at the time you accept it, identified as a security deposit payment (this receipt rule does not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units). Whatever the schedule, the total deposit may not exceed two months' rent, and the only money you may require to start the tenancy is the first full month's rent, the security deposit and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees. If you offer a surety bond instead of some or all of the deposit, the tenant may choose it but you cannot require it, and the bond and any deposit together may not exceed two months' rent. Any installment agreement should be in writing and should say what happens if an installment is missed; an unpaid deposit installment is not rent, so it does not by itself support a 7-day notice for nonpayment of rent.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: In Maine you may not require a new tenant to pay last month's rent in advance. When a lease or tenancy at will begins, the most you may require is the first full month's rent, a security deposit of no more than two months' rent, and any properly disclosed mandatory recurring fee. Calling extra money "last month's rent" or "prepaid rent" does not get around this, and any advance whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance is treated as a security deposit regardless of its label, so it counts toward the two-month cap and must be held and returned under the deposit rules. Maine has no statute forbidding a tenant from using the deposit as the last month's rent, and none requiring you to accept that; the lease may require the last month's rent to be paid when due. If a tenant does not pay the final month, unpaid rent is a lawful reason to keep part of the deposit, listed in your itemized statement, and you may also pursue the tenant for any balance. A domestic violence victim who ends a tenancy early is not owed a refund of rent prepaid for the month in which the tenancy ends. The deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units, but the start-of-tenancy limit does.

title: Deposit Refund Not Conditioned on Notice
bodyText: Maine has no rule allowing you to make the security deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out or a forwarding address. Your deadline to return the deposit, or give an itemized statement of what you keep with the balance, runs from the end of the tenancy or the surrender and acceptance of the premises, whichever is later: within the time the written lease states, but no more than 30 days, or within 21 days for a tenancy at will. Mailing the statement and payment to the tenant's last known address satisfies the law, so a missing forwarding address does not excuse a late refund. A lease term that makes the tenant forfeit the deposit for failing to give notice would waive the tenant's deposit rights and is void. What you can do: require notice before the tenant leaves, and if a tenant breaks the lease's notice terms, you may recover your reasonable costs of finding a new tenant and any unpaid rent, subject to your duty to mitigate, and deduct those amounts in the itemized statement. These deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Deposits After a Victim Ends the Tenancy
bodyText: Maine has no special rule on when you return a security deposit after a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking ends a tenancy early, and no rule that the deposit clock waits until all remaining occupants leave. The ordinary deadlines apply: within the time stated in a written lease, not over 30 days, or within 21 days for a tenancy at will, counted from the end of the tenancy or surrender and acceptance of the premises, whichever is later. Where the victim shares the lease with others who stay, the statutes do not say how the deposit is divided, so handle it by written agreement or keep it with the continuing tenancy. Two Maine rules affect what you may keep. A victim is not liable for damage caused by the abuse beyond the amount of the victim's security deposit, if the perpetrator is a tenant and the victim gives you written notice of the damage and the required documentation within 30 days after it happens; you may still hold the perpetrator liable. And a victim who ends a lease early under Maine law is not liable for rent beyond the notice period or move-out date. Deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Maine has no special procedure for an early or expedited return of the security deposit and no fee for one. None is needed: Maine's deadlines are outer limits, so you may return the deposit, or the itemized statement with the balance, as soon as you can determine what you have actual cause to keep. For a written lease the deadline is the time stated in the lease, which may not exceed 30 days; for a tenancy at will it is 21 days, counted from the end of the tenancy or the surrender and acceptance of the premises, whichever is later. Do not charge a processing or administrative fee for returning the deposit early. A charge tied to the tenant's leaving is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice unless it only recovers reasonable re-renting costs when the tenant broke the lease's notice terms, unpaid rent, or reasonable repair costs for damage the tenant caused, and deducting an unauthorized fee from the deposit is wrongful retention, which costs double damages plus attorney's fees. Deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Surety Bonds Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: Maine's only statutory alternative to a security deposit is a surety bond the tenant buys. You may offer a tenant the option of a surety bond in place of some or all of the deposit, but you may not require it, and the bond and any deposit together may not exceed two months' rent; demanding more lets the tenant recover up to three times the excess plus attorney's fees. Before purchase, the tenant must be told in writing of their rights, including that the premium is nonrefundable (printed in 16-point bold type, on the first page and above the signature line), that the bond is not insurance for the tenant, and that the tenant stays responsible for rent and damage. To claim on the bond, you must first mail the tenant, at least 10 days ahead and within the deposit return deadline, a written list of damages, your actual costs, the surety's name and address and how to dispute; missing it forfeits your claim. The tenant may pay you directly or have you use any deposit first. If the tenant disputes the claim, the surety may not report it to a credit bureau before getting a judgment. If a buyer takes over the property, the new landlord must accept the bond. Maine has no statute authorizing a monthly fee charged in place of a deposit; if you consider one, it must satisfy the recurring-fee and total price disclosure rules, so get legal advice first.

title: Furnished Units
bodyText: Maine has no statute specifically about furnished rentals: no list of required furnishings, and no larger deposit allowed for a furnished unit. The security deposit for a furnished unit is capped at two months' rent like any other, and a separate "furniture deposit" counts toward that cap because any advance whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit. You may charge the deposit for damage to furniture and other items you own beyond normal wear and tear, which Maine defines as deterioration from intended use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse of the premises or the equipment or chattels by the tenant, household or guests. List the furnishings in the lease or an attached inventory, record their condition at move-in, and keep repair or replacement invoices, since you bear the burden of proving any amount you keep. Furnished rentals to people who keep a primary residence elsewhere may be subject to Maine's lodging sales tax (see the rent tax row). Deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Maine has no statute written for holding deposits, earnest money or other money taken to reserve a unit before a lease is signed, so treat such payments carefully. You may not charge an applicant any fee to submit an application or for you to review or approve it, other than the actual cost of one background check, credit check or other screening; a nonrefundable "holding fee" collected with an application risks being treated as a prohibited application fee and an unfair trade practice. When the lease or tenancy at will begins, the most you may require is the first full month's rent, a security deposit of no more than two months' rent and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees. The safest practice: take a holding payment only after you approve the applicant, put the terms in writing, and apply the full amount to the first month's rent or the security deposit at signing, staying within those limits; once the tenancy begins, any part applied to the deposit is subject to every deposit rule. If the applicant backs out, keep no more than your actual, documented loss, and refund the payment if you decline the applicant or cannot deliver the unit.

title: No Inspection Notice Penalty
bodyText: Maine does not require you to tell a tenant about move-in or move-out inspection rights, so there is no penalty for failing to give such a notice. Maine's deposit penalties attach to other duties. If you do not return the deposit, or give the tenant a written itemized statement of what you keep with the balance, within the deadline (the time stated in a written lease, not over 30 days, or 21 days for a tenancy at will), you forfeit the right to keep any part of it. If you then keep it after the tenant's 7-day notice of intent to sue, you are presumed to be withholding it wrongfully, and wrongful retention costs double the amount withheld plus attorney's fees and costs. Failing to hold deposits in a separate protected account, or to tell a tenant on request where it is held, costs at least $500 or one month's rent. For a surety bond, missing the 10-day written damages notice forfeits your claim against the bond and the tenant. Offering a joint move-out inspection is still good practice, because it helps you prove damage. These deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: In Maine no part of a security deposit can be made nonrefundable, so a lease clause or notice designating a nonrefundable portion does not work. Maine treats any advance or deposit of money whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance as a security deposit, whatever you call it, including a "nonrefundable pet deposit" or "cleaning deposit". You must return all of it except amounts you have actual cause to keep, listed in a written itemized statement within the deadline, and you may never keep any part for normal wear and tear. A lease term waiving these rights is void. Labeling the money a fee instead does not help: at the start of a tenancy you may require only the first full month's rent, the security deposit (capped at two months' rent) and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees, so nonrefundable move-in, cleaning, key, pet or administrative fees cannot be required, and application fees are banned except the actual cost of one screening. The one "nonrefundable" notice in Maine's statutes concerns surety bonds: if a tenant buys a bond instead of a deposit, the surety must disclose in 16-point bold type that the premium is nonrefundable. These deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units, but the start-of-tenancy limit does.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposit Notice Rule
bodyText: Maine has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. The reason is that Maine does not allow any part of a security deposit to be nonrefundable. Any money paid in advance mainly to secure the tenant's performance counts as a security deposit whatever it is called, it must be returned except for amounts you have actual cause to keep and itemize in writing within the deadline, it may never be kept for normal wear and tear, and a lease term waiving these rights is void. Giving a tenant a "nonrefundable deposit" notice would not make the money yours and could mislead the tenant. The one separate nonrefundable disclosure in Maine law is for surety bonds a tenant buys instead of a deposit: before purchase the tenant must receive written notice of their rights, with the word "nonrefundable" about the premium in at least 16-point bold type on the first page and again above the tenant's signature. Deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText:
A Maine lease or tenancy at will **may not require a security deposit of more than two months' rent**.

The cap is the same for every type of tenancy and has no exceptions for pets, furniture or higher-risk tenants. Every advance or deposit whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance counts toward it, whatever its name, so a pet deposit, cleaning deposit or furniture deposit must fit within the two months together with the regular deposit.

If a tenant buys a surety bond in place of part of the deposit, the bond and deposit together are also limited to two months' rent. You may not charge any deposit or fee for an assistance animal used by a person with a disability, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes.

Maine's statute does not address raising the deposit after a rent increase; any increase in what you hold should stay within two months of the current rent and rest on a lease term the tenant agreed to. The deposit chapter does not apply to a unit in a building of five or fewer units where you live in one of them, but the start-of-tenancy limit still refers to a deposit within the two-month cap, so stay within it there too.

title: Holding Security Deposits
bodyText: Maine requires you to keep tenants' security deposits separate from your own money. During the tenancy a deposit may not be commingled with your assets or anyone else's; it must be held in an account at a bank or other financial institution on terms that put it beyond the reach of your creditors, including a foreclosing mortgagee or a bankruptcy trustee, and that allow it to be transferred to a new owner or returned to the tenant. You may use a single escrow account for all your tenants' deposits, and one account for buildings owned by different entities if a single landlord substantially controls or owns them. If a tenant asks, you must tell them the name of the institution and the account number where the deposit is held. If a court finds a violation, the tenant recovers actual damages, $500 or one month's rent, whichever is greatest, plus reasonable costs, and the court may add attorney's fees. Maine does not require you to pay interest on deposits or to give notice of the account unless asked, and offers no bond alternative to the account. When you sell, a new owner takes over responsibility for deposits transferred to them. These rules do not apply to a unit in a building of five or fewer units where you live in one of them.

title: No Interest on Deposits
bodyText: Maine does not require you to pay a residential tenant interest on a security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing account. You must still keep the deposit in a separate account at a bank or other financial institution, beyond the reach of your creditors, and tell the tenant where it is held if asked. The statute does not say who keeps any interest the account happens to earn; if you want to avoid questions, say in the lease that no interest will be paid and any account interest belongs to you, or use a non-interest-bearing escrow account. Maine's deposit-interest rule applies only to mobile home park lot rentals, which have their own chapter, not to apartments or houses. If a tenant with a disability makes modifications and you require payments into a restoration escrow under the Human Rights Commission's rule, that escrow is interest-bearing and its interest belongs to the tenant; that is a separate arrangement from the security deposit. Deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Maine tenant cannot give up the protections of the security deposit law. Any provision, oral or written, in or connected with a lease or tenancy at will that waives a deposit right for the tenant or the tenant's household is against public policy and void. That covers the two-month cap, the return deadlines and itemized statement, the bar on keeping money for normal wear and tear, the separate-account rule, the transfer rules on sale and the double-damages remedy. It is also an unfair trade practice to require a tenant to sign a lease containing a provision that has the effect of waiving such a right, and in Maine adding "to the extent permitted by law" does not cure it, because requiring the term is itself the violation. Clauses to avoid include nonrefundable deposits, automatic forfeiture of the deposit for breaking the lease or failing to give notice, preset cleaning charges kept regardless of condition, and promises that the deposit will be returned on a schedule longer than the law allows. Lawful lease terms, such as a return period shorter than 30 days, are fine. The deposit chapter does not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Deposits When Property Is Sold
bodyText: When your interest in a rental ends, whether by sale, assignment, death, a receivership or otherwise, whoever holds the security deposits (you, your agent or your executor) must do one of two things. Either transfer the deposits, or what remains after lawful deductions, to the new owner with an accounting of each tenant's deposit, and mail each tenant notice of the transfer, the new owner's name and address and a copy of the accounting; or return the deposits to the tenants. On a sale, the accounting and transfer must happen no later than the real estate closing, and you must give the buyer written proof of them at closing. Once you comply, you are released from further liability, and the buyer has all the rights and duties of a landlord holding those deposits, including keeping them in a protected account and returning them at the end of each tenancy. If you are buying, insist on the accounting and the funds at closing, because you will be responsible for deposits transferred to you. A buyer must also honor a tenant's surety bond and may not demand an additional deposit or bond during the current rental term. These deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Deposit Penalties
bodyText:
Maine's deposit penalties are strict.

If you do not return the deposit, or give a written itemized statement of what you keep together with the balance, within the deadline (the time stated in a written lease, not over 30 days, or 21 days for a tenancy at will), you forfeit the right to keep any part of it; missing either the statement or the return is enough. Before suing, the tenant must give you at least 7 days' notice of intent to sue; if you still do not return the entire deposit, you are presumed to be withholding it wrongfully.

Wrongful retention makes you liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld (not double the whole deposit), plus the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees and court costs, and in court you must prove your withholding was not wrongful. Forfeiting the right to withhold does not by itself erase a claim for damage or unpaid rent beyond the deposit, but expect that claim to be contested.

Commingling deposits or failing to hold them in a protected account, or to disclose the account on request, costs actual damages, $500 or one month's rent, whichever is greatest, plus costs and possibly attorney's fees. With a surety bond, a late damages notice forfeits any claim against the bond or the tenant. These rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Deposit Return Deadlines
bodyText:
When a Maine tenancy ends, you must either return the full security deposit or give the tenant a written statement itemizing why you are keeping part of it, together with full payment of the balance.

The deadline depends on the tenancy. For a written lease, it is the time stated in the lease, which may not exceed 30 days; for a tenancy at will, including a month-to-month tenancy after a lease expires, it is 21 days after the tenancy ends or the tenant surrenders and you accept the premises, whichever is later. State a period in the lease, since Maine's statute measures a written lease's deadline by the time the lease states.

Reasons you may keep money include unpaid rent, utility charges the tenant was required to pay you directly, the cost of storing and disposing of property the tenant left, and damage beyond normal wear and tear. Mailing the statement and payment to the tenant's last known address is enough to comply. The tenant does not have to ask for the deposit first, and an uncashed refund never reverts to you.

Missing the deadline forfeits your right to keep any of it, and wrongful retention can cost double damages. These rules do not apply to a unit in a building of five or fewer units where you live in one of them.

title: No Rule on Deposit Standards
bodyText: Maine has no rule requiring you to post or give tenants the standards you use to decide how large a security deposit to charge, even if you charge different tenants different amounts. Two limits apply. First, no deposit may exceed two months' rent. Second, fair housing law forbids discriminating in the price, terms or conditions of a rental because of race or color, sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, physical or mental disability, religion, ancestry, national origin, familial status or having sought and received a protection order, and forbids imposing different terms on someone because they receive public assistance, including a housing subsidy. You also may not charge any deposit for an assistance animal or raise the customary deposit for a tenant with a disability. If you vary deposits, use written, objective criteria applied to everyone, such as credit history or a guarantor, and keep a record of how each amount was set, so you can show a legitimate reason if challenged. The fair housing rules have narrow exemptions for an owner-occupied two-family home and for renting up to four rooms in an owner-occupied single-family home.

title: What a Deposit May Cover
bodyText:
Maine law does not give a closed list of what a security deposit may be used for, but it sets firm limits.

You may keep only amounts for which you have actual cause, and you must list each reason in the written itemized statement. The statute names some permitted reasons, without limiting others: unpaid rent, utility charges the tenant was required to pay directly to you, and the cost of storing and disposing of property the tenant left behind. Damage beyond normal wear and tear also qualifies.

You may never keep money for normal wear and tear, which Maine defines as deterioration from the intended use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household or guests. Two charges are expressly outside normal wear and tear: removing articles the tenant abandoned, such as trash, and, if the unit was rented in habitable condition, what you must spend to return it to habitable condition, which may include cleaning, unless the need was caused by you or events outside the tenant's control.

The library's deposit use clause is stricter on cleaning than Maine law requires, which is lawful. Deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Utility Deposits Held by a Landlord
bodyText: Maine has no separate rule for a "utility deposit" that a landlord holds. If you collect money to secure the tenant's payment of utility charges under the lease, Maine treats it as part of the security deposit, because any advance whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever it is called. It therefore counts toward the two-month-rent cap, must be held in the protected deposit account, and must be returned, or accounted for in the itemized statement with the balance, on the ordinary schedule: within the time stated in a written lease, not over 30 days, or 21 days for a tenancy at will. You may deduct utility charges the tenant was required to pay directly to you. Charges the tenant owes a utility company directly are between the tenant and the utility, and you may not deduct them unless the lease made the tenant pay you. You also cannot collect a utility deposit at signing on top of the first month's rent and the security deposit. Deposits that utility companies themselves require are governed by utility rules, not by this law. These deposit rules do not apply to an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Disability Modifications
bodyText:
Your lease may require your written consent before a tenant alters the property, but Maine fair housing law limits that for tenants with disabilities.

You must permit reasonable modifications of the premises that a person with a physical or mental disability needs for full enjoyment of the home, at that person's expense; Maine does not shift the cost to larger or subsidized landlords. Where reasonable, you may condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Under the Maine Human Rights Commission's rule, you may also require a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with any required permits.

You may not raise the usual security deposit for a tenant with a disability; if needed to ensure restoration funds, you may negotiate payments into an interest-bearing escrow, over a reasonable period, up to the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant.

Separately, you must make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies, and a lease may not bar a tenant from using a clothesline or drying rack, subject to reasonable safety restrictions.

The fair housing rules do not apply to renting one unit of an owner-occupied two-family home or up to four rooms in an owner-occupied single-family home.

title: Bed Bug Duties
bodyText:
Maine gives landlords specific bed bug duties.

When a tenant tells you, orally or in writing, that the unit may have bed bugs, you must inspect within 5 days. If you find an infestation, you must contact a pest control agent within 10 days and take reasonable measures to identify and treat it, using a certified commercial applicator who carries current liability insurance.

Before renting a unit, you must disclose whether any adjacent unit is currently infested or being treated, and on request the last date the unit and adjacent units were inspected and found free of bed bugs; you may not offer for rent a unit you know or suspect is infested. If a tenant cannot comply with requested inspection or treatment preparation, you must offer reasonable assistance and disclose the likely cost; you may charge a reasonable amount for that help, repayable over up to 6 months unless you agree to longer. You need not provide other lodging or replace the tenant's belongings.

Failing these duties is treated as unreasonably failing to remedy a health and safety condition and costs $250 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Tenants must report suspected bed bugs, allow access on reasonable notice and follow treatment measures, and pay for treatments caused by unreasonable noncompliance; a court can order access and compliance.

title: No Cold-Weather Absence Notice Rule
bodyText: Maine law does not require a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit vacant during cold weather. If you want that notice, for example so you can check that pipes do not freeze, put it in the lease; the library's extended absence notice clause can serve this purpose. Keep the clause practical: require notice of an absence, and a request that the tenant keep heat at a safe minimum, rather than penalties. Your own duty matters more here. If the lease or agreement makes you responsible for heat, it is a breach of Maine's implied warranty of habitability if the heating facilities are not operated so as to protect the building's equipment and systems from freezing, or cannot keep the unit at 68 degrees Fahrenheit under the statutory test. Any entry to check on the unit needs reasonable notice, presumed to be 24 hours, except in an emergency. A tenant's prolonged absence alone is not abandonment; property left behind must be handled under Maine's unclaimed property procedure.

title: Common-Area Lights on a Tenant Meter
bodyText: If hallway, stairway, basement or other common-area lights, or any other common-area utility, are wired to a tenant's electric service in a Maine multi-unit building, you may not make that tenant solely responsible for the cost unless you and the tenant agree in writing that the tenant will pay it in return for a stated reduction in rent or other specified fair consideration that approximates the actual cost of supplying those areas. The same rule covers heat and any other utility serving areas outside the tenant's unit, including shared furnaces and water heaters. It applies to buildings of any size with more than one unit, not just two- or three-unit buildings, and the statute does not limit it to new tenancies; use the library's separate common-area utility agreement whenever this situation exists. A tenant cannot waive the rule except through that written agreement. If you violate it, the tenant may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees and costs, and you are presumed to have known the tenant was paying for common areas; if you overcome that presumption, you still must comply but owe only actual damages. The better fix is to move common-area circuits to a house meter in your name.

title: Liens for Tenant Improvements
bodyText: In Maine, a contractor or supplier who works on a building under a contract with the owner, or with the owner's consent, gets a lien on the building and land to secure payment. If you consent to a tenant's improvement and the tenant does not pay its contractor, the contractor may try to place a lien on your property. Maine has no rule that a lease clause, even a recorded one, keeps your interest free of such liens. What the statute does give you is a notice: when the work is not being done under a contract with you, you can prevent a lien for work not yet performed by giving the contractor or supplier written notice that you will not be responsible for it. Also, a claimant who did not contract with you can enforce a lien against your property only up to the balance you owe the person you contracted with, though how that applies when you contracted with no one is unclear, and the limit does not apply to work furnished to premises for a business, commercial or industrial purpose unless the owner lives there, which may include a rental you do not live in. Practical steps: require written approval of any alteration, get the contractor's name before work starts, send that written non-responsibility notice, and require the tenant to provide lien waivers or proof of payment. How courts treat a landlord's consent is a case-law question not covered here.

title: Disturbances and Nuisance
bodyText:
Maine has no statute imposing a general duty on tenants not to disturb neighbors, so the lease's no-disturbance clause supplies that duty.

Maine law then gives you two routes.
- If the tenant, the tenant's family or an invitee causes or permits a nuisance, or violates the law regarding the tenancy, a tenancy at will may be ended on 7 days' written notice stating the ground, and you must prove the cause; a written lease without its own termination language may use the same notice.
- A lesser disturbance that is a material lease breach can support a 30-day notice for a tenancy at will, or termination as the lease provides.

Every termination notice must tell the tenant of the right to contest it in court and must attach the court's form notice. You may not evict a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking because incidents of that abuse, or the victim's reports of them, are treated as a nuisance, disturbance or lease violation, although you may act against the perpetrator.

Where a tenant, guest or dangerous pet has harmed or threatened tenants or the property, you may petition the court for a protection order. Keep dated records of complaints, warnings and police reports.

title: Move-In Condition Acknowledgments
bodyText:
A lease clause in which the tenant acknowledges that the property is in good, satisfactory condition is useful evidence of the unit's condition at move-in, but in Maine it cannot take away the tenant's habitability rights.

Every Maine rental carries an implied warranty that the unit is fit for human habitation, and the law voids any agreement waiving it, with one exception: a written agreement in which the tenant accepts specified conditions that may violate the warranty in return for a stated reduction in rent or other specified fair consideration. A general statement that the unit is in good repair is not that kind of agreement, so if a condition later proves to endanger health or safety, the tenant keeps the right to complain, to raise it as a defense to nonpayment, and in many buildings to repair and deduct.

If you are renting with a known defect you will not fix, use the library's separate accepted-conditions clause, describe each condition specifically, and state the rent reduction. Never require a tenant to sign a waiver of habitability rights; doing so is an unfair trade practice.

Note any existing damage in the lease or a move-in record so you do not later charge the tenant's deposit for it.

title: Tenant Absences
bodyText:
Maine has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, and none giving you extra rights to enter while the tenant is away. A lease may require such notice, as the library's extended absence clause does, and may let you recover actual damages from a willful failure to give it, such as frozen-pipe damage that notice would have let you prevent.

Your entry rights do not change because the tenant is away: you must give reasonable notice of your intent to enter, presumed to be 24 hours, and enter at reasonable times, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, including an emergency when an animal's welfare is at risk. A tenant cannot waive these entry rules.

An absence is not abandonment. If you believe the tenant has left for good, end the tenancy through the proper notice or court process, and handle any property left behind under Maine's unclaimed property procedure: safe storage, mailed notice and a 7-day claim period before sale or disposal. Changing the locks or removing belongings without that process is an illegal eviction.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to allow a tenant to run a family child care business in your rental, and none setting the terms on which you may permit one, such as liability waivers or insurance. Your lease may therefore limit or prohibit business use, including child care, as the library's residential-use clause does. If you choose to allow it, put your conditions in writing: compliance with state licensing (family child care providers are licensed by the Maine Department of Health and Human Services), any local zoning approval, adequate liability insurance naming you where available, limits on use of common areas, and responsibility for added wear. Two Maine rules follow automatically. While a private residence is used as a day care or babysitting service, smoking is prohibited in the residence during operating hours and in other areas the law lists, which affects your smoking policy and other tenants. And if a licensed family child care provider carries separate business liability insurance, an insurer may not refuse or cancel coverage on the provider's primary residence because of the child care business. Fair housing law still applies, so decisions must not be based on familial status or another protected characteristic.

title: Home Businesses in a Rental
bodyText: Maine has no statute that makes running a home-based business a protected use of a rented home, so your lease may limit or prohibit business use, as the library's residential-use clause does, or allow it on conditions. Maine statutes mention home-based businesses and home occupations only in zoning and land-use contexts, such as treating them as outside "commercial use" in certain zoning rules, and local ordinances usually decide whether a home occupation is allowed at a particular address; check local zoning before you permit one. If you allow a business, set written conditions: no employees or customer traffic beyond what you approve, no signs, no hazardous materials, compliance with licensing and zoning, insurance for business liability, and no use of common areas. Keep fair housing in mind: an accommodation for a tenant with a disability, such as working from home, may be required even where your lease restricts business use. A business use that creates a nuisance or violates the law regarding the tenancy can support a 7-day termination notice for a tenancy at will.

title: Co-Tenant Liability
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that sets how co-tenants share responsibility under a residential lease, so the lease's joint-and-several liability clause governs: each tenant who signs can be held responsible for the full rent and all obligations.

Maine law does create exceptions and procedures to know.
- A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may end the lease early on 7 days' notice (30 days for a lease of a year or more) with the required documentation and is then not liable for unpaid rent under the lease; you may bifurcate the tenancy to evict or end the tenancy of the perpetrator without regard to whether the victim signed the lease, and the perpetrator remains liable for property damage and can be liable to the victim.
- When you file an eviction against multiple occupants, name all adults whose names appear on the lease or whose tenancy you acknowledged by accepting rent or otherwise, plus "all other occupants", so the judgment covers everyone.
- Accepting rent from an adult not on the lease can make that person a tenant you must name.
- A co-tenant who pays more than their share must look to the other co-tenants, not to you.

title: Assigning Yard and Upkeep Chores
bodyText:
Maine has no rule that tenant chores such as mowing, raking or watering must be in a separate signed document or supported by extra payment, so your lease may assign routine upkeep to the tenant, as the library's landscaping clause does.

Two Maine limits apply. First, you cannot shift your duty to keep the unit fit for human habitation. Any agreement waiving it is void unless it is a written agreement in which the tenant accepts specified conditions in return for a stated rent reduction or other specified fair consideration, so do not use chore clauses to make the tenant responsible for things like heat, plumbing, structural repairs or conditions that endanger health or safety.

Second, in a multi-unit building, if the tenant's utility account pays for water, electricity or heat used in common areas, such as an outdoor spigot or shared lighting used for landscaping, you need a written agreement with a stated rent reduction or fair consideration approximating the cost.

Keep chores reasonable and specific, and supply needed equipment if you expect it used. A tenant who fails to do assigned chores is in breach of the lease, but the remedy must go through Maine's notice and court process.

title: Shifting Landlord Duties to a Tenant
bodyText: Maine does not have a list of minimum housing standards that a lease may assign to the tenant item by item. Your duties come mainly from the implied warranty of habitability and the ban on dangerous conditions, and Maine allows them to be shifted only in three specific ways. First, a written agreement in which the tenant accepts specified conditions that may violate the warranty, in return for a stated reduction in rent or other specified fair consideration; any other waiver is void. Second, in a multi-unit building, a written agreement that the tenant will pay for heat, electricity or other utilities serving common areas, in return for a stated rent reduction or fair consideration approximating the actual cost. Third, if you provide heat, a separate signed agreement, not part of the lease, in at least 12-point plain English, to heat to a stated temperature below 68 but not below 62 degrees Fahrenheit for a stated rent reduction, revocable on reasonable notice and not allowed if anyone over 65 or under 5 lives there. The library has a separate clause for each. Routine chores like lawn care can be assigned in the lease, but not responsibility for conditions that endanger health or safety.

title: Tenant Utility Bills and Liens
bodyText: In Maine, a tenant's unpaid water bill can become your problem even when the account is in the tenant's name. A water utility has a lien on the real estate it serves to secure payment of unpaid rates, and sewer and sanitary district charges can also become liens on the property; such liens can ultimately be foreclosed. Maine has no lease clause or filing that shields an owner from these liens. Instead, Maine gives you a right to information: if a tenant is billed for water, municipal sewer or storm water, sewer district or sanitary district service and nonpayment could lead to a lien on the property, the utility, municipality or district must, on your request, tell you or your agent the current status of the tenant's account, including amounts due or overdue. Check those accounts periodically, require the tenant to keep them paid and to show proof of payment on request (the library's utility payment evidence clause), and consider keeping water and sewer accounts in your own name and billing the tenant, which then must be disclosed in the total price disclosure. Electricity and gas work differently: a utility cannot collect your unpaid bills from the tenant. Unpaid utility charges the tenant owed you directly may be deducted from the deposit.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText:
