Maine has no statewide limit on how many people may live in a rental unit and no statutory standard based on bedrooms, floor area or air space; local building, housing or fire codes may set limits, so check the municipality's rules. The lease may name the tenants and authorized occupants, as the library's permitted occupants clause does.

Two Maine rules shape how you use it. First, fair housing law bars discrimination because of familial status, so occupancy rules must not be a way to exclude families with children; Maine's Human Rights Act expressly leaves reasonable local, state or federal limits on the maximum number of occupants in force, so an occupancy rule tied to a genuine code limit is safest.

Second, if a person who is not an authorized occupant is living in the unit, Maine allows a tenancy at will to be ended on 7 days' written notice on that ground, and a written lease without its own termination language may use the same notice.

A guest who stays briefly is not an unauthorized occupant just because they are not on the lease; define guests and their permitted stay clearly. Accepting rent from an adult occupant can make that person a tenant.

title: No Statutory List of Prohibited Tenant Acts
bodyText: Maine has no statute that lists acts a residential tenant must not commit, such as damaging the property, disturbing neighbors or refusing entry, so your lease clauses supply those rules. Maine law then backs them up in several ways. A tenancy at will may be ended on 7 days' written notice if the tenant, family or an invitee caused substantial damage the tenant has not repaired, caused or permitted a nuisance or made the unit unfit, violated the law regarding the tenancy, committed or threatened violence against another tenant, a guest, you or your staff, or if an unauthorized person is occupying the unit; a written lease without its own termination language may use the same notice. A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry for inspections, repairs, services or showings, and may not change the locks without notice and a duplicate key within 48 hours; refusing to provide the key can support a 7-day notice. Other conduct that breaches the lease supports a 30-day notice for a tenancy at will. You may also petition the court for protection when a tenant, guest or dangerous pet has harmed or threatened tenants or property. See the tenant statutory duties row for the duties Maine law itself imposes.

title: Unlawful Use of the Premises
bodyText: Maine has only one statute that voids a lease because of how the premises are used: if the tenant of a dwelling house is convicted of keeping it as a house of ill fame, you may choose to treat the lease as void and recover possession by the same court process used against a tenant holding over after the lease ends. The lease is not void automatically; it is your option, and it requires a conviction. For other unlawful uses, such as drug dealing or running an illegal business, Maine law does not void the lease. Instead, a tenancy at will may be ended on 7 days' written notice if the tenant, family or an invitee caused or permitted a nuisance or violated or permitted a violation of the law regarding the tenancy, and a written lease without its own termination language may use the same notice; you must prove the ground in court. The library's optional Maine criminal activity clause makes such conduct a material breach. You may not treat a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking victim's situation, or the victim's reports to police, as a nuisance or lease violation. Possession can be recovered only through the court process, never by lockout.

title: Enforcing a Residential-Use Clause
bodyText:
Apart from the illegal nuisance uses described below, Maine has no statute that sets a special consequence when a tenant uses a rental for something other than a home, so a residential-use clause like the library's is enforced like any other lease term.

For a tenancy at will, a breach can support a 30-day written notice; for a written lease, termination follows the lease's own default terms, and if the lease has no termination or notice language for a material breach, Maine lets you terminate only on the 7-day grounds of the tenancy-at-will statute, not by a 30-day notice. A faster 7-day notice is available only if the non-residential use amounts to a nuisance, makes the unit unfit, or violates the law regarding the tenancy, such as an illegal business.

A tenant who uses the premises for a purpose Maine's nuisance law names (a house of ill fame, the illegal sale or keeping of liquor or scheduled drugs, lewdness or gambling) forfeits all rights to them, and you may then use the court eviction process; a conviction for keeping the premises as a house of ill fame also lets you treat the lease as void. Every notice must state the right to contest in court and attach the court's form notice, and possession must be recovered through court, not by lockout.

Keep in mind that renting to short-term guests through a platform, home businesses and child care are not protected uses in Maine, but a reasonable accommodation for a tenant with a disability may still be required.

title: Smoking Policy Disclosure
bodyText:
Maine requires every landlord renting a home used as a tenant's primary residence to give the tenant or prospective tenant a written smoking policy. It must say whether smoking is prohibited on the premises, allowed on the entire premises, or allowed only in limited areas, and if limited, identify where.

You may put the policy in a written lease, or give a separate written notice when renting under a tenancy at will.

Before the tenant signs or pays a deposit, you must get the tenant's written acknowledgment of the policy; the library's Maine smoking clause supplies the disclosure in the lease, but get the signed acknowledgment (for example, on a copy of the policy) before the lease is signed or any deposit is paid; the disclosure checklist then records it. A tenant cannot sue you solely because you failed to give the disclosure, or because another tenant broke the policy.

For medical cannabis, you may not refuse to rent to or penalize someone just for being a qualifying (certified) patient or a caregiver, unless renting to them would put you in violation of federal law or cost you a federal contract or funding, and you may prohibit smoking medical cannabis only if you prohibit all smoking on the premises and post notice of that on the premises; you may restrict administration or cultivation inconsistent with the premises' general use. Maine has no statute treating smoke drift as a nuisance. Smoking is banned in a home while used as a day care.

Changing the policy mid-lease requires the tenant's agreement or a proper change in a tenancy at will.

title: Subletting and Assignment
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that governs whether a residential tenant may sublet or assign, so the lease controls. You may require your written consent and, under Maine statutes, may withhold it in your discretion; there is no rule that you must be reasonable, and no rule that silence counts as approval.

Three Maine rules matter.
- An assignment of a lease creating more than a tenancy at will must be made by a writing signed by the person assigning it.
- If someone the lease does not authorize moves in, a tenancy at will may be ended on 7 days' written notice on that ground, and a written lease without its own termination language may use the same notice; accepting rent from an occupant can make that person a tenant you must name in any eviction.
- And if you refuse a sublet and the tenant then leaves early, you must still make reasonable efforts to re-rent before recovering lost rent, so a blanket refusal does not protect the rent stream.

If tenants sublet short-term through online platforms, the stays may be subject to Maine's lodging tax and local short-term rental ordinances. A lease clause that a tenant's mere request to sublet is grounds for eviction would be unwise.

title: Forwarding Notices of Proceedings
bodyText:
Maine law does not require a tenant to tell you, or send you, a notice of a lawsuit or other proceeding affecting the property, and has no statute on attornment, meaning a tenant's acknowledgment of someone else as landlord. The lease may require the tenant to notify you promptly and deliver any written notice, as the library's clause does; a tenant who fails to do so is in breach, but Maine sets no statutory penalty.

In practice, make sure you receive legal papers directly: anyone authorized to sign a residential lease for the owner is the owner's agent for service of process and for receiving notices and demands, so keep your agent's contact details current and give tenants an address for notices. If the property is in foreclosure, the foreclosing lender, not the tenant, has statutory duties to notify residential tenants, and bona fide tenancies in foreclosed buildings may be ended only under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act. If a tenant receives papers addressed to you, ask in the lease that they be forwarded within a set number of days.

title: Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: Maine has no statute on whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renter's insurance, or on filing a claim against a tenant's policy. Related Maine rules set the boundaries. You may not use the lease to escape liability for your own or your agent's negligence; such a clause is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice, so you cannot require a tenant's insurance to absorb losses you cause. You also cannot shift your duty to keep the unit fit for human habitation onto the tenant or the tenant's insurer, except through a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration. You may require the tenant to carry renter's insurance for the tenant's own belongings and liability if the lease says so, and you may hold the tenant responsible, directly or through the deposit, for damage the tenant or guests cause beyond normal wear and tear. Pursuing a tenant's insurer generally requires the tenant's cooperation or a court judgment against the tenant. A surety bond a tenant buys instead of a deposit is not insurance for the tenant, and the surety must say so.

title: Tenant Upkeep and Well and Septic Systems
bodyText:
Maine has no statute requiring tenants to keep the unit clean, make repairs or preserve the property, so those duties come from the lease, such as the library's tenant maintenance clause.

Maine law limits what the lease can shift: you may not make the tenant responsible for keeping the unit fit for human habitation, except through a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction or fair consideration.

For homes on a private well, Maine puts the testing duty on you, not the tenant: starting in 2022 and every 5 years, you must have each private drinking water well serving a tenant tested by a certified laboratory for arsenic and the other contaminants the state specifies, give each tenant the results within 10 days of receiving them, and tell new tenants the most recent results. A 2026 law (2025 Me. Laws ch. 746) separately requires a PFAS test of such wells by January 1, 2027.

Maine has no statute on septic system care by tenants; a lease may ask tenants not to flush harmful items and to report backups, but repairs remain your responsibility when the system affects habitability.

A tenant who causes substantial damage and does not repair it can be given a 7-day termination notice in a tenancy at will.

title: Tenants' Duties Under Maine Law
bodyText: Maine has no single list of tenant duties, but several statutes put obligations directly on tenants, whatever the lease says. Access: a tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry, on reasonable notice, to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, tenants or contractors. Locks: a tenant who changes a lock must notify you and give you a duplicate key within 48 hours (72 hours for a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking victim, who may change locks at the victim's expense); refusing to provide the key can support a 7-day termination notice. Detectors: a tenant must keep the smoke, carbon monoxide and fuel gas detectors working by keeping them connected or keeping charged batteries in them, testing them periodically and not disabling them, and should report problems to you in writing. Bed bugs: a tenant must promptly report a known or suspected infestation, allow inspection and treatment on reasonable notice, and follow reasonable control measures, and pays for treatments caused by unreasonable noncompliance. Defects: a tenant who wants to sue over habitability, reduce rent in your rent action or use repair-and-deduct must first give you written notice of the condition (for a habitability suit, actual notice to whoever customarily collects your rent also counts; and, for the first two, have been current on rent when notice was given); the nonpayment-eviction defense needs only your actual or constructive notice. The library's Maine clauses repeat these duties.

title: Agreements for Tenants to Make Repairs
bodyText: Maine has no statute that lets you hand your repair and maintenance duties to a tenant through a separate agreement, and no special formalities for such arrangements. Your duty to keep the unit fit for human habitation and free of conditions endangering health or safety cannot be waived, with one exception: a written agreement in which the tenant accepts specified conditions that may violate the warranty, in return for a stated rent reduction or other specified fair consideration. So if a tenant will do work in exchange for reduced rent, describe the specific conditions or tasks, state the rent reduction or other consideration, and keep the arrangement in writing; a general promise by the tenant to handle all repairs is void as to habitability. Separately, Maine gives tenants a statutory repair-and-deduct right for dangerous conditions you fail to fix: small repairs (less than $500 or half a month's rent, whichever is greater), after written notice and 14 days following certified mail, done with professional care and licensed trades for electrical, oil burner and plumbing work, with an itemized statement, and with no reimbursement for the tenant's own labor. When repairs are undertaken by or for the tenant under that statute, you are free from liability for resulting injuries. That right does not apply in an owner-occupied building of five or fewer units.

title: Tenant Utility Accounts
bodyText:
Maine lets the lease make the tenant responsible for arranging and paying utilities to the unit, as the library's Maine utilities clause does, with limits.

Utilities serving common areas or other units cannot be put on one tenant without a written agreement giving a stated rent reduction or fair consideration approximating the cost.

If an account is in your name, you must pay it: a utility may not demand payment from the tenant for your unpaid bill, and a tenant who pays to keep service may deduct that from rent, and can recover the amount paid or $100, whichever is greater, plus costs. If electric service is in the tenant's name and is about to be disconnected, you can ask the electric utility in advance for an agreement to transfer the service automatically into your name to protect the building, for a reasonable fee; the utility tells you within 72 hours of a transfer but will not share the tenant's account details without consent.

Water and sewer charges a tenant leaves unpaid can become a lien on your property, so monitor those accounts. Maine law does not make a tenant's unpaid utility bill a separate eviction ground; treat it as a lease breach.

You may never cut off or cause interruption of a tenant's utilities to force them out.

title: No Right to Cut Off Submetered Utilities
bodyText: Maine has no statute that allows a landlord who submeters, allocates or resells electricity, gas or water to a tenant to cut off service when the tenant does not pay. The opposite rule applies: a landlord may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service being supplied to a tenant, including water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, sewer, elevator or refrigeration, whether or not you control the service, except for a temporary interruption needed while actual repairs are being made or during a temporary emergency. Doing so is an illegal eviction, and the tenant may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. If you bill a tenant for utilities through a submeter or an allocation, treat unpaid charges as a debt: they are not rent, so they cannot support a 7-day nonpayment notice, but utility charges the tenant was required to pay you directly may be deducted from the security deposit, and you may sue for them. Charges you bill must appear in the total price disclosure, and common-area usage cannot be passed to one tenant without a written rent-reduction agreement. Maine utilities must give tenants and owners past consumption and cost data on request.

title: Checking Tenant Utility Payments
bodyText:
Maine law helps you confirm that a tenant is paying utilities that could become a lien on your property. If a tenant is billed for water, municipal sewer or storm water, sewer district or sanitary district service and nonpayment could result in a lien against the property, the water utility, municipality or district must, on your or your agent's request, tell you the current status of the tenant's account, including amounts due or overdue; you do not need the tenant's permission.

Electricity is different: an electric utility generally may not share a tenant's personal or account information with you without the tenant's consent, even under an automatic-transfer agreement, beyond telling you service was transferred to your name.

That is why the library's utility payment evidence clause, which requires the tenant to give you reasonable proof of payment on request, is useful; you may also ask the tenant to sign a consent letting the utility share account status with you. Keep requests reasonable and use the information only for managing the property; Maine separately penalizes disclosing tenants' personal information to harass or force them out without a legitimate business purpose.

title: Keeping Utilities On
bodyText:
Maine law bars you, not the tenant, from cutting off utilities: you may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service supplied to the tenant, whether or not you control it, except for a temporary interruption needed while actual repairs are underway or during a temporary emergency. Violations are illegal evictions costing actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees.

Maine has no statute requiring a tenant to keep the tenant's own utilities on, so the library's utility continuity clause supplies that duty; a tenant who lets heat or water service lapse and causes freezing or other damage is liable for it under the lease and may face termination for substantial damage.

Two tools protect the building.
- If an electric account in the tenant's name would be disconnected, an agreement you make in advance with the electric utility can transfer the service automatically to your name.
- And if an account in your name is unpaid, the tenant may assume the service and deduct the payments from rent, so keep your accounts current.

If you provide heat, you must keep the heating facilities running enough to protect the building's systems from freezing.

title: Smoke, Carbon Monoxide and Fuel Gas Detectors
bodyText:
Maine requires you to provide working smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors at the start of each tenancy, and, in a multifamily building or a mixed-use building containing a dwelling unit, a fuel gas detector in every room with an appliance that burns propane, natural gas or other liquefied petroleum gas. In multifamily buildings, each unit needs smoke detectors, and any smoke detector installed or replaced within 20 feet of a kitchen or a bathroom with a tub or shower must be photoelectric (ionization is still allowed in bedrooms); buildings over three stories also need detectors in each corridor and hallway. Carbon monoxide detectors go in each area within or giving access to bedrooms and, in multifamily buildings, must have both electrical and battery power or a sealed 10-year or qualifying battery.

After a tenant notifies you in writing of a problem, you must repair or replace the detector. If a deaf or hard-of-hearing occupant asks, you must provide a suitable alarm or the occupant may install one and deduct the cost from rent.

The tenant must keep detectors working by keeping them connected and keeping charged batteries in them, testing them periodically and not disabling them. Inspect detectors after installation and before each new tenant: doing so limits your liability unless you had 24 hours' actual notice of a defect and failed to act.

Violations carry civil fines up to $500 each. A buyer of a multiapartment building must install missing detectors within 30 days.

title: Alternate Housing During Repairs
bodyText: Maine has no general rule requiring you to provide a hotel room or another unit when a condition makes the home unlivable, whether or not the tenant asks. Three specific rules apply. First, in a habitability case, the court may allow the tenant to move out temporarily while necessary repairs require the unit to be vacant, and the tenant owes no use and occupation charge until moving back; if you offer reasonable alternative housing, the court may not charge you for the tenant's alternate housing during the repairs, so offering it limits your exposure. Second, if the state orders lead hazards removed while a tenant occupies the unit, you must move the tenant on reasonable notice to a lead-safe substitute unit of similar size and location, pay reasonable moving expenses and any occupancy charges above the tenant's rent, unless the Department of Health and Human Services waives the requirement; you also may not evict a family with children because previously unknown lead is discovered. Third, bed bug treatment does not require you to provide other lodging. After a fire or other unavoidable casualty, the tenant owes no rent while the unit is unfit, but you have no duty to rehouse. Check local codes, which may add relocation duties.

title: Excluding Appliances
bodyText: Maine has no statute that presumes appliances left in a unit are supplied by you, or that limits which appliances a lease may exclude from your responsibility. List the appliances you supply and will maintain in the lease, as the library's appliances clause does, and say plainly that any other item, such as a washer the tenant owns or a refrigerator left by a former occupant, is not supplied or maintained by you. That exclusion cannot reach your habitability duties. You must keep the unit fit for human habitation, including the systems needed for heat, water and safe living, and a written agreement excusing a condition is binding only if it specifies the condition and gives a stated rent reduction or other specified fair consideration. Maine also makes it a breach of the warranty of habitability to offer for rent a unit with a leaking event (such as a failed appliance, roof, window, door, plumbing system or foundation) or chronic moisture or humidity, outside the tenant's control, that results in mold, bacteria or other biological growth. If you leave an appliance you will not maintain, remove it or note its status in writing at move-in. Damage a tenant causes to your appliances beyond normal wear and tear may be charged to the tenant.

title: Listing Supplied Appliances
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that lists appliances a landlord must supply, such as a stove or refrigerator, and none that turns the appliances named in a lease into a separate statutory duty. When you list appliances in the lease, as the library's appliances clause does, your promise to maintain them is a contract term the tenant can enforce.

Maine's habitability rules apply on top of it: you must keep the unit fit for human habitation and free of conditions that endanger health or safety, and offering a unit for rent where a leak, such as from a failed appliance, outside the tenant's control has led to mold or other biological growth is a breach of the warranty of habitability. If a listed appliance breaks and you do not fix a condition that endangers health or safety, a tenant in most buildings may use Maine's repair-and-deduct remedy after written notice.

Tenants must use appliances reasonably and are responsible for damage they cause beyond normal wear and tear. A tenant who will pay for appliance-related utilities should know the costs before signing through the total price or energy efficiency disclosures.

title: Rent After Condemnation
bodyText: Maine has no statute that, in general terms, bars you from collecting rent once a building has been condemned or ordered vacated by a code official. Several Maine rules reach the same result in common situations. You may not knowingly rent a dwelling that the state has posted and ordered cleared of lead-based substances unless the Department of Health and Human Services waives it, and a tenant in a unit with an active lead order must be moved to a lead-safe substitute unit at your expense for moving and any extra occupancy cost. No action for rent can be maintained for a period when fire or other unavoidable casualty has made the premises unfit for use or habitation, and a residential lease cannot override that. When a unit is unfit for habitation for other reasons, courts can reduce the rent to the unit's fair value from the time you had notice until repairs are made, a tenant may raise that as a defense to a nonpayment eviction, and you may not raise rent while the warranty of habitability is breached. Municipal housing and building codes often govern condemnation and placarding, and local ordinances may bar occupancy or rent; this library does not track them. Do not accept rent for a unit no one may lawfully occupy.

title: Habitability Rules Maine Does Not Have
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Maine counterpart. (1) No air-conditioning or cooling duty: Maine's 68°F heat standard applies only when you are obligated by the lease or agreement to provide heat. (2) No right for a tenant to withhold rent or pay it into escrow on the tenant's own: the tenant's routes are a court complaint, a defense to a nonpayment eviction, a reduction in a rent action, and repair-and-deduct for small repairs. Rent goes into a court escrow only when a tenant appeals an eviction judgment and the rent is disputed. (3) No general repair deadline, except that repair-and-deduct opens 14 days after the tenant's certified-mail notice and a reported bedbug problem must be inspected within 5 days. (4) No duty to provide substitute housing; a court may let the tenant move out temporarily while necessary repairs are made, owing nothing for use and occupation until the tenant returns. (5) No right to end a tenancy because a repair costs too much. Maine's statutes, 2025-2026 session laws, constitution, civil procedure rules and seven agency rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Local housing codes may add duties, so check the municipality.

title: No Rule on Designated Repairers
bodyText: Maine has no statute that lets, or forbids, a lease naming who must make repairs. You may require repair requests to come to you and use your own contractors for work you do. What a lease cannot do is cut off the tenant's statutory repair-and-deduct remedy. If a condition endangers or materially impairs health or safety, the fix costs less than $500 or half a month's rent (whichever is greater), and you do not act within 14 days after the tenant's written notice by certified mail (or as promptly as an emergency requires), the tenant may have the work done with due professional care and deduct the actual, reasonable cost after giving you an itemized statement. Electrical, oil burner and plumbing work must be done by a professional licensed in Maine, and the tenant cannot charge for the tenant's own or family labor. A lease term waiving this remedy is void, and requiring a tenant to sign one is an unfair trade practice. The remedy does not apply in an owner-occupied building of 5 or fewer units, to damage the tenant caused, or where you were unreasonably denied access.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Under the Maine Human Rights Act it is unlawful housing discrimination to refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when they are necessary to give a person with a physical or mental disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing, or to refuse reasonable modifications of the premises, at the tenant's expense, that may be necessary for full enjoyment. In a rental you may, when reasonable, condition a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior afterward, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Maine's statute does not require that condition to appear in the lease. The Human Rights Commission's housing rule adds that you may not raise the usual security deposit for a tenant with a disability, but may negotiate payments into an interest-bearing escrow account, not over the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant. Accommodation also matters in eviction: the court must deny possession if you had a duty to offer a reasonable accommodation, failed to, and the request is causally linked to the conduct you are evicting for. Owner-occupied 2-family dwellings and rentals of up to 4 rooms in an owner-occupied home are outside most of the Act. Assistance animals have separate rules.

title: No Rule on Double Letting
bodyText: Maine has no statute on renting the same room or unit to two different tenants for the same period, and no special rent-abatement remedy for it. General rules apply instead. Once you have rented a unit, keeping that tenant out other than through court process is an illegal eviction, for which the tenant recovers actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. Maine also has no statute on a landlord's failure to deliver possession at the start of a lease, so the lease and contract law govern a late or failed move-in. Avoid signing overlapping leases; if a prior occupant stays past the end of the tenancy, use the forcible entry and detainer process rather than self-help.

title: No Staff Screening Requirement
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to run background checks on apartment employees, maintenance staff or managers, and none forbidding it. Related rules still reach your staff as your agents. Entry into a unit must follow Maine's entry rules: reasonable notice (24 hours is presumed reasonable), entry only at reasonable times, except in an emergency or when notice is impracticable. You, your agent and anyone acting under your direction may not disclose a tenant's, applicant's or occupant's personal information to harass or intimidate them or to push them out outside the court process, without a legitimate business purpose; the remedy is actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater. And you and your agents may not subject a tenant to sexual harassment, which also lets the tenant end the lease early.

title: Building and Fire Code Editions
bodyText: Maine's statutes generally do not freeze an outside code at a named edition; they hand the choice to agencies. The Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code is built from the International Building, Existing Building, Residential, Energy Conservation and Mechanical Codes plus ASHRAE ventilation and energy standards and a radon-control standard, adopted by board rule, and each must be either the most recent edition or the edition before it. It must be enforced in towns of more than 4,000 residents; smaller towns need not enforce it but may not adopt a different building code. Fire-safety rules for buildings are adopted by the Commissioner of Public Safety, and smoke detectors must carry a UL or Factory Mutual listing. The editions now in force are the 2021 International Building, Existing Building, Residential, Energy Conservation and Mechanical Codes with Maine amendments, the 2019 ASHRAE 62.1, 62.2 and 90.1 standards and ASTM E1465-08 for radon control, now administered by the Maine Office of Community Affairs; the fire rules adopt the 2018 NFPA 101 and NFPA 1. Check the current rule before relying on a particular code section, because the board can move to a newer edition. One statute names an edition: a town may adopt the swimming-pool fencing standards in Appendix G of the 2009 International Residential Code.

title: No Disaster Rule; Casualty Rule Applies
bodyText: Maine has no statute that ends a tenancy, or suspends rent, because of a declared natural disaster or emergency. The rule that applies is Maine's casualty rule: while the premises are destroyed or damaged by fire or other unavoidable casualty so that they are unfit for use or habitation, you cannot sue for rent, or for damages for breach of the lease's conditions, for that period. The statute keeps contrary agreements contained in a lease alive only for nonresidential leases and leases securing Maine Guaranty Authority obligations, so do not rely on a residential lease term that keeps rent running. The statute does not itself end the lease or set notice periods, so a casualty clause should say how each party may end it. Separately, the Public Utilities Commission's consumer rule lets the Commission declare a moratorium on utility disconnections when an emergency makes disconnection a clear danger to health or safety.

title: What Makes a Unit Unfit
bodyText: Maine measures habitability by effect on health and safety. Your implied warranty that the unit is fit for human habitation is breached by a condition that endangers or materially impairs the health or safety of the tenants, if the tenant did not cause it, gave you written notice without unreasonable delay (actual notice to the person who usually collects your rent also counts), was current on rent when giving notice, and you unreasonably failed to take prompt, effective steps to repair it. The same test defines the dangerous conditions you may not maintain or permit, which a tenant may fix through repair-and-deduct when the cost is small. Maine has no list of qualifying defects, but the statutes name some breaches outright: heating that cannot hold 68°F when you must supply heat, a system not run to prevent freezing, offering a unit for rent with mold from a leak or chronic moisture outside the tenant's control, failing to give the radon notice, and failing to follow the bedbug law. A defect that does not endanger or materially impair health or safety does not trigger these remedies, though the lease or a local code may still require you to fix it.

title: Changing Habitability Duties by Agreement
bodyText:
Maine lets the parties change the habitability duty in only one way: a written agreement in which the tenant accepts specified conditions that may violate the warranty of fitness, in return for a stated rent reduction or other specified fair consideration. That agreement binds both of you.

Any other waiver of the warranty, of your duty to keep the premises free of dangerous conditions, or of the repair-and-deduct remedy is void, and requiring a tenant to sign a waiver of a statutory right is an unfair trade practice.

Two cases have their own rules.
- Heat below 68°F needs a separate signed document in at least 12-point type, revocable on reasonable notice, with a minimum of at least 62°F and a fair stated rent reduction, and it is not allowed if anyone over 65 or under 5 lives there.
- Making one tenant pay for heat or utilities serving common areas needs a written agreement for a stated rent reduction or fair consideration approximating the cost.

Maine has no statute on assigning routine chores to tenants, but a chore clause cannot shift your duty to keep the unit fit.

title: Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Maine law gives tenants several presumptions in habitability and utility disputes. When a court reviews a habitability complaint, or a tenant proves an unfit condition in your action for rent, the agreed rent is presumed to equal the fair value of the unit free of the defect, so the court cuts the rent owed from the notice date by the gap between the rent and the unit's actual value. If a tenant has been paying for heat or utilities serving common areas or other units, you are presumed to have known it. If a utility account in your name goes unpaid, you are presumed to have failed knowingly, which exposes you to damages of at least $100 plus costs. Failing to follow the bedbug law counts automatically as an unreasonable failure to repair. And an eviction begun within 6 months after a tenant complains in writing about repairs, reports code problems or asserts habitability rights is presumed retaliatory, unless it is based on a 7-day ground or a lease violation and the tenant did not use repair-and-deduct. Each presumption can be rebutted, so keep repair records, notices and payment proof.

title: No Lease Habitability Statement Required
bodyText: Maine does not require the lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. The warranty is implied: in any written or oral rental agreement you are deemed to covenant and warrant that the unit is fit for human habitation, whether or not the lease says so, and it can be narrowed only by a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration. A statement in the lease that the unit is habitable is optional. Avoid wording that has the tenant acknowledge that the lease or rules are fair and reasonable, or that waives the warranty: those terms are unenforceable, and using them is an unfair trade practice. The Attorney General is required to publish a model residential lease that complies with current law, which is a useful cross-check.

title: No Health District Rental Rules
bodyText: Maine has no health districts that issue rental regulations, and no duty to give tenants health or housing regulations on request. What exists instead: a local health officer receives public complaints about conditions posing a public health threat (meaning a risk of exposure to a communicable disease), may enter and inspect with the owner's, agent's or occupant's consent or, if refused, under a District Court inspection warrant, and may order nuisances suppressed after consulting the state; municipal building officials and fire inspectors may enter buildings at reasonable hours and order fire hazards removed; and towns may adopt stricter heat and mold standards than state law. A tenant's good-faith complaint to a code-enforcement body within 6 months before you file an eviction raises a presumption of retaliation.

title: Heat Standards
bodyText:
Maine does not require you to supply heat; the lease decides who does.

If you are obligated by the lease or agreement to provide heat, you breach the warranty of habitability if you keep the unit so cold it is injurious to the health of ordinary occupants, if the heating system cannot hold at least 68°F (measured 3 feet from exterior walls and 5 feet above the floor, at minus 20°F outside), or if you do not run it so as to protect the building's systems from freezing. Towns may set stricter heat standards.

A lower setting needs the separate heat agreement (minimum at least 62°F, revocable, fair rent reduction, never where anyone over 65 or under 5 lives). You are not responsible if a tenant who controls the thermostat turns it down below 68°F, as long as the system can meet the standard.

If you fail to meet the heat standard, a tenant may buy heating fuel and deduct it under the repair-and-deduct remedy. You may not make one tenant pay for heat to common areas without a written agreement for a stated rent reduction, and you may never willfully cut off heat to force a tenant out.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: When you breach the lease or your statutory duties, a Maine tenant has several routes. If a written lease has no termination provision, or no written-notice-of-termination term for a material breach, the tenant may end it on 7 days' written notice when you have substantially breached the lease (the same gap lets you terminate on the 7-day at-will grounds). For unfit conditions the tenant may sue for an injunction ordering repairs and a rent rebate, defend a nonpayment eviction, get rent reduced in your rent action, or use repair-and-deduct for small repairs. Many duties carry minimum damages plus attorney's fees: illegal eviction or utility shutoff and unlawful or harassing entry ($250 or actual damages), making a tenant pay for common-area utilities ($250), failing to pay a utility account in your name ($100), bedbug-law violations ($250), mishandling the deposit account ($500 or a month's rent) and wrongful deposit retention (double the amount withheld). Maine gives tenants no lien on your property for your breach. Including termination language, with written notice of termination for a material breach, in the lease keeps the 7-day statutory exit from applying.

title: Your Repair and Habitability Duties
bodyText:
In every Maine rental, written or oral, you warrant that the unit is fit for human habitation, and you may not maintain or permit any condition that endangers or materially impairs tenants' health or safety.

Specific duties include heat standards when you supply heat, mold-free conditions where leaks or chronic moisture are outside the tenant's control, bedbug inspection within 5 days of a report and treatment by a licensed pest control agent, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, radon testing and notice, and paying any utility account in your name. You may not offer for rent a unit you know or suspect has bedbugs, or one with leak- or moisture-driven mold.

These duties cannot be waived except by a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction, and requiring any waiver of a statutory tenant right is an unfair trade practice. Maine has no air-conditioning duty and no statutory list of imminently dangerous conditions.

Outside the landlord-tenant law, a town may step in to provide heat, utilities or repairs when habitability is imminently threatened and you cannot be reached or do not act, then hold a lien for its costs; and a town may declare a dangerous building a nuisance, order it disposed of and recover costs by special tax.

title: No Self-Cure Billed as Rent
bodyText: Maine has no statute letting you fix a tenant's breach yourself and bill the cost as rent. Calling a repair charge "additional rent" in the lease does not work in Maine: the statute defines rent to exclude fees and charges that reimburse you for reasonable costs, so an unpaid repair bill cannot support the 7-day nonpayment notice. What you can do instead: enter on reasonable notice to make necessary repairs (a tenant may not unreasonably refuse); give a 7-day notice if the tenant, the tenant's family or an invitee caused substantial damage that the tenant has not repaired; charge reasonable costs of repairing damage the tenant caused when the tenancy ends, or deduct them from the deposit; and, for bedbugs, recover treatment costs caused by the tenant's unreasonable failure to cooperate or ask the court for an order.

title: Facilities Maine Requires
bodyText: Beyond the general duty to keep the unit fit for human habitation, Maine's statutes name few specific facilities you must supply. The ones they do name: working smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors at each new occupancy, repaired after the tenant's written notice, with alarms suitable for a deaf or hard-of-hearing occupant on request; fuel gas detectors in each room with a propane or natural gas appliance in multifamily buildings; and, if you have agreed to provide heat, heating that meets the 68°F standard. Maine has no statute requiring particular locks, deadbolts, door viewers, window screens, garbage receptacles, hot-water temperatures or appliances such as a stove or refrigerator. Those can still be required by a local housing code or by the lease, and a missing or broken facility that endangers or materially impairs health or safety breaches the warranty. Check local codes for added standards.

title: No Rule on Repair Promises
bodyText: Maine has no rule requiring a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing, carry a completion date or be made before the lease is signed. A promise still matters. A tenant's good-faith written request for repairs that the rental agreement requires, made within 6 months before you file an eviction, raises a presumption that the eviction is retaliatory. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to make agreed repairs, on reasonable notice. And if a written lease has no termination provision, a tenant may end it on 7 days' written notice when you substantially breach it, which an unkept repair promise can be. Put any promised work in the lease or an addendum, with what will be done and by when, so both sides know what was agreed.

title: No Quiet Possession Statute
bodyText: Maine has no statute creating a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment for residential tenants. Several statutes protect the same interest. You may not willfully cut off a tenant's utilities, lock the tenant out or hold the tenant's belongings outside court process; the tenant recovers actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. Entering in violation of the entry rules, entering in an unreasonable manner or making repeated entry demands that harass the tenant also carries $250 or actual damages and an injunction. You and your agents may not sexually harass a tenant, and you may not disclose a tenant's personal information to harass or push them out. If a written lease lacks termination language, a tenant may end it on 7 days' notice for your substantial breach. A common-law covenant of quiet enjoyment may exist in Maine case law.

title: No Rent-Receipt Anti-Waiver Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute like the one in some states that bars a lease, assignment, deed or security instrument from letting someone collect the rent free of the duty to keep the unit habitable. Related Maine rules point the same way. The habitability duties run to the landlord under any written or oral rental agreement and cannot be waived except by a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction. Anyone authorized to sign leases for the owner is the owner's agent for service of process and for receiving notices. Security deposits must sit in an account beyond the reach of your creditors, including a foreclosing mortgagee, and pass to a new owner, who becomes responsible for them. A town that steps in to provide basic necessities gets a lien against the landlord. If you assign rents to a lender, keep the repair and utility duties funded.

title: Code Inspections of Rentals
bodyText: Maine has no statewide rental registration, licensing or periodic inspection program; some municipalities run their own, so check locally. State law gives officials inspection powers: a building official, the fire inspector and municipal officers may enter buildings at reasonable hours to examine them and must order dangerous combustible conditions or heating equipment fixed, and a local health officer may inspect for public health threats with the owner's, agent's or occupant's consent or, if refused, under a District Court warrant. No Maine statute lets a lease authorize a housing inspector to enter without the tenant's consent. What you can rely on is the tenant's duty not to unreasonably refuse your own entry to inspect, or to show the unit to workers or contractors, on reasonable notice (24 hours is presumed reasonable); a lease cannot waive the tenant's entry protections. A tenant's good-faith complaint to a code-enforcement body within 6 months before an eviction raises a presumption of retaliation, except in an eviction for a 7-day ground or a lease violation unless the tenant has used the repair-and-deduct remedy.

title: Small Owner-Occupied Building Exemptions
bodyText: Maine has three small-landlord exemptions but requires no notice or lease statement about them. In a building of no more than 5 dwelling units where you live in one: the tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy does not apply, the rule requiring written receipts for cash rent and deposit payments does not apply, and the security-deposit chapter (the 2-month cap, return deadlines, separate account and double damages) does not apply. The implied warranty of habitability and its court remedies, the entry rules, late-fee limits, illegal-eviction protections and fair housing law still apply, and Maine has no statutory rent escrow to exempt. The fair housing exemption is narrower: only one unit of an owner-occupied 2-family dwelling, or up to 4 rooms in your own home. Stating in the lease that the building is owner-occupied with 5 or fewer units is optional but can head off disputes.

title: No Termination for Costly Repairs
bodyText: Maine gives you no right to end a tenancy because a repair would cost too much compared with the rent. Under a fixed-term lease you must keep the unit fit for the rest of the term unless the lease ends it (Maine's casualty rule does not end a lease); while fire or other unavoidable casualty leaves the unit unfit, you cannot recover rent for that period. In a tenancy at will you may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice without a reason, but if the tenant complained in writing about repairs, complained to code enforcement or asserted habitability rights within the prior 6 months, an eviction is presumed retaliatory, and no writ issues unless you rebut it. A tenant may also accept specified conditions in writing in return for a stated rent reduction.

title: Repair Request Notice Rules
bodyText:
Maine's repair remedies turn on notice, and the rules differ by remedy.
- A habitability lawsuit needs written notice given without unreasonable delay to you or to whoever usually collects the rent, though actual notice to the rent collector also satisfies it.
- The rent-reduction defense in your action for rent needs written notice given while the tenant was current on rent.
- Repair-and-deduct needs written notice of the tenant's intent to fix the problem and 14 days after written notice by certified mail.
- The nonpayment-eviction defense needs only actual or constructive notice to you or your agent.
- A bedbug report may be written or oral, and smoke or carbon monoxide detector problems need written notice.

You may accept oral or online repair requests; doing so does not cost you anything the statutes give you, but once you actually know of a problem, a defense that turns on knowledge can apply. A lease term requiring written requests cannot narrow these statutory defenses, because a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights.

Keep a log of every request and your response.

title: No Security Device Mandate
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring deadbolts, door viewers or peepholes, window locks or rekeying between tenants, whatever the building's age. Maine's lock rules run the other way, limiting tenants: a tenant may not change a lock without notifying you and giving you a duplicate key within 48 hours; a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may change the locks at the tenant's own expense and give you a key within 72 hours; if a tenant changes a lock and won't provide a key, you may enter in an emergency by reasonable means, charge reasonable costs for resulting damage, and end the tenancy on 7 days' notice. Rekeying at turnover is still sensible practice, and a local code may require specific hardware.

title: No Senior Housing Staff Card Rule
bodyText: Maine has no work-card, licensing or background-check requirement for staff of housing for older persons. Maine's senior-housing law is a fair housing exemption: the familial-status protections do not apply to housing for older persons, meaning housing under a qualifying government program for the elderly, housing intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit, with at least 80% of units so occupied and published policies showing that intent. All other fair housing protections, including disability accommodation, still apply. If you operate 55+ housing, keep your age-verification records and published policies current.

title: Services and Utilities You Provide
bodyText:
When the lease says you provide a service or utility, Maine law attaches duties to that promise.

If you agreed to provide heat, the 68°F heat standard applies. A utility account you open in your own name is yours to pay, and if it goes unpaid the tenant may take over the service and deduct the payments from rent, plus damages of at least $100. You may not willfully interrupt any utility or service the tenant receives, whether or not you control it, except temporarily for actual repairs or emergencies.

If the lease requires the tenant to pay a recurring charge, other than rent or utility costs, for a service or common area, it is a mandatory recurring fee that must appear in the signed total price disclosure, and an optional service fee must be opt-in with the right to stop at any time; without a required signed disclosure the lease is unenforceable. A promised service the tenant asks you in writing, in good faith, to repair counts as a repair required by the rental agreement for the retaliation presumption.

List clearly which services and utilities you provide and which the tenant pays.

title: No Appliance Supply Duty
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to supply a stove, refrigerator or other kitchen appliance in a rental. Whether appliances come with the unit is a lease term. If you supply them, Maine law does not set a separate repair deadline, but a defective appliance that endangers or materially impairs health or safety, such as a leaking gas range, breaches the warranty of fitness and can trigger the tenant's court and repair-and-deduct remedies. On a citizen's complaint that a stove, oven, furnace or boiler is defective or so placed as to endanger a building, the Commissioner of Public Safety (or the officers of a town of not more than 2,000 inhabitants) gives the owner or occupant written notice, and failing to fix it within 3 days carries a forfeiture of $10 to $100. Say in the lease which appliances are included and who repairs them.

title: No Housing Receivership; Town Remedies
bodyText: Maine has no statute letting a court appoint a receiver to collect rents and repair substandard rental housing. Instead, towns have three tools. If leased premises face an imminent threat to habitability, municipal officers may, after documenting a good-faith attempt to reach you, provide heat, utilities, maintenance or repairs themselves and then hold a lien against you, recorded at the registry of deeds, for the cost plus interest and administrative costs. After notice and hearing, municipal officers may declare a building a nuisance or dangerous (structurally unsafe, unsanitary, a fire hazard or unfit for its use) and order its disposal, recovering their expenses by demand, special tax on the land or a civil action. And building officials and fire inspectors may order dangerous combustible conditions or heating equipment removed or fixed, with daily fines for noncompliance. Local code-enforcement ordinances may add repair orders.

title: Cable and Antenna Access
bodyText: In any building with 2 or more apartments, a Maine tenant may subscribe to cable television or use an over-the-air reception device, such as a satellite dish or antenna, installed by a service operator. The operator needs your written consent to attach equipment, and you may refuse only for good cause, such as the operator's failure to honor earlier written commitments or to repair damage from a prior installation. If you do not answer, consent is deemed given once the operator delivers a copy of the statute, a signed statement agreeing to be bound and a plain-language notice of your rights, in person or by certified mail. Installation must be at no cost to you; the operator must indemnify you for damage, follow your reasonable installation requests and day-to-day rules, and carry insurance unless you waive it. You may not charge tenants who subscribe different rent or fees from those who do not, or take payment for the installation except reasonable compensation from the operator, which is presumed to be $1 unless you give notice by certified mail within 20 days and prove a specific loss.

title: Tenant Repair Remedies
bodyText: A Maine tenant facing an unfit condition has four routes, all requiring that the tenant did not cause it. (1) A lawsuit: if the condition endangers or materially impairs health or safety, the tenant gave written notice without unreasonable delay, was current on rent, and you unreasonably failed to act promptly, the court may order repairs, set the fair value of the unit from the date you had notice and order a rebate, let the tenant move out temporarily during repairs owing nothing, and issue other orders, but no consequential damages. (2) A defense to a nonpayment eviction if you had actual or constructive notice and failed to act, letting the tenant either end the lease or stay at a reduced rent. (3) A rent reduction in your action for rent, after written notice. (4) Repair-and-deduct for repairs costing under $500 or half a month's rent, whichever is greater, 14 days after certified-mail notice. These rights cannot be waived. Maine has no rent escrow during repairs; escrow arises only when a tenant appeals an eviction judgment. Repair-and-deduct does not apply in owner-occupied buildings of 5 or fewer units.

title: Utilities You Pay
bodyText:
If the lease makes you responsible for a utility, Maine law holds you to it. When you apply for and receive utility service, you must pay for it; the utility may not demand payment from the tenant for your unpaid bill and may disconnect the tenant only after giving the tenant notice and a chance to take over future service. A tenant who takes over and pays may deduct those payments from rent, and a court must award the tenant at least $100 or the amount paid, plus costs, presuming you failed to pay knowingly. The utility also gets a lien on the rental property for your unpaid bills.

You may never willfully interrupt a utility the tenant receives, even one in your name, except temporarily for actual repairs or emergencies; doing so is an illegal eviction carrying at least $250 in damages plus fees. If the utility is heat, the 68°F standard applies.

Utilities you pay need no entry in the total price disclosure unless the tenant pays something toward them.

title: No Utility Allowance Rule
bodyText:
Maine has no statute or utility-commission rule in the searched corpus on utility allowances, where you pay a utility up to a set amount and the tenant reimburses the overage.

Such an arrangement is a lease term, and Maine's general rules shape it. Overage charges are utility service costs, not rent, so they must be listed in the signed total price disclosure when one is required, an unpaid overage cannot support a 7-day nonpayment-of-rent notice, and the late-fee rule for rent does not cover it; you may deduct unpaid utility charges the tenant was required to pay you from the deposit.

Maine's utility statutes expressly allow electric submetering only at campgrounds and electric vehicle charging stations, and whether passing master-metered electricity through to tenants by allowance is permitted was not located.

Utility tariffs and other commission rules were not searched either.

title: Utility Transfer and Account Status Requests
bodyText: Maine offers landlords a different tool from a disconnection-notice authorization. On your request, the electric transmission and distribution utility must enter into an agreement with you for a rental receiving service in the tenant's name: if the tenant's service would otherwise be disconnected, it transfers automatically into your name and the utility notifies you within 72 hours. The utility may charge a reasonable fee for the transfer and may not tell you anything else about the tenant or the tenant's account without the tenant's consent. For water service, and for municipal, sewer-district and sanitary-district sewer service, where an unpaid tenant bill can become a lien on your property, the provider must on request tell you or your agent the current status of the tenant's account, including amounts due or overdue. No Maine statute or rule in the searched corpus provides for a separate document authorizing a utility to warn you of a tenant's pending disconnection.

title: Unpaid Utilities in Your Name
bodyText: When a utility account for a tenant's home is in your name and goes unpaid, Maine protects the tenant. You are responsible for any service you applied for; the utility may not make the tenant pay your bill or demand a deposit based on your credit, and it may disconnect only after giving the tenant notice and a chance to take over future service. Under the Public Utilities Commission's rules, an electric, gas or water utility that knows the premises are rented may not disconnect at your request or for your nonpayment unless the tenant agrees in writing, you sign a statement that the premises are vacant, the utility confirms vacancy by inspection, or it gives tenants notice at least 14 days before the disconnection date, delivered in person to an adult in each unit where possible (electric and gas) and posted at the building's entrances for single-meter buildings. A tenant who takes over service may deduct payments from rent and recover at least $100 or the amount paid, plus costs. The utility can lien your property for the unpaid bill. Maine has no rent-receivership remedy for unpaid utilities.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Maine's utility shutoff protections come mainly from Public Utilities Commission rules adopted under statute. The statute requires the Commission's rules to give residential customers written notice of an unpaid bill and of a prospective disconnection, a right to reasonable installment arrangements, an informal hearing with an appeal to the Commission, and no disconnection during a limited medical emergency. For electric and gas service, the rules set a winter disconnection period from November 15 to April 15. During it a utility may not send a notice setting a disconnection date, and may not disconnect a residential customer without the advance permission of the Commission's consumer assistance division, after notice and an opportunity to be heard; this is a near-moratorium, not just a longer notice period. The Commission may also declare an emergency moratorium. For rented premises, separate tenant protections apply when the account is yours. These protections run between the utility and its customer; you may never interrupt a tenant's utility yourself.

title: Shared and Common-Area Utilities
bodyText:
In a multi-unit building, Maine bars a lease or tenancy at will agreement that makes one tenant solely responsible for heat, electricity or any other utility serving common areas or areas outside the unit (hallways, stairwells, basements, attics, storage areas, or a furnace or water heater shared with other tenants), unless you both agree in writing that the tenant will pay in return for a stated rent reduction or other specified fair consideration approximating the actual cost. Any other waiver is void, and you owe actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees and costs; you are presumed to know the tenant has been paying.

Maine has no statute or rule in the searched corpus on dividing a shared meter's bill among units by ratio or formula, and no rule voiding a term that has tenants pay for utilities not separately metered.

If you do bill shared costs, they are utility service costs, not rent, and belong in the signed total price disclosure when one is required. Fix shared-meter wiring where you can, and use the common-area utility agreement where you cannot.

title: Submetering and Utility Billing
bodyText: Maine has no statute or Public Utilities Commission rule on submetering, ratio (RUBS) billing or other landlord billing of utilities to residential tenants, and none prescribing a lease disclosure, type size, billing cap or building-size threshold for it. Maine's utility law expressly allows electric submetering only at campgrounds (where it is not treated as resale) and at electric vehicle charging stations; whether a landlord may submeter or allocate electricity, gas or water among units, and whether doing so makes the landlord a regulated utility, was not located. If you bill any utility charges, Maine's general rules apply: they are utility service costs, not rent, so they must be listed in the signed total price disclosure when one is required, cannot support a 7-day nonpayment-of-rent notice, and fall outside the rent late-fee rule; unpaid charges you required the tenant to pay you may come out of the deposit. Prospective tenants who will pay for energy are entitled to a 12-month usage and cost history, which the electric, gas and water utilities must give free on request. If a utility account is in your name and you fall behind, the utility may not shut off a rented home without the tenant's written consent, a vacancy statement or inspection, or at least 14 days' notice delivered to each unit (and posted at the entrances of a single-meter building) that offers the tenant service in the tenant's own name, and it cannot make the tenant pay your arrears. Get advice before submetering. Maine's statutes, 2025-2026 session laws, constitution, civil procedure rules and seven agency rules were searched, and Public Utilities Commission rules chs. 320, 620, 660 and 815 were read at sync; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Utility Cutoff to Force Transfer
bodyText: Maine does not allow a landlord to cut off a utility in the landlord's name because the tenant has not transferred the account. You may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption of any utility service the tenant receives, whether or not you control it, except temporarily during actual repairs or emergencies; doing so is an illegal eviction carrying actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. The utilities' own rules also stop them from disconnecting rented premises at your request unless the tenant agrees in writing, you certify the unit is vacant, the utility confirms vacancy, or it gives the tenants at least 14 days' notice and a chance to take service in their names. What you can do: require in the lease that the tenant open accounts in the tenant's name by a set date, treat a failure as a lease breach, and arrange with the electric utility for automatic transfer into your name if the tenant's service would otherwise be disconnected.

title: Victim Lock Changes
bodyText: A Maine tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may change the locks to the unit at the tenant's own expense, without your permission, and must give you a duplicate key within 72 hours of the change (other tenants get 48 hours and must notify you first). The tenant does not have to give you the documentation required for other victim protections when changing locks. You have no statutory duty to change the locks for the victim or pay for it, and a lease cannot take this right away; any waiver of the entry and lock rules is void. If a lock is changed and no key is provided, in an emergency you may enter by reasonable means and charge reasonable costs of resulting damage, and if a tenant refuses to provide a key you may end the tenancy on 7 days' notice, but a victim who is within the 72-hour window has not refused. Handle the victim's information carefully: disclosing a tenant's status as a crime victim to harass or push the tenant out carries damages of at least $1,000.

title: Entry Rules
bodyText:
A Maine tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors.

You must give reasonable notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times; 24 hours is presumed reasonable unless shown otherwise. No notice is needed in an emergency, including an animal-welfare emergency, or when notice is impracticable.

Entering in violation of these rules, entering in an unreasonable manner or making repeated harassing demands for entry exposes you to actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, an injunction, and attorney's fees if the tenant wins after a contested hearing. These rights cannot be waived in the lease, so a term letting you enter without notice for showings or scheduled services is void, and no Maine statute treats a tenant's repair request as waiving notice; agree on a time instead.

Maine has no rule for landlord-initiated temporary relocation. If a tenant unreasonably denies access, the tenant loses repair-and-deduct, and refusing a key after changing locks allows a 7-day termination notice.

title: No Scheduled-Service Entry Exception
bodyText: Maine has no exception letting you enter without notice for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes or pest treatment, even if the lease says so. Every non-emergency entry needs reasonable notice of your intent to enter, at a reasonable time; 24 hours is presumed reasonable. A lease term giving up that notice is void. In practice, send a written notice of each scheduled visit at least 24 hours ahead, or agree with the tenant on a specific date and time. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to supply necessary or agreed services, and for bedbug inspection or treatment the tenant must allow access on reasonable notice that states the reasons for and scope of the entry. No notice is needed in an emergency or when notice is impracticable.

title: No Smart Lock Law
bodyText: Maine has no statute specifically regulating smart locks, keyless entry, app-based access or entry logs in residential rentals. Maine's general rules apply to them. An electronic lock does not change the entry rules: you must give reasonable notice (24 hours is presumed reasonable) and enter at reasonable times except in an emergency, and using remote access to enter without notice exposes you to damages of at least $250. Tenants may not change locks without notice and a duplicate key within 48 hours (72 hours for a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking), so decide in the lease how codes or credentials will be handled. Data a smart-access system collects, such as names, phone numbers or entry patterns, falls under Maine's limit on disclosing tenants' personal information to harass or push them out.

title: Duty to Re-Rent After Abandonment
bodyText: If a tenant moves out early without justification and stops paying, or is removed for nonpayment or another breach, you may recover rent and damages from that tenant, except what you could have avoided by reasonable efforts to re-rent, unless you expressly agreed to accept a surrender and end the tenant's liability. Your recovery is reduced by the net rent obtainable by re-renting the way you would have if the unit had been vacated normally, in line with local practice; you may also recover reasonable listing and advertising costs. You must allege and prove your efforts, but the tenant bears the burden of proving they were unreasonable and how much more could have been obtained. Entering to inspect, preserve, repair, remodel or show the unit, re-renting with the proceeds credited to the tenant, or using it yourself for up to a year with prompt written notice that you will credit its reasonable value, does not count as accepting a surrender. You may fill your other vacant units first if a new prospect did not come from the departed tenant. A lease term waiving your duty to mitigate would waive a tenant right and is risky.

title: Attorney Fee Rules
bodyText:
A Maine residential lease or rule **may not make the tenant pay your legal fees for enforcing it**. Such a term is unenforceable, and using it is an unfair and deceptive trade practice.

The only exception: a lease may provide that the prevailing party gets attorney's fees after a contested hearing to enforce the lease in cases of wanton disregard of its terms; it works both ways by its own words. There is no other closed list and no percentage cap, because no other fee-shifting term is allowed.

Many Maine statutes instead award tenants their attorney's fees when you violate them, including illegal eviction, unlawful entry after a contested hearing, common-area utilities, unpaid landlord utility accounts (in the court's discretion), bedbugs, rent-increase notice, rent increases during habitability violations, wrongful deposit retention and deposit-account violations. A court may award you fees if a tenant's illegal-eviction suit was frivolous or brought only to harass, and may assess fees against a party who fails to mediate in good faith. Collection costs passed through a debt collector are limited to what the agreement and law allow.

title: Property Left Behind
bodyText:
Maine has one mandatory procedure for a tenant's belongings left after a judgment for possession or after the tenant vacates.

Store them in a safe, dry, secured place. Send written notice of your intent to dispose by first-class mail with proof of mailing: to the unit if the tenant is still in possession (giving at least 7 days after mailing or 48 hours after the writ is served, whichever is longer), or to the last known address with an itemized list if the tenant has left. If the tenant claims within 7 days, release everything without charge, as long as the tenant arranges retrieval by day 14; keep storing for at least 14 days. If no timely claim, or no retrieval by day 14, you may require payment of arrears, damages and storage costs, sell at a reasonable fair market price (sending any surplus to the Treasurer of State) or dispose of items with no reasonable value.

A tenant may waive these rights only after or upon vacating, and an oral waiver must be confirmed in writing; the lease may let you dispose without liability only if you follow the notice rules. Holding property any other way is an illegal eviction. Storage and disposal costs may come out of the deposit.

title: Fire and Casualty Rules
bodyText:
Under Maine's casualty rule, while a residential building or unit is destroyed or damaged by fire or other unavoidable casualty so that it is unfit for use or habitation, you cannot bring an action for rent, or for damages for breach of the lease's conditions, for that period. The statute's exceptions for contrary agreements are written for nonresidential leases and leases securing Maine Guaranty Authority obligations, so do not rely on a residential lease term that keeps rent running through a casualty.

The statute does not itself end the lease, set a notice period, or require you to rebuild, return the tenant's belongings by a set date or provide other housing; the lease decides how either party may terminate. A tenant whose unit was rendered unfit may also use the habitability remedies if you unreasonably fail to repair a repairable condition.

A casualty the tenant, an occupant or a guest caused is not unavoidable as to them, and you may recover damages from whoever caused it. Return the deposit, less lawful deductions, within the statutory time once the tenancy ends.

title: Condo and Subsidy Conversions
bodyText: Two Maine conversion rules matter to landlords. Condominium conversion: the declarant must give each residential tenant and subtenant notice of the conversion and the public offering statement at least 120 days before requiring them to leave; during that time no tenant may be made to vacate except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct disturbing other tenants, and the tenancy terms may not change. For 60 days the tenant has the exclusive offer to buy the unit, and for the next 180 days you may not offer it to others on better terms. A conversion notice that sets a vacate date and complies with Maine's eviction-notice rules also serves as the notice to vacate, but no lease may be ended early in violation of its terms. Failing to give notice is a defense to eviction, and towns may adopt stricter conversion rules. Subsidized housing: an owner of low-income rental housing with 5 or more units must give tenants 90 days' notice before a sale or other action ending affordability restrictions or financial assistance, notice at least 2 years before restrictions expire, and must let tenants stay 6 months at the same rents or relocate them under state rules; a missed notice carries a penalty of at least $2,500.

title: Crime at the Property
bodyText:
Maine has no special fast-track eviction or mandatory-eviction duty for crime, but its notice rules let you move quickly.

In a tenancy at will, 7 days' written notice ends the tenancy if the tenant, family or an invitee caused or permitted a nuisance or violated the law regarding the tenancy, or if the tenant, a guest or invitee committed violence, a threat of violence or sexual assault against another tenant, a guest, you or your staff; there is no cure right for these grounds. A fixed-term lease ends for crime as its own terms provide.

Separately, a place used for the illegal sale or keeping of scheduled drugs, as a house of ill fame, or for lewdness or gambling is a common nuisance: the Attorney General, a district attorney or 7 voters of the county may sue to abate it, two drug sales there within 3 years prove the nuisance, and anyone who keeps or allows a place declared a nuisance commits a crime. A tenant who uses the premises that way forfeits the tenancy, and if a tenant is convicted of keeping a house of ill fame you may treat the lease as void.

A victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may not be evicted for that violence or for reporting it. No statute requires the lease to describe these rights.

title: Eviction Grounds and Cure
bodyText: Maine has no general right for a tenant to cure a lease violation before termination. For a tenancy at will, you may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice for any reason that is not retaliatory or discriminatory, or on 7 days' written notice for listed grounds: substantial damage the tenant has not repaired, a nuisance, making the unit unfit, violating the law regarding the tenancy, rent 7 or more days in arrears, being a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking perpetrator against another tenant, violence or threats against others, or an unauthorized occupant.
