Only rent has a cure: paying the full rent due before a 7-day rent notice expires voids it, and after expiry an at-will tenant who pays all arrears, current rent and your filing and service fees before the writ issues gets the tenancy reinstated. Refusing you a key after a lock change also supports a 7-day notice. For a fixed-term lease, termination for breach follows the lease's own terms; if a written lease has no termination provision or written-notice term for a material breach, you may use the 7-day notice rules for the listed grounds (the 30-day no-cause notice does not apply to a fixed term). A 7-day notice must state the specific ground; every notice must tell the tenant of the right to contest the termination in court and have the court's form notice attached.

title: Ending a Tenancy for Default
bodyText:
How you end a Maine tenancy for the tenant's default depends on the tenancy.

A fixed-term written lease ends for breach as the lease provides, and if the lease has no termination provision or written-notice term for a material breach, you may use the tenancy-at-will 7-day notice for the listed grounds only; the 30-day no-cause notice does not apply, which is why the lease should contain its own termination term. Possession comes only through a forcible entry and detainer case, which may start without notice within 7 days after the term expires or is forfeited.

Every termination notice must tell the tenant of the right to contest in court (and a 7-day notice must state the specific ground), attach the court's form notice, and be served with the court's information sheet and mediation form. The lease may not make the tenant pay your legal fees, except a prevailing-party fee award after a contested hearing for wanton disregard of the lease, and may not charge a fee for ending the tenancy beyond reasonable re-renting costs where the tenant broke the notice terms, unpaid rent, or tenant-caused repair costs.

You must mitigate damages. Maine has no repeat-breach rule and no trebling of damages, and requiring the tenant to waive these protections is an unfair trade practice.

title: No Drug-Free Addendum Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute on drug-free or crime-free lease addenda: none requires one, sets its wording or bars it. A drug-free term is an ordinary lease term, and violating it can support termination under the lease, or, in a tenancy at will, a 7-day notice where the conduct is a nuisance or a violation of law regarding the tenancy. Limits to keep in mind: you may not refuse to rent to or penalize someone solely for being a qualifying (certified) medical cannabis patient or a caregiver (unless federal law or funding requires it), though you may restrict cannabis use or growing inconsistent with the general use of the premises, and may ban smoking medical cannabis only if you ban all smoking and post notice. The addendum must not penalize a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking victim, and federally assisted housing has its own federal rules.

title: Victim Eviction Protections
bodyText: Maine protects tenants who are victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking in eviction. You may not evict a victim because of actual or threatened violence at the premises, or because the victim reported it, on the theory that it was a nuisance, property damage or a lease violation from a nuisance, disturbance or damage. A victim is not liable for damage to the property from that violence beyond the security deposit, if the perpetrator is a tenant and the victim gives written notice and documentation within 30 days. You may split the lease to evict the perpetrator, whether or not the victim signed it, without interfering with property rights set by a court order, and you may evict a perpetrator who is a tenant on 7 days' notice when the victim is also a tenant. An eviction filed within 6 months after a tenant tells you, before being served with an eviction notice, that the tenant or the tenant's minor child is a victim is presumed retaliatory, unless the eviction is for a 7-day cause or a lease violation and the tenant has not used the repair-and-deduct remedy. You may still evict a victim for unrelated reasons and hold the perpetrator liable for damage. Refusing to rent because someone obtained a protection order is housing discrimination.

title: Victim Early Termination
bodyText: A Maine tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may end the victim's tenancy early because of an incident or threat. For a tenancy at will or a lease shorter than one year, the tenant gives 7 days' written notice; for a lease of one year or more, 30 days' written notice; either way with the required documentation. The victim owes no rent beyond the date the notice expires or the date the victim moves out, whichever is later, though you need not refund rent the victim prepaid for that month. A tenant sexually harassed by you or your agent has the same early-termination right. The statute speaks of the victim's own tenancy and does not say whether co-tenants' obligations end; consider how a remaining household will continue. Domestic violence for this purpose covers listed crimes against a family or household member or dating partner, while sexual assault and stalking cover anyone. You may still evict a perpetrator, including by splitting the lease, and recover damages from the perpetrator. Do not charge an early-termination fee or keep the deposit beyond lawful deductions for a victim's termination.

title: Victim Documentation
bodyText: When a tenant invokes Maine's victim protections (other than changing the locks), the tenant must give you documentation of the alleged conduct by the perpetrator, including the perpetrator's name. Acceptable documentation includes, but is not limited to: a statement signed by a Maine sexual assault counselor, domestic violence advocate or victim witness advocate; a statement signed by a health care provider, mental health care provider or law enforcement officer, with a license number if licensed; a protection from abuse complaint or a temporary or final protection order; a protection from harassment complaint or order; a police report from an investigation of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking; or a criminal complaint, indictment or conviction for such a charge. Because the list is not exclusive, judge other reasonable proof case by case rather than insisting on one form. Keep the documents confidential: a victim's status is personal information you may not disclose to harass or push the tenant out, and doing so costs at least $1,000.

title: Early Termination Rules
bodyText:
Maine bars any lease or rule term making a tenant pay a fee, penalty or other charge for the act of ending a tenancy, except to recover reasonable expenses of finding another tenant when the tenant broke the lease's notice-before-leaving terms, to collect unpaid rent, or to recover reasonable costs of repairing damage the tenant caused. A flat buy-out or early-termination fee is therefore unenforceable and an unfair trade practice, whatever the lease or an addendum says; keeping part of the deposit for reasons the deposit law allows is not such a fee.

If a tenant leaves early without a lawful reason, you may recover rent and damages, reduced by what reasonable re-renting would bring in.

Tenants have statutory early-exit rights you cannot contract away: victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, and tenants sexually harassed by you or your agent (7 or 30 days' notice), either party after a radon test at or above 4.0 picocuries per liter (30 days' notice), a court-ordered termination for an unfit unit, and, from January 1, 2030, a tenant who never received the signed energy efficiency disclosure (30 days' notice).

title: No Eminent Domain Lease Rule
bodyText: Maine has no general statute saying what happens to a residential lease or the rent when the property is taken by eminent domain, and no statute letting the court in a condemnation case cancel the lease. The lease and general law govern, so a lease should say whether it ends on a taking and how any award is shared. One state program helps tenants directly: when the Department of Transportation acquires a dwelling for a project, a tenant who lawfully lived there at least 90 days before negotiations began can receive a payment to rent a comparable replacement dwelling for up to 42 months (or apply it toward buying one), within federal limits. Other condemning authorities follow their own statutes, which were not reviewed for tenant payments.

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord
bodyText: Most business entities that own Maine rentals need a lawyer to bring an eviction. Maine's unauthorized-practice law lets a non-lawyer appear for a limited liability company in a forcible entry and detainer case only if the person is the company's sole member, or a member of a company owned by a married couple, domestic partners, or an individual and that individual's issue. Separately, an officer or authorized employee of a corporation, partnership or sole proprietorship, or a member, manager or authorized employee of an LLC, may appear for it in a small claims case, such as one to collect unpaid rent or damages within small claims limits. An individual owner may always represent himself or herself. Anyone else who appears for an entity in an eviction without being a lawyer risks a Class E crime, and the filing may be challenged. Court rules may add conditions; check the clerk's requirements.

title: No Environmental Event Termination Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute giving a landlord or tenant the right to end a lease after an environmental event such as a wildfire, smoke, flooding or contamination. Related rules may apply. If the event destroys or damages the unit so it is unfit for use or habitation, the casualty rule bars rent actions for that period. Offering a unit for rent with mold from a leak, flooding or chronic moisture outside the tenant's control breaches the warranty of fitness. If a radon test shows 4.0 picocuries per liter or more, either party may end the lease or tenancy at will on 30 days' notice, and you may not keep the deposit except for lawful deductions. Beyond those, any termination right for an environmental event must come from the lease, so an opt-in clause would need to be drafted with Maine's limits on fees and waivers in mind.

title: No Hardship Stay; Limited Delays
bodyText: Maine has no general hardship stay that lets a court delay an eviction because moving would be hard on the tenant. The delays that do exist are specific. The writ of possession issues 7 calendar days after judgment, and a tenant has 48 hours after a sheriff or constable serves it to leave. A tenant who appeals can get the writ stayed while the appeal is pending, but only by paying the current month's unpaid rent or the arrearage (whichever is less) and keeping rent paid into court or to you as it comes due, and the stay can be lifted for nonpayment, nuisance or damage. If a National Guard or Reserve member is ordered to military duty, an eviction from that member's family dwelling needs the court's permission, and the court may stay the case or postpone rent if service materially affects the ability to pay; you may ask for relief, including later payment of arrears. A court may also continue a hearing for good cause.

title: Eviction Process
bodyText: Maine evictions use the forcible entry and detainer (FED) process in District Court; self-help is illegal. Start with a written notice: 30 days for a tenancy at will, 7 days for listed grounds such as rent 7 or more days late, or the notice your lease provides. A 7-day notice must state the specific ground, and every notice must state the tenant's right to contest in court, attach the court's form notice, and come with the court's information sheet and mediation request form. Serve it in hand, or after 3 good-faith attempts by first-class mail plus leaving it at the home. The summons must give at least 14 days to the return day; file the complaint at least 3 days before the hearing with copies of the lease and notice. The court may order mediation and must hold the hearing within 10 days after the return day unless continued for good cause. The tenant may not counterclaim in the FED, and Maine has no for-cause rule, rent escrow on adjournment, or legislative-only rule for procedure. The writ issues 7 days after judgment; the tenant must leave within 48 hours after service, or is a trespasser and the belongings follow the abandoned-property rules. A tenant who appeals must pay rent and file an affidavit to stay the writ.

title: No Eviction Sealing; Limited Online Access
bodyText: Maine has no statute sealing, expunging or removing eviction records, and no procedure for a landlord to object to sealing. A court rule instead limits remote access: before judgment, or at any time if the parties agree, records in eviction (forcible entry and detainer), small claims and foreclosure cases can be seen by the public only at a courthouse; after a judgment against the defendant, the case index is available remotely for three years, and other records only when the court approves remote access. So a dismissed case, or one the parties settle with an agreement to limit access, will generally not appear in online court searches, though it remains public at the courthouse. If you use tenant-screening reports, federal and Maine credit-reporting laws govern how eviction information is reported and used. The court rule is cited from the corpus copy of the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems.

title: No Lease-Named Recipient for Court Papers
bodyText: Maine has no rule letting a lease name a person to accept eviction court papers for the tenant. Service on a tenant follows the ordinary civil rules: in hand, or, after at least 3 good-faith attempts on 3 different days, by both first-class mail to the last known address and leaving the papers at the tenant's last and usual place of abode, with an affidavit of that service filed with the court. Termination notices may likewise be served by mail plus leaving them at the home after 3 good-faith attempts, and a notice served by a sheriff, constable or other authorized server is admissible to prove service, with the server allowed to testify remotely. On your side, anyone authorized to sign leases for you is your agent for service of process and for receiving notices and demands, so tenants and courts can serve that person.

title: No Expedited Criminal Eviction
bodyText: Maine has no special expedited eviction track for criminal activity. Speed comes from the ordinary rules. In a tenancy at will, a 7-day written notice ends the tenancy for a nuisance, a violation of law regarding the tenancy, or violence, threats of violence or sexual assault by the tenant, a guest or invitee against another tenant, a guest, you or your staff, and a fixed-term lease ends as its terms allow. The summons must give at least 14 days to the return day, the hearing must be held within 10 days after the return day unless continued for good cause, and the writ issues 7 days after judgment. Where you need protection sooner, you may petition the court against a tenant, guest or owner of a dangerous pet who has harmed or threatened you, your staff, your property or your tenants, and a temporary order is available if your property faces immediate danger of substantial damage. Drug and similar common-nuisance cases can also be brought by public officials or 7 voters.

title: No Just Cause Requirement
bodyText: Maine has no just-cause or good-cause eviction law for ordinary residential rentals. You may end a tenancy at will on 30 days' written notice without stating a reason, and a fixed-term lease simply ends at the end of its term unless it renews by its own terms; Maine has no rule converting an expiring lease to month-to-month or requiring an advance non-renewal notice. The limits are indirect: an eviction is presumed retaliatory if filed within 6 months after the tenant asserted listed rights, complained in good faith to code enforcement or to you in writing about repairs, filed a fair housing complaint, told you of domestic violence, or reported sexual harassment, unless it rests on a 7-day ground or a lease violation; you may not evict for a protected characteristic, receipt of public assistance or a protection order; and condominium conversion, subsidized-housing and foreclosure rules add notice periods. Mobile home park lot tenancies have their own statute with listed termination reasons. Local rent ordinances may add limits (flag).

title: Tenants in Foreclosure
bodyText: Foreclosure does not let a lender or buyer simply remove your tenants. In Maine a bona fide tenancy in a building under a pending foreclosure, or after a foreclosure judgment, may be ended only under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act. In a power-of-sale foreclosure, the lender must give a copy of the foreclosure notice to any residential tenant it knows or should know of, and may not evict until an eviction case is begun at least 21 days after that notice. After a judicial foreclosure judgment, the lender must give tenants a copy of the judgment and notice of all later proceedings, and may evict only through an eviction case after that notice and after the redemption period ends. As the landlord, you must give the lender your tenants' names and contact information on request. While a foreclosure is pending or after judgment, tenants may use repair-and-deduct for repairs up to 2 months' rent. Tenants' security deposits must sit in an account beyond the reach of a foreclosing mortgagee and pass to the new owner. Maine has no separate landlord disclosure duty to tenants about a pending foreclosure.

title: Reinstatement for Nonpayment
bodyText: Maine's statutory right to undo a forfeiture for nonpayment belongs to tenants at will. If the tenant pays the full rent due before a 7-day rent notice expires, the notice is void. After it expires, the tenant can still reinstate the tenancy by paying all arrears, all rent due as of the payment date and the filing and service fees you actually paid, any time before the writ of possession issues; a written assurance of payment from a general assistance program counts as payment, and no writ may issue once the tenant has paid. There is no limit on how often a tenant at will may do this. Fixed-term leases have no statutory pay-to-reinstate right; whether a court would relieve a tenant from forfeiture of a lease is a matter of the Superior Court's equity powers and case law. A 30-day termination is not undone by your accepting money before the writ issues. Track payments carefully and send receipts.

title: No Guarantor Statute
bodyText: Maine has no statute on residential lease guaranties: nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires renewal terms to be stated, or requires a maximum amount or end date. The guaranty is an ordinary contract, so write it clearly, including whether it covers renewals, extensions and holdover periods and any cap. Two Maine rules still bear on guarantors. Any advance or deposit, whatever it is called, whose main purpose is to secure performance of the lease is a security deposit, so money you take from a guarantor to secure the lease likely counts toward the 2-month deposit cap together with the tenant's deposit and is subject to the return rules; the up-front money limit is written for tenants. And a lease may not make the tenant pay your legal fees, so do not route those fees through the guaranty for the tenant's obligations. Maine law does not settle whether a guarantor can be charged legal fees for enforcing the guaranty itself.

title: Tenants Who Stay Past the Term
bodyText:
When a Maine lease term ends and the tenant stays without your agreement, you may start an eviction case without any notice if you file within 7 days after the term expires or is forfeited.

If you wait longer, or accept rent for a period after the term, give a written termination notice as for a tenancy at will before filing, since Maine's month-to-month tenancy is a tenancy at will that needs 30 days' written notice to end. Accepting money after a 30-day notice does not undo that termination before the writ issues.

Maine has no statute setting holdover damages or a double-rent penalty; you may recover rent or the reasonable value of the holdover period and damages, and the lease may set an agreed holdover charge. You may never remove a holdover tenant or the tenant's belongings yourself.

title: Holdover Charge Limits
bodyText:
Maine has no statute capping or setting a holdover rate, so a lease may set an agreed daily holdover charge, as the optional holdover clause does.

Keep it defensible: tie it to a reasonable estimate of your loss rather than a punishment, do not collect both the holdover charge and rent for the same day, and say that accepting it does not create a new tenancy. Maine's limits on late fees (4% of a month's rent, after 15 days, with written notice at signing) apply to rent paid late, not to a holdover charge, but a charge that is really a penalty may be challenged under general contract law.

A holdover charge is not rent, so nonpayment of it cannot support a 7-day notice for rent arrears. Federal program rules may cap holdover charges in assisted housing.

title: No Exemption Waivers
bodyText: Maine has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the exemptions that protect a debtor's property from attachment and execution, and no statute addressing such a waiver at all. The exemptions themselves are statutory: among others, a residence interest up to $80,000 (more for older or disabled debtors or with minor dependents), up to $10,000 in one vehicle, household goods, furniture, appliances and clothing up to $500 per item, a cooking stove and heating stoves and fuel, tools of the trade, health aids and public benefits, adjusted periodically for inflation. A lease also may not require the tenant to give a lien on the tenant's property for rent or other sums, which is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice. Do not include an exemption waiver in a Maine lease; collect a judgment through the ordinary process, where the tenant can claim exemptions.

title: No Infirmity Termination Right
bodyText: Maine has no statute letting a tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability, admission to a nursing home or assisted living, or death. Unless the lease provides an exit, a tenant who leaves early owes rent and damages reduced by what you could obtain by reasonably re-renting, and you may not charge a fee for the act of ending the tenancy beyond reasonable re-renting costs, unpaid rent and tenant-caused repairs. A tenant with a disability may ask you to change a rule, policy or practice, and Maine's Human Rights Act requires reasonable accommodations that are necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing; treat such a request seriously. A tenancy at will can always be ended by the tenant on 30 days' written notice. Consider offering an optional infirmity or death clause.

title: No Landlord Lien
bodyText: Maine gives residential landlords no lien on a tenant's belongings and forbids creating one by contract. A lease or rule term requiring the tenant to give a lien on the tenant's property for rent or other sums is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice. You also may not seize, hold or deny a tenant access to the tenant's property outside court process; that is an illegal eviction carrying actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus fees. Maine has no distress for rent and no statute for a UCC security interest in household goods. The only point at which you may hold property for payment is after the abandoned-property procedure: if the tenant does not claim within 7 days after your notice, or claims but does not retrieve by day 14, you may condition release on payment of arrears, damages and storage costs, or sell it and apply the proceeds. A separate old statute gives a lien on buildings for unpaid land rent where a tenant owns a building on leased land, which does not apply to ordinary apartment rentals. Collect unpaid rent through a court judgment.

title: Possession and Money Claims
bodyText: In Maine, possession and money are pursued separately. The eviction case (forcible entry and detainer) decides only who gets possession: it may not be joined with any other action, and the tenant may not counterclaim in it. To recover unpaid rent or damage to the premises, you bring a civil action, which can be a small claims case within its limits, specifying the items and amounts claimed; you need not wait for the tenancy to end to sue for rent already due. Your recovery for rent after an early departure or eviction is reduced by what reasonable re-renting would bring in, and you may not recover rent for any period when fire or other unavoidable casualty made the unit unfit. A tenant may defend a rent claim by proving an unfit condition, after written notice, that you unreasonably failed to fix. You may also keep part of the security deposit for lawful reasons, with an itemized statement in time. Self-help, liens and fee-shifting are not available.

title: No Liquidated Damages Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute permitting or forbidding a liquidated-damages clause in a residential lease, but several rules sharply limit one. A lease may not charge any fee, penalty or other charge for ending the tenancy except reasonable costs of finding a new tenant when the tenant broke the lease's notice terms, unpaid rent, and reasonable costs to repair damage the tenant caused, so a fixed amount owed for leaving early is barred. Late fees are capped at 4% of a month's rent and allowed only for rent 15 or more days late with written notice at signing. You may keep a security deposit only for actual causes, never as a set forfeit, and a tenant's surety bond is expressly not liquidated damages. A holdover charge set in the lease is not covered by any statute, but a charge that is really a penalty may be challenged under general contract law. Write damage terms as actual, itemized costs.

title: No Lockouts
bodyText: Maine forbids locking out a tenant for unpaid rent, even if the lease allows it. Any eviction outside the court process is illegal and against public policy. You may not willfully interrupt the tenant's utilities, seize or deny the tenant access to the unit, or seize or hold the tenant's belongings except through proper judicial process. The court must award the tenant actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, and/or the tenant's costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and these remedies add to any others the tenant has. A lease clause authorizing a lockout or changing locks for nonpayment is void as a waiver of tenant rights and using it is an unfair trade practice. For unpaid rent, serve a 7-day notice once rent is 7 days late and then file an eviction case.

title: Whom to Name in an Eviction
bodyText: Maine's eviction statute says whom to name: an eviction case is effective against all occupants of a unit if you name "all other occupants" together with all adults whose names appear on the lease or rental agreement, or whose tenancy you acknowledged by accepting rent or otherwise. Minors are not named individually; naming "all other occupants" reaches them. Maine has no statute barring a filing against a minor as such or setting special rules for minor tenants, and capacity questions are handled by the general court rules, which were not reviewed for this row. Be careful about the domestic violence rules if a minor child in the household is a victim: an eviction filed within 6 months after a tenant tells you that the tenant or the tenant's minor child is a victim is presumed retaliatory unless it rests on a 7-day ground or a lease violation.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: When rent is 7 or more days late, Maine lets you end a tenancy at will on 7 days' written notice, and a written lease without its own termination terms can use the same notice. The notice must state that rent arrearage is the ground, state the amount of rent 7 or more days in arrears as of the notice date, and include the statute's paragraph word for word: "If you pay the amount of rent due as of the date of this notice before this notice expires, then this notice as it applies to rent arrearage is void. After this notice expires, if you pay all rental arrears, all rent due as of the date of payment and any filing fees and service of process fees actually paid by the landlord before the writ of possession issues at the completion of the eviction process, then your tenancy will be reinstated." It must also tell the tenant of the right to contest in court and attach the court's form notice, with the court's information sheet and mediation form. Unintentional clerical errors that do not mislead do not void it. Paying all rent due before it expires voids it; general assistance payments or written assurances count as cash. You may combine it with a 30-day notice. A lease cannot replace or waive this notice.

title: Notice Fees
bodyText: Maine has no statute that allows, caps or bans a fee charged to the tenant for preparing or serving a termination notice. Treat such a fee with caution. A lease may not require the tenant to pay your legal fees for enforcing the lease, and any term requiring a tenant to waive a statutory right is an unfair trade practice; whether a notice fee counts as a barred legal fee has not been settled by statute. A notice or service charge is not rent, so it cannot support a 7-day rent notice or be required to cure one, and a 7-day rent notice is voided by paying the rent due. What Maine does allow: a tenant at will who reinstates after a rent notice expires must pay the court filing fees and service-of-process fees you actually paid, and you may recover court costs as the court allows.

title: No Advance Waiver of Notice
bodyText: A Maine lease cannot shorten or waive the notice needed to end a tenancy at will. Either party may waive the 30-day notice in writing only at the time the notice is given, and at no other time before the notice is given, so a waiver signed in the lease or at move-in has no effect. The 7-day notices for listed grounds, including unpaid rent, are fixed by statute, and the rent notice must carry the statutory wording. Requiring a tenant to agree to a lease term that waives these rights is an unfair trade practice, and other notice periods, such as the 45-day and 75-day rent-increase notices, are expressly made non-waivable. A fixed-term lease may set its own termination terms for breach, but they cannot strip the tenant of the right to court process, the right-to-contest statement or the court's forms.

title: Nuisance Evictions and Abatement
bodyText: Nuisance matters to Maine landlords in two ways. As an eviction ground, a tenancy at will can be ended on 7 days' written notice if the tenant, the tenant's family or an invitee caused or permitted a nuisance within the premises, and a fixed-term lease can treat it as a breach under its terms; a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking victim cannot be evicted on a nuisance theory for that violence. As public abatement, places used as houses of ill fame, for illegal sale or keeping of liquor or scheduled drugs, or for lewdness or gambling are common nuisances. The Attorney General, a district attorney or 7 legal voters of the county may ask the Superior Court to abate one; the injunction runs against the building itself, and an owner may move to lift it after 6 months by proving the nuisance has ended. A tenant who uses the premises for those purposes forfeits the tenancy, and after a court declares a common nuisance you may take possession without further process or as the court orders. Keeping or allowing a declared nuisance is a strict-liability crime. Maine has no nuisance receivership or rent-escrow remedy and no rule requiring the lease to summarize these laws.

title: No Owner Move-In Rule
bodyText:
Maine has no statute giving an owner the right to end a lease early to move in, and none limiting it.

For a tenancy at will you may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice for any lawful reason, including moving in yourself, so long as it is not retaliatory or discriminatory. A fixed-term lease cannot be ended early for owner occupancy unless the lease itself reserves that right; Maine law does not supply one.

If you want the option, an opt-in lease clause should state the notice you will give (no less than Maine requires to end a tenancy at will is a sensible floor), that the tenant owes rent only through move-out, and that no fee or penalty applies to the tenant. Possession still requires the court process if the tenant does not leave.

Local ordinances may restrict owner move-in terminations.

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: Maine has no possession bond for residential evictions, at the end of a term or otherwise, and no confessed-judgment mechanism. The immediate-writ-on-bond procedure in Maine's eviction law applies only to commercial leases: there, a landlord who wins may get a writ right away by posting a surety bond to cover the tenant's damages if the tenant later prevails. In residential cases the writ issues 7 days after judgment. On appeal, the courts may require security, which can include a bond, an escrow account, a lien, a mortgage or an order to keep paying rent, to protect either party while the appeal is pending, and may waive or change it for good cause.

title: Late Move-In
bodyText:
Maine has no statute on what happens if you cannot deliver possession when a lease begins, for example because a prior tenant holds over or work is unfinished. The lease and contract law govern, so the lease should say whether rent abates, when the tenant may cancel and what refund is due.

Do not collect more up front than Maine allows (first month's rent, a deposit up to 2 months' rent and any properly disclosed mandatory recurring fee), and refund promptly if the tenancy never starts. If a prior occupant stays, remove them only through the eviction process.

During a tenancy, Maine has no general duty to provide alternate housing when a unit becomes unfit; a court hearing a habitability complaint may let the tenant move out temporarily during necessary repairs, owing nothing for use and occupation until returning, and will not charge you for the tenant's alternate housing if you offered reasonable alternative accommodations.

title: Belongings After the Writ
bodyText: After a judgment for possession, the writ issues 7 days later and is served by a sheriff or constable. If the tenant does not remove themselves and their belongings within 48 hours of service, the tenant is a trespasser and the belongings are treated as abandoned and handled under the abandoned-property procedure: store them in a safe, dry, secured place, mail written notice with proof of mailing (if the tenant is still in possession, the notice may not give less than 7 days after mailing or 48 hours after service of the writ, whichever is longer), release them free if claimed within 7 days and retrieved by day 14, and only then condition release on payment, sell at a reasonable price (surplus to the Treasurer of State) or dispose of items with no reasonable value. Animals left behind: you may contact a person the tenant authorized, a humane agent, animal control or a shelter to take the animal, and if you mail the tenant that person's name, phone number and address within 5 days you are not liable to the tenant for occurrences involving the animal. Maine gives no general immunity for executing the writ beyond these rules, and does not set a separate warehouse-storage option.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Maine's redemption right protects tenants at will evicted for unpaid rent. Paying the full rent due before a 7-day rent notice expires voids the notice. After it expires, and even after judgment, the tenant can reinstate the tenancy by paying all rental arrears, all rent due as of the payment date, and the filing and service-of-process fees you actually paid, at any time before the writ of possession issues (7 days after judgment); once that payment is made no writ may issue. Payment or a written assurance through municipal general assistance counts as cash. Maine sets no required wording for accepting partial rent and no limit on how often a tenant may redeem. Accepting money does not undo a 30-day termination before the writ issues, but accepting the full reinstatement amount in a rent case does. Fixed-term leases have no statutory redemption right. A tenant who appeals must pay the rent the statute requires to keep the writ stayed.

title: Rent Into Court on Appeal
bodyText: In a Maine eviction case, the tenant may not file a counterclaim, and the case may not be joined with any other action, so the tenant raises defenses (such as an unfit unit, retaliation or failure to accommodate) without paying rent into court first. Rent goes into court only on appeal. When a tenant appeals, the tenant must pay you, or the District Court if the rent is disputed, the unpaid portion of the current month's rent or the arrearage, whichever is less, and file an affidavit saying so with the notice of appeal. The Superior Court may stay the writ while the appeal is pending, but must condition the stay on those payments and on rent that comes due during the appeal, paid to you or into an escrow account held by the clerk if disputed; it may also require the tenant to refrain from nuisance or damage. If the tenant violates the conditions, the stay is vacated. A long adjournment of the trial does not itself require rent to be paid into court.

title: False Applications and Sealed Records
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that lets you end a tenancy specifically because an applicant gave false information on a rental application. A false application is handled through your lease terms and Maine's ordinary termination rules: a 30-day notice for a tenancy at will, or the breach terms of a written lease (and, if the lease has no termination term for a material breach, only the 7-day tenancy-at-will grounds, which a false application usually does not meet).

One Maine rule limits what counts as false. A person whose eligible criminal conviction has been sealed by court order may answer inquiries from anyone other than criminal justice agencies and authorized entities by not disclosing the conviction, with no sanction under Maine law, and a person whose juvenile case records are sealed may answer as if the juvenile crimes never occurred. Do not treat silence about a sealed conviction or sealed juvenile record as a misrepresentation or a lease breach.

Common-law fraud and rescission rules were therefore not reviewed.

title: Retaliation Presumption
bodyText: Maine presumes an eviction is retaliatory if you start it within 6 months after the tenant did any of these: asserted rights under Maine's rent-increase notice, rent-increase limit, habitability, radon or recurring-fee rules; complained in good faith to a code-enforcement body about the unit (or that body filed a notice of violation); asked you in writing, in good faith, for repairs required by code, the habitability law or the lease; filed a reasonably based fair housing complaint with the Maine Human Rights Commission or HUD before your eviction notice; told you before the eviction notice that the tenant or the tenant's minor child is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking; or reported sexual harassment by you or your agent before the notice. Asserting bedbug rights before the eviction notice also counts, except in evictions for unpaid rent or substantial damage. No writ of possession issues unless you rebut the presumption. It does not apply to evictions on the 7-day grounds or for a lease violation, unless the tenant used repair-and-deduct. Separately, no writ issues if the tenant proves retaliation for membership in a tenants' organization, and the Maine Human Rights Act bars retaliation for opposing discrimination. Keep a documented, legitimate reason for every notice and rent change.

title: No Seasonal Tenancy Rules
bodyText: Maine has no special rules for seasonal tenancies. A seasonal rental to someone who lives in the unit is still a lease or tenancy at will under Maine's landlord-tenant law, with the usual deposit, notice, habitability and eviction rules, and any estate longer than a tenancy at will needs a signed writing. A few rules turn on short stays. Radon testing does not apply to a building used only for short-term leases of 100 days or less with no renewal or extension. Anyone advertising or renting short-term lodging (transient occupancy such as a vacation rental, typically under 30 days) must show the total price including mandatory fees. Vacation rentals are excluded from state lodging-place licensing, and municipalities may regulate short-term rental units offered through rental platforms. Whether a short vacation guest is a tenant at all is not settled by statute.

title: Self-Help Eviction Banned
bodyText: Maine bans every form of self-help eviction: removing a tenant without the court eviction process is illegal and against public policy. You may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service to the tenant, including water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, sewerage, elevator or refrigeration, whether or not you control the service, except temporarily while actual repairs are under way or during a temporary emergency. You may not seize or deny the tenant access to the unit, or seize or hold the tenant's belongings, other than through proper judicial process. A court that finds an illegal eviction must award the tenant actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, or the tenant's costs and reasonable attorney's fees, or both, on top of any other remedy; a frivolous or harassing suit can bring a fee award against the tenant. Related floors: an unlawful or harassing entry costs actual damages or $250 plus an injunction, and if you fail to pay for utility service in your name the tenant may pay it and deduct it from rent, with damages of at least $100. A lease term allowing a lockout, shutoff or seizure is void. The only way to remove a tenant is a court judgment and a writ served by a sheriff or constable.

title: Military Tenants
bodyText: Maine's protections for military tenants work through the courts, not a lease-termination right. When a member of the National Guard or the Reserves of the U.S. Armed Forces is ordered to military duty under federal or state orders, you may not bring an eviction case for a home occupied mainly by the member, the member's family or other dependents except with the court's leave. The court may stay the case, on its own or on the member's motion, if military service materially affects the ability to pay rent, and may postpone full payment; you may ask the court for just relief, such as an order to pay the arrears after release from service. Maine's Servicemembers' Civil Relief Act also lets a court stay any civil case involving a Guard or Reserve member during service or within 60 days after, and requires remote testimony or an expedited hearing on the member's motion when duties prevent appearing. Maine has no statute letting a servicemember end a lease early, no shortened military notice and no deadline for deciding military applications. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which does give lease-termination rights, applies separately and was outside the searched corpus.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Maine has no rule giving a tenant a continuance or a defense in a nonpayment eviction because a social security check, other benefit or housing voucher payment arrived late. Related rules help such tenants. Payment or a written assurance of payment through the general assistance program, authorized by the State or a municipality, has the same effect as cash. A 7-day notice for unpaid rent is void if the tenant pays the full rent due before it expires, and in a tenancy at will the tenancy must be reinstated if, before the writ issues, the tenant pays all arrears, all rent due as of that date and the filing and service fees you actually paid. The statutory reinstatement right is written for tenancies at will. The court may grant a continuance for good cause shown and may refer the parties to mediation.

title: Statutory Termination Rights
bodyText: Maine sets several termination rights by statute that a lease cannot remove. For tenants: if a written lease has no termination or written-notice term for a material breach, the tenant may end it on 7 days' written notice when you have substantially breached it; victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, and tenants sexually harassed by you or your agent, may end the tenancy on 7 or 30 days' notice; either side may end it on 30 days' notice after a radon test at or above 4.0 picocuries per liter; a court finding a unit unfit may let the tenant end the agreement; and from January 1, 2030, a tenant who never received the signed energy efficiency disclosure may end the lease on 30 days' notice. For you: the lease may be treated as void at your option if the tenant is convicted of keeping the unit as a house of ill fame, and a tenant who changes the locks and refuses you a key may be given a 7-day notice. Missing paperwork also has consequences: a lease is unenforceable if you do not receive the tenant's signed total price disclosure when one is required, and no late fee may be charged without written notice at signing. Maine has no statute letting a tenant end a lease for your fraudulent misrepresentation.

title: Surrender at the End of the Term
bodyText:
When a fixed-term lease ends, Maine law does not require either side to give notice, and if the tenant stays you may file an eviction case without notice within 7 days after the term expires.

Several rules shape the hand-back.
- An estate in land can be surrendered only by a writing signed by the person giving it up, so put any early surrender in writing.
- If a tenant leaves early, you keep the right to rent and damages, reduced by what reasonable re-renting would bring, unless you expressly agree to accept the surrender and end the tenant's liability; entering to inspect, repair or show the unit, or re-renting it, does not by itself accept a surrender.
- For a tenancy at will the deposit is due back within 21 days after termination or your surrender and acceptance of the premises, whichever is later; for a written lease, within the period the lease states, not over 30 days.
- You may not charge the deposit for normal wear and tear, and belongings left behind must be stored and handled under Maine's unclaimed-property notice rules.

Maine has no good-cause renewal rule, but removal still requires a court judgment.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: In Maine, a tenancy without a written lease for a fixed term, including the usual month-to-month arrangement, is a tenancy at will; no estate in land greater than a tenancy at will can be created without a signed writing. Either side ends it with at least 30 days' written notice, and if the tenant has paid rent past that point the notice must run at least to the paid-through date. The 30 days can be waived in writing only when the notice is given, never in advance. You may instead give 7 days' notice for the listed grounds, and the two notices may be combined. Several rules differ from a fixed-term lease: the deposit is due back within 21 days after termination or surrender and acceptance, whichever is later; a tenant behind on rent can reinstate the tenancy before the writ issues by paying all arrears, current rent and your filing and service fees; a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may leave on 7 days' notice; and the smoking-policy notice may be a separate written notice. No reason is needed for a 30-day notice, but an eviction within 6 months after protected tenant activity is presumed retaliatory.

title: No Tenant Bankruptcy Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute on what happens to a residential tenancy, a security deposit or an eviction when a tenant files for bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law, including the automatic stay, governs that situation and was outside the searched corpus, so get advice before you serve a notice, start or continue an eviction, or collect pre-filing rent from a tenant in bankruptcy. The Maine rules that mention bankruptcy point the other way: security deposits must be held in an account beyond the reach of your own creditors, including a trustee in bankruptcy, and a defendant in a Maine action may plead a discharge in bankruptcy. Ordinary Maine eviction, deposit and unclaimed-property rules otherwise continue to apply.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: Maine law treats damage the tenant causes differently in several places. Substantial damage caused by the tenant, the tenant's family or an invitee, and not repaired before notice, is a ground for a 7-day termination notice. Tenant-caused conditions are excluded from the tenant's habitability remedies: the court complaint, the rent defense, the rent deduction and repair-and-deduct all require that the tenant or someone under the tenant's control did not cause the condition, and a tenant-caused violation does not block a rent increase. When a tenant leaves, a lease may charge reasonable repair costs for damage the tenant caused, and you may keep deposit money for damage beyond normal wear and tear, which excludes deterioration from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests. Maine's casualty rule bars rent claims only while fire or other unavoidable casualty leaves the unit unfit; the statute does not say whether a tenant-caused fire counts. One limit: a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking is not liable beyond the deposit for related damage when the perpetrator is a tenant and the victim gives notice and documentation within 30 days; you may still pursue the perpetrator.

title: Termination Notice Periods
bodyText: Maine notice periods depend on the tenancy. A tenancy at will, including month-to-month and week-to-week arrangements, ends on at least 30 days' written notice from either side, extended to the paid-through date if rent was paid past it; there is no separate weekly period. You may give 7 days' written notice for the listed grounds, such as rent 7 or more days late, substantial damage, nuisance, violence or an unauthorized occupant; a rent notice is void if the full rent is paid before it expires. A fixed-term lease needs no notice to end at expiration, and you may file without notice within 7 days after it ends; for a breach during the term follow the lease, or, if the lease has no termination or notice term for a material breach, a 7-day notice on one of the statutory 7-day grounds (there is no 30-day no-cause notice during the term). Notice periods cannot be shortened in advance: the 30 days may be waived only in writing when the notice is given. A 7-day notice must state the specific ground; every termination notice must tell the tenant of the right to contest in court and attach the judicial branch form notice. Serve in hand, or after 3 good-faith attempts by first-class mail plus leaving it at the home. Maine has no extra notice for elderly or disabled tenants, no payment-plan offer requirement and no mandatory nonrenewal notice.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: Maine has a specific rule on taking money after a termination notice. For a tenancy at will ended by a 30-day notice, accepting money, whether back rent or payment for current use and occupation, does not undo the termination up to the issuance of the writ of possession, so you may accept payments without waiving that notice. Be careful with rent for a period after the termination date: a terminated tenant is subject to eviction without further notice unless the tenant paid, after the notice was served, rent that accrued after the termination. A 7-day notice for unpaid rent is void if the tenant pays the full rent due before it expires, and a tenant at will who pays all arrears, current rent and your filing and service fees before the writ issues must be reinstated. If you accept money then, give a written receipt and a written reservation of rights. Re-renting, entering to show or repair, or using the unit while mitigating does not by itself accept a surrender.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that ends a lease when a tenant dies, sets a special procedure for a deceased tenant's belongings, or lets a lease name someone to collect the deposit or remove property.

A tenant's death does not by itself end the tenancy; deal with the estate's personal representative or heirs, give any termination notice the tenancy requires, and handle belongings left in the unit under Maine's unclaimed-property rules (safe storage, mailed notice, 7 days to claim). Return or account for the deposit under the usual rules to whoever is entitled on the tenant's behalf.

One rule is specific: you may require a tenant to give information about animals in the unit and the name of one or more people authorized to enter and retrieve an animal if the tenant dies or becomes disabled. If you then have an authorized person, humane agent, animal control officer or shelter take the animal and, within 5 days, mail the tenant notice of who has it, you are not liable to the tenant in a civil action for injuries or damage arising from the animal.

A contact-person clause for other purposes is optional.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Maine has no fast-track squatter procedure. To remove someone with no right to the unit, use the court eviction process, which may be brought against a person who took possession without right, and name "all other occupants" along with every adult on the lease or whose tenancy you acknowledged so the judgment reaches everyone. A tenant who lets an unauthorized person occupy gives you a ground for a 7-day termination notice. Criminal trespass law also applies: knowingly entering a dwelling place without license or privilege is a Class D crime, and remaining in a place in defiance of a lawful order to leave, personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person, is a Class E crime, so police may act against a trespasser who was never a tenant. You may also seek a criminal no-trespass order against a nontenant who commits domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking at the premises. Do not lock out or remove the belongings of anyone who may be a tenant or a tenant's household member: self-help eviction is illegal, with damages of at least $250.

title: No Agreed Method for Legal Notices
bodyText: Maine's landlord-tenant statutes do not let you and the tenant add an agreed method, such as a text message, that counts as legal notice where a statute requires notice. Each statute names its own method. Termination notices go to the tenant in hand, or, after at least 3 good-faith attempts, by first-class mail to the last known address plus leaving the notice at the tenant's home; a tenant ending a lease for your breach uses a similar fallback. Unclaimed-property notices go by first-class mail with proof of mailing, repair-and-deduct notices by certified mail with return receipt, and a deposit statement is complete when mailed to the tenant's last known address. Where a statute speaks of actual notice, such as notice of a defect to the person who customarily collects the rent, proof that the person actually knew is enough. Maine's electronic transactions law lets a mailing requirement in another law be varied by agreement only where that other law allows it, and the tenancy statutes do not allow it.

title: Addenda and Separate Documents
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that makes an addendum or other separate document control over the lease, so an order-of-precedence clause is a matter of contract.

Several Maine documents must sit outside the lease, and no precedence clause can override what they do.
- An agreement for you to provide heat below 68°F must be a separate written document, clear and conspicuous, in plain English and at least 12-point type, signed by both of you.
- The total price disclosure, required when the tenant pays any mandatory or optional recurring fee, is a separate statement signed by both of you, and the lease is unenforceable if you do not receive the signed copy.
- The energy efficiency disclosure and radon notice come before the lease or deposit, and the smoking policy may be in the lease or in a separate written notice the tenant acknowledges in writing.

Keep the lease and these documents consistent on rent, fees and terms.

title: Notices of Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: Maine's only statutory notices to tenants about a proceeding against the property come in foreclosure, and they fall on the lender. In a power-of-sale foreclosure the lender must give a copy of the foreclosure notice to any residential tenant it knows or should know of, by sheriff, first-class mail or posting at each entrance, and may not evict until it starts an eviction case at least 21 days after that notice. After a judicial foreclosure judgment the lender must give the tenant a copy of the judgment and written notice of all later proceedings through the sale. On request you must give the lender each tenant's name, address and other contact information. Maine has no statute requiring you to tell tenants about a tax lien, municipal lien, receivership or other claim against the property, or requiring a tenant to tell you about papers the tenant receives; a lease may require either.

title: No Automatic Renewal Rules
bodyText: Maine has no statute on automatic renewal of residential leases: no required reminder before a fixed-term lease renews, no limit on renewal terms and no formatting rule for renewal clauses. Maine's automatic-renewal law covers online subscriptions and health club memberships, not leases. If your lease renews itself, the renewal is a contract term, and any estate longer than a tenancy at will must rest on a signed writing. Maine has no statute on what tenancy arises when a tenant stays after the term with your consent; case law was not searched, so treat the holdover as a tenancy at will that needs 30 days' written notice to end. Any rent or mandatory fee increase at renewal still needs 45 days' written notice, or 75 days for increases totaling 10% or more in 12 months. State in the lease how and by when either side may stop a renewal.

title: Other Rules Maine Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states do not exist in Maine. (1) No statute bars renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy when you cannot deliver possession on the start date; the lease and contract law apply. (2) No statute makes compliance with the detector rules inadmissible or limits what an insurer may do; but if you did not know and had not been told that a smoke detector needed repair or replacement, your failure to repair or replace it may not be considered evidence of negligence in a later civil action for death, property loss or personal injury. (3) No statute gives you a special right to end a tenancy because the rental application was false, and an applicant may lawfully withhold a sealed conviction. (4) No Maine rule on a tenant's bankruptcy; federal law governs. (5) No statutory lease type-size, initialing or translation rule.

title: Whole-Code Checks
bodyText: Maine's statutes, 2025-2026 session laws, constitution, civil procedure rules and seven agency rules were searched, not only the landlord-tenant chapters, for three things landlords ask about. (1) Maine has no fast squatter-removal procedure: use the eviction process, which may be brought against a person who took possession without right, together with criminal trespass law. (2) Maine does require a receipt for cash: for each rent or security deposit payment made partly or fully in cash you must give a written receipt at the time, showing the date, amount, payer, period covered, whether it is rent or deposit, and the signature and printed name of the person receiving it; a rent card the tenant keeps can serve. This does not apply in an owner-occupied building of 5 or fewer units. (3) No state statute makes landlord registration or a rental license a condition of getting a possession judgment; some municipalities run registration or licensing programs, so check local rules. General business law can still hold up your case if you own through an out-of-state entity: an out-of-state corporation transacting business in Maine without authority may not maintain any court proceeding until it files an application for authority, and an out-of-state limited liability company conducting activities here without a statement of foreign qualification on file may not maintain a proceeding to collect its debts, such as unpaid rent; each also owes a $500 civil penalty for each year (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 13-C, §§ 1501-1502; tit. 31, §§ 1622, 1629). Owning property without more is not transacting business; whether renting it out is, and whether an eviction seeking only possession is a proceeding to collect debts, are case-law questions.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations
bodyText: Maine moved its protection-from-abuse law into a new chapter of Title 19-A in a 2021 recodification, and the landlord-tenant cross-references have been updated. The landlord-tenant definition of domestic violence now points to the current Title 19-A, section 4102 definitions of abuse, family or household members and dating partners, and stalking points to the criminal stalking statute. In 2025 the Legislature corrected the Maine Human Rights Act so that the protected class for people who sought and received a protection order refers to a final protection order under the current statute, an order under the former section, or a similar order from another state. If your forms, policies or screening criteria cite old section numbers, update them. Documentation a victim may give you includes a protection-from-abuse or protection-from-harassment complaint or order, a police report, a signed statement from an advocate, counselor, health care provider, mental health care provider or law enforcement officer, or a criminal complaint, indictment or conviction. A victim changing locks need not give documentation.

title: Electronic Leases and Signatures
bodyText:
Maine's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you sign leases and deliver required writings electronically, but only with a tenant who has agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and the parties' conduct.

An electronic record or signature cannot be denied effect just because it is electronic, and it satisfies a law requiring a writing or a signature. A tenant who agreed to transact electronically may refuse to do so for other transactions, and that right cannot be waived.

When a law requires you to deliver information in writing, an electronic record works only if the tenant can print or store it. If a statute requires a particular method, such as in-hand service, first-class mail, certified mail or posting, you must still use that method.

The Act excludes only wills and most of the Uniform Commercial Code, so it has no carve-out for eviction, default or cure notices; those notices simply keep their own statutory service methods. Keep a paper option for tenants who decline electronic signing.

title: No Emergency Contact Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency phone number, post a 24-hour contact or make tenants name an emergency contact. Related rules apply. Whoever is authorized to sign leases for the owner is the owner's agent for service of process and for receiving notices and demands, so tenants can always serve or notify that person. You may require a tenant to tell you about animals in the unit and to name people authorized to retrieve an animal if the tenant abandons it, dies or becomes disabled. In an emergency you may enter without the usual notice, and a tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy moves as promptly as conditions require. Giving tenants a working emergency contact is still good practice.

title: Entire Agreement and Lease Changes
bodyText:
Maine has no statute letting you amend an existing lease by notice to bring it into line with a new law, so a clause saying the lease may be changed only by a signed writing gives up nothing in Maine.

New laws apply on their own terms whatever the lease says, and a lease term that waives a Maine tenant right is unenforceable however it is worded.

Some documents must sit outside the lease and still bind you: an agreement for heat below 68°F must be a separate signed document, the total price disclosure is a separate signed statement, and the tenant's acknowledgment of the smoking policy may be separate. Write the entire-agreement clause so it includes those documents rather than excluding them.

Rent and mandatory recurring fee increases you are allowed to make still need 45 days' written notice (75 days for increases of 10% or more in 12 months), whatever the clause says about signed amendments.

title: Governing Law
bodyText:
Maine has no statute on governing-law or venue clauses in residential leases. A lease of a Maine dwelling should name Maine law.

Maine's landlord-tenant protections apply to the tenancy whatever the lease says: requiring a tenant to sign a term that waives a right under those chapters is an unfair and deceptive trade practice, and any waiver by a consumer of the Unfair Trade Practices Act is void. Eviction cases go to the District Court, which must hold the hearing within 10 days after the return day unless it grants a continuance for good cause. Do not use a clause choosing another state's law or courts to avoid Maine rules.

title: Mediation and Dispute Resolution
bodyText: Maine has no statute on lease clauses requiring the parties to try to settle informally before going to court. What Maine has is court mediation. In any residential eviction case the court may refer the parties to mediation on any issue at any time, the notice of termination and the summons must be served with the court's information sheet and mediation request form, and either party may ask for mediation. An agreement reached in mediation must be written, signed and approved by the court as an order. If a party fails to make a good-faith effort to mediate, the court may order mediation, dismiss, enter a default, award fees or impose another sanction. A lease clause that delayed your eviction case or the tenant's statutory remedies would risk being an unenforceable waiver of tenant rights. Commercial landlords and tenants may agree to binding arbitration of possession disputes; no statute gives residential parties that option, and whether Maine's consumer arbitration law, which covers contracts for goods or services, reaches residential leases was not resolved.

title: No Statewide Landlord Registration
bodyText: Maine has no statewide landlord registration or rental licensing requirement, no county or assessor registration, and no rule that an out-of-state owner must hire an in-state broker or keep an in-state contact for tenants. If you own through an out-of-state corporation or limited liability company, though, it must file with the Secretary of State, naming a registered agent or clerk, before it transacts business or conducts activities here (an application for authority or a statement of foreign qualification); owning property without more does not count, but renting it out may, and until the entity files it may be unable to sue (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 5, § 105; tit. 13-C, §§ 1501-1502; tit. 31, §§ 1622-1623, 1629; see `edu-owner-agent-me`). And a sole proprietor or partnership engaged in a mercantile enterprise under a name other than the owner's own must file a certificate with the town or city clerk before starting, on pain of a $5-a-day fine; whether renting out property is a mercantile enterprise is unclear (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 31, §§ 1, 2, 5). Some Maine municipalities run their own rental registration, licensing or inspection programs, so check the local rules where the property is. What state law does require: whoever is authorized to sign leases for the owner is the owner's agent for service of process and for notices, and certain disclosures (radon, energy efficiency, smoking policy, total price) must be given before the lease. Real estate brokerage licensing for third-party managers was not reviewed.

title: No Lease Completeness Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring every blank in a written lease to be filled in before signing, and no rule that an incomplete lease is a breach by you. Fill in or strike every blank anyway, because the terms Maine ties to the lease work only if the lease states them: the deposit return period (up to 30 days for a written lease), any late fee notice (required at signing for a fee up to 4% of a month's rent), termination or written-notice terms for a material breach (without them only the 7-day tenancy-at-will grounds apply), any prevailing-party attorney's fee term, and any term permitting disposal of abandoned property after the statutory notice. A blank or missing term usually falls back to the statute, not to your preferred figure.

title: No Lease Copy Duty
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no rule that failing to do so is a defense to enforcing it. Several copy rules sit nearby. The total price disclosure, when one is required, must be signed by both of you with a copy to each, and the lease is unenforceable if you do not receive the signed copy. You must keep the signed energy efficiency disclosure for at least 3 years. An applicant who pays for a screening check gets a complete copy of what it found. A surety or landlord must give the tenant copies of surety bond documents the tenant signs. If you file an eviction, a copy of any written lease and of the termination notice must be filed with the complaint. Give the tenant a signed copy of the lease anyway; it is the best evidence of the terms.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Maine statute requires a tenant to initial a lease term for it to bind the tenant; the signatures on the lease are enough as far as the statutes go. Initials cannot save a term the law forbids: a term waiving a tenant right under Maine's landlord-tenant chapters is unenforceable, and requiring it is an unfair trade practice. Two Maine documents have their own signing rules instead. An agreement for heat below 68°F must be a separate written document in at least 12-point type, signed by both of you. A tenant's written waiver of the 30-day notice before lead-disturbing repair work in a pre-1978 building must be in plain language, in at least 12-point boldface type, and must immediately precede the adult tenant's signature. Having a tenant initial an unusual but lawful term can still help show it was noticed.

title: Lease Length and Recording
bodyText: Maine sets no maximum or minimum length for a residential lease, and Maine's landlord-tenant protections apply to long leases as well as short ones. Length matters for recording: a lease for more than 2 years or for an indefinite term binds only you, your heirs and devisees and people with actual notice unless the lease, or a memorandum of lease naming the parties, describing the property, stating the date and term and describing any renewal, extension or purchase options, is acknowledged and recorded in the registry of deeds. Record it if the tenant needs protection against a later buyer or lender. Rent-to-own and option arrangements for a purchaser-occupied home of up to 4 units, where the occupant pays more than 4 times the monthly payment up front or is promised future ownership, are governed by a separate statute that requires a written contract with listed terms, including a habitability certification.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Maine requires a signed writing for any tenancy greater than a tenancy at will: no estate in land greater than a tenancy at will can be created, and no estate can be granted, assigned or surrendered, except by a writing signed by the person granting it or that person's attorney. An oral agreement for a fixed term therefore creates only a tenancy at will, ended on 30 days' written notice. Separately, no action may be brought on an agreement that is not to be performed within one year, or on a contract concerning an interest in land, unless the agreement or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party being charged. Electronic signatures satisfy these writing rules when both sides agreed to deal electronically. Maine has no long-lease exclusion from its landlord-tenant law, and its more-than-2-years rule is a recording rule, not a validity rule: an unrecorded long lease still binds you and anyone with actual notice.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Maine sets no minimum type size for a printed lease and no evidence rule penalizing small print in a lease. Type-size rules apply only to particular side documents. An agreement for heat below 68°F must be a separate, clear and conspicuous document in plain English and at least 12-point type. A tenant's written waiver of the 30-day notice before lead-disturbing work in a pre-1978 building must be in at least 12-point boldface type and immediately precede the adult tenant's signature. If a tenant buys a surety bond instead of paying a deposit, the surety's disclosure must show the word "nonrefundable" in at least 16-point bold type on the first page and again just above the tenant's signature line. Use a readable size for the whole lease anyway: the statutes that require plain, readily understandable disclosures show what a court will expect.

title: Lease Signer as Agent for Service
bodyText: Maine does not make a nonresident individual owner appoint an in-state agent or file anything before suing, and it does not require tenants to withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. An out-of-state entity is different. An out-of-state corporation transacting business in Maine must file an application for authority with the Secretary of State and may not maintain any court proceeding until it does; an out-of-state limited liability company conducting activities here must file a statement of foreign qualification, naming a registered agent or clerk, and may not maintain a proceeding to collect its debts, such as unpaid rent, until it does; and each owes a $500 civil penalty for every year it operates without filing (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 13-C, §§ 1501-1502; tit. 31, §§ 1622, 1629). Owning property without more is not transacting business; whether renting it out is, is a case-law question. And whoever you are, owning real estate in Maine lets a Maine court hear a claim arising from it, with the summons served on you personally outside the state (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 704-A(2)(C), (3)). Instead, one rule covers every owner, resident or not: anyone authorized to sign a residential lease or tenancy-at-will agreement for the owner is treated as the owner's agent for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. If a property manager or leasing agent signs your leases, tenants and courts may serve that person, so make sure the agent forwards papers promptly and that the lease gives a current address for notices.

title: How Notices Must Be Delivered
bodyText:
Maine prescribes how key notices are delivered, and a lease cannot substitute other methods.

Termination notices go to the tenant in hand; after at least 3 good-faith attempts, you may instead both mail the notice first-class to the tenant's last known address and leave it at the tenant's home. The statute does not limit who may serve a notice, but if it is served by an officer authorized to serve civil process, the notice is admissible to prove service and the server may testify remotely. A tenant ending a lease for your substantial breach uses the same fallback.

Unclaimed-property notices go by first-class mail with proof of mailing; repair-and-deduct notices by certified mail, return receipt requested; deposit statements are complete when mailed to the last known address; a deposit transfer on sale must be mailed to the tenant. Maine has no special e-mail notice addendum; electronic delivery works only with a tenant who agreed to deal electronically, only for documents the tenant can keep, and never where a statute names another method.

The court's information sheet and mediation form must accompany termination notices.

title: No Move-Out Form Rules
bodyText: Maine has no statute on a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to what the tenant's notice needs. A tenant at will ends the tenancy with at least 30 days' written notice, the same as you; a tenant ending a written lease for your substantial breach (when the lease lacks termination terms) gives 7 days' written notice. Do not use the form to obtain waivers: a term waiving a tenant right under Maine's landlord-tenant chapters is unenforceable, requiring it is an unfair trade practice, and a fee for the act of moving out is barred except reasonable re-renting costs when the tenant broke the lease's notice terms, unpaid rent, and repair costs for tenant-caused damage. One statute makes another document a notice to vacate: a condominium conversion notice that sets a vacate date and meets the eviction-notice rules also serves as the notice to vacate.

title: Rules That Depend on the Lease
bodyText: Several Maine rules turn on what your lease says, and a silent lease gets the statutory default. (1) Deposit return: a written lease may set a return period up to 30 days; a tenancy at will gets 21 days. (2) Breach: if a written lease has no termination or written-notice term for a material breach, either side may use the statutory route (the 7-day tenancy-at-will grounds for you, a 7-day notice for the tenant). (3) Late fees: none may be charged unless you gave written notice at signing that a fee up to 4% of a month's rent may apply. (4) Attorney's fees: only a prevailing-party fee after a contested hearing in cases of wanton disregard of the lease is allowed. (5) Abandoned property: the lease may let you dispose of it without liability if you follow the statutory notice steps. (6) Heat: the 68°F standard applies when the lease or agreement obligates you to provide heat. (7) Animals: you may make emergency entry to check on an animal a condition of the tenancy. (8) Property taxes: the half-sharing rule applies unless there is an agreement to the contrary. (9) Returned checks: a written agreement controls over the bad-check statute. (10) Smoking: the policy may go in the lease.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Maine's plain-language law for consumer agreements does not reach residential leases: it covers consumer loans and consumer leases of goods, not leases of housing. Maine has no readability test, no required statement listing the tenant's waivers and no Attorney General preapproval for residential leases.
