Plain-language rules do apply to particular landlord documents: the total price disclosure must be plain and readily understandable by the general public; an agreement for heat below 68°F must be readable in plain English; a tenant's waiver of the 30-day lead-work notice must be in plain language; and the court's eviction form notice is written in plain language. The Attorney General posts a model residential lease, updated every other year, that you may compare your lease against.

title: Building-Size Exemptions
bodyText: Maine's size tests look at the building, not how many units you own, and each uses its own test. (1) Owner-occupied building of no more than 5 dwelling units, one of which you live in: the cash-receipt rule, the tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy and the whole security-deposit chapter do not apply. Both parts must be met: a 6-unit building, or a 5-unit building you do not live in, gets no exemption. (2) Fair housing: the Maine Human Rights Act does not reach renting one unit of a 2-family dwelling you occupy, or up to 4 rooms in a one-family home you occupy, though advertising and other listed rules still apply. (3) The firearms rule for federally subsidized apartments excludes owner-occupied housing of 4 units or fewer. (4) The common-area utility rule applies to multi-unit buildings. (5) Rent-to-own rules cover purchaser-occupied homes of up to 4 units. Maine has no rule scaled to the size of your portfolio.

title: No Renter's Insurance Rules
bodyText:
Maine has no statute on renter's insurance in residential leases: nothing requires or forbids a renter's insurance clause, limits force-placed coverage or administrative fees, requires a notice that you do not insure the tenant's belongings, or requires a flood or renter's insurance notice before signing.

Related rules still matter. If the lease makes the tenant pay a cost, the total price disclosure (when one is required) must list any other cost the tenant will pay under the lease, so list a required policy's cost or a landlord-placed coverage charge there. A lease may not absolve you of liability for your own or your agent's negligence, so an insurance clause cannot shift that risk to the tenant's policy. Up-front money at move-in is limited to the first month's rent, the deposit and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees.

title: Tenant Property Losses and Insurance
bodyText:
Maine has no statute stopping you from pushing repairs that are your responsibility onto the tenant's renter's insurance, and no statute making you the insurer of the tenant's belongings.

Other rules set the limits.
- A lease or rule absolving you of liability for your own or your agent's negligence is unenforceable, and using it is an unfair trade practice, so a clause saying you are never liable for the tenant's property loss fails where you were negligent.
- Your repair and habitability duties cannot be waived except by a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction.
- In a bedbug treatment you need not replace the tenant's personal property, and you may not seize or hold the tenant's belongings outside court process.

A lease may ask the tenant to insure the tenant's own property and may say the tenant's insurer, not you, covers losses you did not cause.

title: Selling or Changing Management
bodyText: Selling a Maine rental, or changing who manages it, triggers several rules. Deposits: when your interest ends by sale, assignment, death, receivership or otherwise, whoever holds the deposits must either transfer them to the successor with an accounting and mail each tenant notice of the transfer, the new owner's name and address and the accounting, or return them to the tenants; on a sale this happens at closing, and the buyer then answers for the deposits. Tenancies: a buyer cannot evict a tenant at will without a termination notice from you or the buyer, and a lease binds a buyer with notice; a lease over 2 years should be recorded. Showings: the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry, on reasonable notice, to show the unit to purchasers or lenders. Information: you may share tenant personal information when reasonably necessary for a sale or refinancing. Condominium conversions need 120 days' notice and a purchase offer, and lease options trigger the seller property disclosure. Maine has no general duty to notify tenants of a sale or a new manager, other than the deposit-transfer notice and a 90-day notice before selling low-income rental housing (5 or more units with affordability restrictions or government financial assistance) in a way that ends those restrictions or assistance, and no rule on a receiver rejecting a residential lease.

title: What Maine's Landlord-Tenant Law Covers
bodyText: Maine's landlord-tenant chapters cover residential rentals of dwelling units, defined to include mobile homes, apartments, buildings and other structures rented for human habitation, with their common areas, under written leases or tenancies at will. Several arrangements fall outside or follow other rules. Hotels and motels: an innkeeper is not a landlord, and a hotel or lodging-house guest is not a tenant, under the landlord-tenant laws. Mobile home park lots follow their own Title 10 chapter. Commercial tenancies have a separate subchapter. A certified recovery residence with an approved discharge policy may discharge a resident without the eviction process when needed for welfare or safety. Employee housing is covered: eviction may be brought against a tenant whose occupancy is incidental to employment. Some rules also exempt owner-occupied buildings of 5 or fewer units. Maine has no farm carve-out, no long-lease exclusion, no population or county limits and no local-adoption requirement; municipalities may add ordinances.

title: Required Statutory Texts and Forms
bodyText: Maine prescribes verbatim text or official forms for side documents, not for the lease itself. Verbatim text: a 7-day notice for unpaid rent must include the statutory paragraph telling the tenant that paying the rent due before the notice expires voids it and that paying all arrears, rent due and filing and service fees before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy; an application may use the statutory sentence that the tenant may get a 12-month energy history from the supplier instead of a full energy disclosure; a tenant's waiver of the 30-day lead-work notice follows a statutory form in 12-point boldface. Official forms: the judicial branch form notice must be attached to every notice to terminate, the court's information sheet and mediation request form go with the notice and summons, and the radon disclosure uses the Department of Health and Human Services form. The Attorney General posts a model residential lease, updated every odd-numbered year, but its use is not required.

title: Tenant Portals
bodyText: Maine has no statute on tenant portals. Whether you may require tenants to sign, pay or receive notices through an online portal turns on general rules. Maine's electronic transactions law applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically; that right cannot be waived, so a lease term requiring every future signature or notice to go through a portal cannot take it away. Electronic delivery of a required writing works only if the tenant can print or store it, and notices with a prescribed method, such as termination notices, must still be served that way. If a tenant pays rent partly or fully in cash, you must give a written receipt unless the building is owner-occupied with 5 or fewer units. Any portal fee is a cost the total price disclosure must list, and an optional convenience fee must meet the optional recurring fee rules if it recurs. Offer a non-electronic way to pay and sign.

title: Tenant Records and Data
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to keep a rent ledger or give tenants one on request, though cash payments need written receipts (except in owner-occupied buildings of 5 or fewer units) and a 7-day rent notice must state the amount 7 or more days in arrears. Several rules govern tenant data. If you keep applicants' or tenants' names with social security, driver's license or state ID numbers, financial account numbers with access, or passwords in computerized form, Maine's breach-notice law applies: on learning of a breach you must investigate promptly and, if misuse has occurred or is reasonably possible, notify affected Maine residents within 30 days of learning of it and its scope, unless law enforcement requires a delay. You may not pass a consumer report to anyone other than the applicant it covers. You may require a social security number for a landlord background check. You and your agents may not disclose a tenant's or applicant's personal information to harass, intimidate or push them out without a legitimate business purpose; the penalty is actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater. Keep the signed energy disclosure for 3 years.

title: Notice of Changes to Terms and Fees
bodyText: Maine regulates notice for some changes but not others. Raising rent or any mandatory recurring fee needs at least 45 days' written notice; a rent increase of 10% or more, or increases that add up to 10% or more in 12 months, needs 75 days, except in deed-restricted affordable and subsidized housing. The 75-day rule speaks of rent, so a mandatory fee increase needs the 45 days. An optional recurring fee can be imposed only after written notice, before it starts, that the tenant may opt in and stop paying at any time without penalty. A fixed-term lease can be changed during the term only as the lease allows or by agreement. Maine has no statute on changing other terms of a tenancy at will, such as house rules, and does not treat such a change as a termination; to impose a new term over a tenant's objection, end the tenancy with 30 days' written notice and offer a new one, keeping in mind the retaliation presumption. Waivers of the increase-notice rules are void.

title: No Sunset on Tenant Laws
bodyText: None of Maine's core landlord-tenant statutes, the eviction, rental property and security deposit chapters in Title 14, carries a repeal or expiration date as of October 2026. The dated changes run forward instead. From January 1, 2030, a tenant who did not receive a signed residential energy efficiency disclosure may end the lease on 30 days' written notice, and you may not keep any fee or deposit for that termination except as the deposit statute allows. In the 2026 session the Legislature added the ban on disclosing a tenant's personal information to harass or push out a tenant and raised the minimum award for unlawful or harassing entry from $100 to $250. Plan for current rules to stay in force until the Legislature changes them, and check each session's laws.

title: No Translation Duty
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to translate a lease or notice into another language, even if you advertise or negotiate in that language, and no type-size and translation rules for leases. Maine's translation rules found in the search apply elsewhere, such as legal funding contracts. The documents Maine regulates must still be clear: the total price disclosure must be plain and readily understandable by the general public, and the heat agreement must be in plain English. If you negotiate in another language, giving the tenant a translation is good practice and helps show the tenant understood the terms; fair housing law bars treating applicants differently because of national origin.

title: Notices That Must Be Written
Assistance Animals
bodyText:
Under the Maine Human Rights Act you may not refuse to permit an assistance animal, or otherwise discriminate against a person with a disability who uses one, unless you show the animal poses a direct threat to others' health or safety, would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, or would substantially interfere with others' reasonable enjoyment of the housing. An assistance animal includes an animal that a physician, psychologist, physician associate, nurse practitioner, licensed social worker, licensed professional counselor or other licensed health professional with knowledge of the disability-related need has determined necessary to mitigate a disability (so untrained emotional support animals of any species count), and an animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks.

You may not charge a fee or deposit for it, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes.

A separate law gives a person with a disability who has a service animal full and equal access to housing without extra charge, and interfering with that right is a crime. Knowingly misrepresenting an animal as a service or assistance animal is a civil violation.

You are not liable for injuries or damage involving an assistance animal unless you were grossly negligent, reckless or at fault intentionally, or the animal is yours. Owner-occupied 2-family homes and some room rentals are exempt.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet Requirement
bodyText: Maine does not require you to give a tenant a state fact sheet about pets and eviction, or any pet-specific notice, when you know the tenant has a dog or cat. Maine does have related animal rules. You may require the tenant to tell you about animals in the unit and to name people authorized to retrieve an animal if the tenant abandons it, dies or becomes disabled, and you may make emergency entry to check on an animal's welfare a condition of the tenancy. If a tenant leaves an animal or cannot care for it, you may have an authorized person, humane agent, animal control officer or shelter take it and must mail the tenant notice within 5 days of who has it to gain liability protection. You may not seize or hold a tenant's pet as you may not seize other belongings, and you may petition the court about a dangerous pet.

title: Pet Deposits and Fees
bodyText:
**In Maine a pet deposit is a security deposit.** Any advance or deposit whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance counts, whatever you call it, so a pet deposit is subject to the deposit rules and must fit within the 2-month cap together with any other deposit, sit in a protected account and come back on time with an itemized statement.

At move-in you may collect only the first month's rent, the deposit and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees, so a one-time pet fee or nonrefundable pet charge cannot be collected up front. A monthly pet charge is either rent or a mandatory recurring fee; either way it must appear in the total price disclosure, and raising it needs 45 days' written notice.

You may not charge any fee or deposit for an assistance animal. Deposit rules do not apply in an owner-occupied building of 5 or fewer units, but the up-front limit and fee rules still do.

title: Pet Liability and Insurance
bodyText:
Maine has no statute on requiring a tenant to carry pet liability insurance.

Related rules frame such a clause. A dog's owner or keeper is liable for damage caused through negligence, and strictly liable when a dog injures a person off the owner's or keeper's premises; a keeper is anyone in possession or control of the animal. A court that finds a dog dangerous may order the owner or keeper to carry at least $100,000 in liability insurance for the dog's life. You may petition the court for protection against a dangerous pet on the premises.

If you require pet insurance, list its cost in the total price disclosure when one is required. Do not require insurance, a fee or a deposit as a condition of an assistance animal; the tenant is liable for damage the animal causes.

title: Pet Rules in Maine
bodyText:
Maine lets you allow, limit or ban pets by lease, with limits.

Assistance animals must be allowed unless a statutory defense applies, with no fee or deposit. A pet deposit counts toward the 2-month deposit cap, and no extra pet charge may be collected at move-in.

You may require the tenant to give information about animals in the unit and the names of people authorized to retrieve an animal, and may make emergency entry to check on an animal's welfare a condition of the tenancy; otherwise entry needs reasonable notice. You may not seize, remove or hold a tenant's pet outside court process, except by following the statute when a tenant has left the animal or cannot care for it because of death or disability.

You may petition the court for protection from a dangerous pet, and a pet that causes substantial damage or a nuisance can support a 7-day termination notice. Maine has no statute giving tenants of elderly housing a right to keep pets. A clause making the tenant liable for the pet's damage is fine; one absolving you of your own negligence is not.

title: Criminal Penalty for Refusing Service Animals
bodyText: Maine makes it a crime to deny or interfere with the housing rights of a person with a disability who uses a service animal. Under Title 17, a person who is blind, visually impaired or otherwise physically or mentally disabled and has a service animal, such as a service dog, is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations, may not be charged extra to keep it, and is liable for damage it does. Interfering with those rights is a Class E crime of strict liability, so good faith is no defense. Housing accommodations are defined broadly, including public and assisted housing, rental units, lodging places and condominiums, but exclude rentals in a building for no more than 2 families where the owner or the owner's family lives, and rooms rented by a resident owner or occupant. Separately, the Maine Human Rights Act bars refusing an assistance animal, with civil remedies. Lease no-pet rules must yield to both.

title: Misrepresenting an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Maine penalizes knowingly misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or an assistance animal, and the rule is not limited to particular places, so it reaches misrepresentations made to a landlord. Misrepresentation includes knowingly creating or providing documents that falsely say an animal is a service or assistance animal, fitting a non-service animal with a harness, collar, vest or sign used to mark service animals, and claiming an animal is a service animal when it has not completed training for disability-related tasks. It is a civil violation with a fine of up to $1,000 per occurrence, not a crime. Do not assume misrepresentation: an untrained animal that a qualified health professional has determined necessary to mitigate a disability is a legitimate assistance animal in housing. If you doubt a request, follow the fair housing accommodation process rather than accusing the tenant.

title: Charging for Parking
bodyText:
Maine has no statute requiring you to provide parking or setting how it is assigned, so parking is a lease term.

Maine's fee rules decide how you may charge for it. A parking charge paid on a set recurring basis under the lease is either part of the rent or a mandatory recurring fee, or, if parking is an added feature the tenant may take or drop, an optional recurring fee; an optional fee requires written notice before it starts that the tenant may opt in and stop paying at any time without penalty, and you may not end the tenancy because the tenant opts out. Any recurring parking charge goes in the total price disclosure, and increases in a mandatory fee need 45 days' written notice. No parking charge may be collected at move-in beyond the first month's rent, deposit and disclosed mandatory recurring fees.

A lease may not absolve you of your own negligence in the lot. Fines and removal of vehicles are covered separately.

title: Parking Fines and Notices
bodyText:
Maine has no rule requiring you to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, prescribing a heading, limiting mid-term changes or limiting what vehicle data you may ask for.

A 2025 Maine law does govern parking fines on property accessible to the public for parking. Anyone who owns, operates or manages such property may impose a fine, fee or charge for breaking a parking rule only if the amount is reasonable and conspicuously posted so it is visible at every entrance and exit of the lot, and only after written notice to the vehicle's registered owner giving the date and time, the rule broken, the amount, a due date at least 10 business days after the notice, payment instructions and a contact. Automated license plate readers are generally barred there. A violation is an unfair trade practice, with damages of 3 times the charge.

Whether a tenants-only lot is accessible to the public is not settled; if you fine for parking violations, follow these steps anyway and put the parking rules and fines in the lease.

title: Tenant Storage Space
bodyText:
Maine has no statute on storage space provided with a residential tenancy. Maine's self-service storage law lets storage facility operators assert a lien and sell stored goods after notice, but it is written for real property rented for individual storage spaces under a written rental agreement where occupants store and remove their own goods; whether it reaches a locker you lease as part of an apartment is not settled.

Treat tenant storage as part of the tenancy.
- You may not seize or withhold a tenant's property outside court process, and belongings left behind after the tenant moves out, including in storage, must be stored and handled under the unclaimed-property notice rules.
- Storage areas are common areas for the rule that a tenant may not be made solely responsible for common-area heat or utilities without a written agreement and rent reduction.
- A lease may not absolve you of your negligence for stored goods.
- A separate storage charge must follow the recurring-fee and disclosure rules.

title: Towing and Abandoned Vehicles
bodyText:
Maine has no private-property towing statute requiring signs, written tow authorization or rate caps, and no landlord kickback ban.

What Maine has is the abandoned-vehicle law. It covers a vehicle towed after being left on property without permission, or left on property without the permission of the owner or person in charge, and a vehicle left on an individual's residential property for more than 6 months. The owner of the premises, or the owner's agent, holding such a vehicle must notify the Secretary of State in writing on the state form; the Secretary notifies the owner and lienholder, and if they do not retrieve it and pay reasonable towing, storage and repair charges within 14 days, ownership passes to the premises owner (with newspaper notice when no record exists).

A tenant's own car parked with your permission is not clearly within this law, so enforce parking rules through the lease.

Parking fines on publicly accessible lots need posting and written notice. Police may remove vehicles parked illegally on public ways.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Maine has no rule requiring you to price parking separately from rent, to offer units without parking, or to let tenants opt out of a parking charge, except that a parking charge you structure as an optional recurring fee must let the tenant opt in and stop paying at any time without penalty. Maine's 2025 parking law points the other way at the municipal level: in a designated growth area a municipality may not require more than one off-street parking space per dwelling unit for residential development, and must let developers meet parking requirements through off-site parking agreements within a quarter mile. If you charge for parking separately, list it in the total price disclosure.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Maine gives tenants no right to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental. The only Maine charging-rights law, effective January 1, 2026, makes void any condominium or common interest community declaration or bylaw that prohibits or unreasonably restricts a unit owner's installation or use of a charger in a unit or limited common element parking space; it protects owners and long-term purchasers, not ordinary tenants, though it may affect what a condominium association can stop you, as a unit owner, from installing for your tenant. Whether to allow a tenant's charger is a lease and alteration question. If you agree, address who pays for installation, electricity and removal, and remember that a tenant may not be made solely responsible for electricity serving common areas without a written agreement and rent reduction.

title: EV Chargers at Move-Out
bodyText: Maine has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends: no rule on removal, restoration, reimbursement or transfer to you. Settle it in a written agreement before installation. Without one, ordinary rules apply: the deposit may cover damage beyond normal wear and tear but not normal wear and tear, the itemized statement and return deadlines apply, and personal property the tenant leaves behind is handled under the unclaimed-property notice rules. Whether a hard-wired charger becomes part of the building is a fixtures question for case law.

title: No EV Charger Installation Rules
bodyText: Maine sets no conditions for a tenant's installation of an electric vehicle charger, because tenants have no statutory right to install one. Conditions such as approval of plans, a licensed installer, permits, insurance, separate metering and payment terms are matters for your written agreement with the tenant. Two Maine rules shape that agreement: a recurring charge for charging access is either a mandatory or optional recurring fee and must appear in the total price disclosure (an optional fee needs written notice that the tenant may stop it at any time without penalty), and a tenant may not be made solely responsible for electricity serving common areas or other units without a written agreement and a rent reduction approximating the cost. The condominium charging law, which limits unreasonable restrictions by associations on unit owners, does not apply to tenants.

title: Shared EV Chargers and Common-Area Power
bodyText: Maine has no statute on electric vehicle chargers in shared parking areas of rental property. The rule that matters is Maine's common-area utility rule: in a multi-unit building you may not make one tenant solely responsible for electricity or another utility serving common areas or areas outside that tenant's unit unless you both agree in writing that the tenant will pay in return for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration approximating the actual cost. A shared charger wired to one tenant's meter therefore needs that written agreement, or separate metering on your account. A violation costs actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, and you are presumed to know when a tenant has been paying for common-area service. A charger fee paid on a predetermined recurring basis is a recurring fee that must be disclosed; a pay-per-use charge, like a coin-operated laundry fee, is not an optional recurring fee, though listing it in any total price disclosure is prudent.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText:
Maine treats medical and adult-use cannabis differently in rentals.

Medical: you may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for being a qualifying patient or caregiver, unless doing so would put you in violation of federal law or cost you a federal contract or funding. You may restrict administration or cultivation that is inconsistent with the general use of the premises, and you may ban smoking medical cannabis only if you ban all smoking on the premises and post notice of the ban there.

Adult use: Maine law lets adults 21 and over possess cannabis and grow up to 6 mature plants where they live, and consume it in a private residence, but gives tenants no protection against a lease that bans adult-use smoking, growing or other use. Anyone growing on land where they do not live and that they do not own needs the owner's written agreement. No one may make cannabis concentrate with an inherently hazardous substance, and you may not knowingly allow it on your property.

Your smoking policy disclosure should state how cannabis smoking and vaping are treated. Federal law was outside the searched corpus.

title: Common Areas
bodyText:
In Maine, common areas are part of the dwelling unit for habitability purposes: the implied warranty of fitness covers apartments and buildings including their common areas, and offering a unit for rent with a leak or chronic moisture outside the tenant's control that results in mold breaches it.

A tenant in a multi-unit building may not be made solely responsible for heat, electricity or other utilities serving common areas such as hallways, stairwells, basements, attics, storage areas or shared furnaces and water heaters, unless you agree in writing to a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration approximating the cost. A lease may not prohibit a renter from installing or using a clothesline or drying rack on leased residential property, except in property owned in common with third parties or condominium common elements, though reasonable safety and building-protection limits are allowed.

In federally subsidized apartments you may impose only reasonable restrictions on firearms in common areas. Maine has no statute giving tenants a right to waterbeds or other flotation bedding.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a disaster or declared emergency as guests notwithstanding the lease, and none limiting your remedies when a tenant does. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms control, but use them carefully: a person occupying the unit who is not an authorized occupant is a ground for a 7-day termination notice, so decide in writing whether you will allow emergency guests and for how long. Fair housing rules still apply to how you treat household members, and any occupancy limit must rest on reasonable local, state or federal occupancy restrictions. State disaster law deals with temporary housing provided by government, not with private tenancies.

title: Grills and Fire Safety
bodyText:
Maine's statutes contain no rule on grills, open-flame cooking or similar devices on rental balconies, decks or porches.

The State's open-burning law lets residential outdoor grills be used for cooking without a burning permit, but only when not prohibited by state rule or local ordinance. Fire-safety rules for buildings are adopted by the Commissioner of Public Safety through the State Fire Marshal's rules, which incorporate national fire codes, and municipalities may enforce local codes; those rules were not in the searched corpus and may restrict grills on multifamily balconies. Check the fire code edition in force and any local ordinance before writing a grill rule, and state your rule in the lease.

title: Firearms Rules
bodyText: Maine limits firearm rules only in federally subsidized apartments. A rental agreement or rule for a subsidized apartment (USDA rural rental assistance, or HUD voucher, new construction, substantial or moderate rehabilitation Section 8 assistance) may not require a tenant, as a condition of tenancy, to accept a ban or restriction on lawfully owning, using or possessing a firearm, firearm component or ammunition inside the tenant's own unit. You may impose reasonable restrictions on possession, use or transport in common areas that do not circumvent that rule, and tenants must store firearms with reasonable care. If you sue to enforce a prohibited term, the tenant, household member or guest may recover actual damages and attorney's fees. You are immune from civil liability for incidents involving firearms you must allow, except for willful, reckless or grossly negligent conduct. The rule does not apply to owner-occupied housing of 4 units or fewer or to restrictions federal or state law requires. For other rentals Maine has no statute on lease firearm rules; the constitutional right to keep and bear arms limits government, and no landlord parking-lot rule exists (the locked-vehicle rule binds employers).

title: Guests
bodyText:
Maine has no statute on tenant guests, guest stay limits or guest fees, so guest rules are lease terms, but several statutes turn on guests.

A tenant is responsible for guests and invitees in several ways: substantial damage, a nuisance or a violation of law by the tenant's invitee, and violence or threats by a guest against another tenant or you, are grounds for a 7-day termination notice, and a person occupying the unit who is not an authorized occupant is also a ground. Tenant-caused conditions, including those caused by guests, are excluded from the tenant's habitability remedies.

When you evict, name "all other occupants" with the adult tenants so the judgment reaches everyone. A long-staying guest whom you have treated as a tenant, for example by accepting rent, may become a tenant.

A guest-limit rule may not be used to discriminate on a protected basis or to penalize a victim of domestic violence, and Maine has no rule for live-in care providers.

title: No Guest Rights Statute
bodyText: Maine has no statute giving tenants or their guests, visitors or service suppliers a right of access in multi-unit buildings, barring guest fees, or limiting your control over who enters common areas. Guest rules are lease terms. Some limits still apply: you may not discriminate on a protected basis in the terms or privileges of a tenancy, including toward a tenant's associates; you may not refuse an assistance animal accompanying a person with a disability; a tenant may not be penalized for status as a medical cannabis caregiver; and rules that charge for guests must appear in the total price disclosure if they are recurring. You may seek a court order protecting the property or tenants against a guest who causes or threatens harm.

title: Keys and Lock Changes
bodyText:
Maine regulates locks rather than keys.

A tenant may not change the lock to the unit without notifying you and giving you a duplicate key within 48 hours. A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may change the locks at the tenant's own expense and must give you a duplicate key within 72 hours, without first providing documentation.

If a tenant changes a lock and you have no key, in an emergency you may enter by whatever reasonable means are necessary and charge the tenant reasonable costs for resulting damage; if a tenant refuses to give you a duplicate key, you may end the tenancy on a 7-day notice. You may not lock a tenant out or change locks to remove a tenant without a court judgment.

Key, fob or lock fees may not be collected at move-in beyond the first month's rent, deposit and disclosed mandatory recurring fees, but a lease may charge the reasonable cost of rekeying for lost or unreturned keys. Maine has no statute requiring you to rekey between tenants. These entry and lock rights cannot be waived in the lease.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Rules
bodyText: Maine has no statute on crime-free lease addenda, requiring tenants to cooperate with police, or limiting penalties for tenants who call for police or emergency help. Related rules shape any such clause. A victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may not be evicted because of incidents of actual or threatened abuse at the premises, or for reporting them, when the eviction would treat them as a nuisance, property damage or a lease violation. You may disclose tenant personal information to state, local or county law enforcement in exigent circumstances or as reasonably necessary to prevent or prosecute a crime, or in response to a valid subpoena or warrant. Criminal activity by the tenant or guests can support a 7-day notice when it is a violation of law regarding the tenancy, a nuisance, or violence or threats. One reporting duty binds every person, landlords and their staff included: anyone who becomes aware of a suspected medical examiner case, as when a tenant is found dead from an injury, poisoning or overdose, dies suddenly while in apparent good health, or has no physician able to certify a natural death, must immediately notify a law enforcement officer or the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, and no one may move or alter the body or objects at the scene before the medical examiner arrives or authorizes it (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 22, §§ 3025(1), 3026(1), 3027(1)). Maine's child and adult abuse reporting duties bind listed professionals, not landlords as such, though anyone may report (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 22, §§ 4011-A(1), (3), 3477, 3479).

title: No Political Access Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to give political candidates or campaign workers access to your building, to allow voter-registration materials, or to permit political signs in rentals. The only sign protection found covers condominium and similar unit owners: an association may not bar a unit owner from displaying a sign supporting or opposing a candidate or referendum question during the period from 6 weeks before to one week after the election. It does not protect tenants. Political sign and access rules for tenants are therefore lease terms, though you may not apply them in a way that discriminates on a protected basis.

title: No Portable Cooling Right
bodyText: Maine gives tenants no right to install a portable or window air conditioner or other cooling device, and requires no lease statement about such limits. You also have no duty to provide air conditioning: Maine's temperature standard is a heating standard that applies when the lease or agreement obligates you to provide heat. Whether to allow window units is a lease term; if you allow them, address installation, weight, window safety and who pays the electricity. Keep in mind that a tenant may not be made solely responsible for electricity serving common areas without a written agreement and rent reduction.

title: Solar Devices and Clotheslines
bodyText: Maine's solar rights law protects renters only for clothes drying. A contract, lease, rule or similar binding instrument adopted after September 30, 2009 may not prohibit a person from installing or using a clothesline, drying rack or other solar clothes-drying device on residential property the person leases or rents, though it may impose reasonable restrictions needed for safety and evacuation, to protect buildings from damage, for historic or aesthetic values when a comparable alternative exists, or for shoreland zoning, and may ban such devices on property owned in common with third parties or condominium common elements. The protection for solar collectors such as panels covers owners, not renters, so a lease may restrict a tenant's plug-in or balcony solar device. A 2026 Maine law lets any electricity customer, including a tenant, install small plug-in solar or battery systems without utility approval, and requires a customer who does not own the building to avoid structural or code harm and restore the building on removal; it governs the utility relationship and does not bar a lease restriction.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to tell tenants where and how to recycle, or to provide recycling at a rental. Recycling and trash collection are usually set by municipal ordinance and your contracts with haulers, so check local rules. Two Maine rules touch trash: normal wear and tear does not include the cost of removing trash and other articles the tenant abandons, so you may charge the deposit for that removal, and a tenant may not be made solely responsible for utilities serving common areas without a written agreement and rent reduction. A recurring trash or recycling fee charged to tenants is a fee that must appear in the total price disclosure.

title: No Religious Display Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on a door frame, and no statute giving tenants a right to fly the United States flag. Display rules are therefore lease terms, subject to fair housing law: you may not discriminate because of religion, national origin, ancestry or another protected class in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, so a display rule must be neutral and applied to everyone, and a rule that singles out religious items invites a discrimination claim. A request to keep a disability-related item may call for a reasonable accommodation.

title: House Rules
bodyText:
Maine has no statute setting when house rules bind a tenant or limiting mid-tenancy rule changes, so rules work through the lease.

Several Maine rules reach them.
- The unfair-agreement list applies to rules as well as leases: a rule that absolves you of your negligence, makes the tenant pay your legal fees (except a prevailing-party award after a contested hearing for wanton disregard), puts a lien on the tenant's property, makes the tenant acknowledge the rules are fair and reasonable, charges a fee for moving out, or imposes recurring fees in violation of the fee rules is unenforceable, and using it is an unfair trade practice.
- A rule that waives a tenant right under Maine's landlord-tenant chapters is likewise barred.
- Rent and mandatory recurring fee changes need 45 or 75 days' written notice.
- Enforcement of a rule violation is a lease violation, and the retaliation presumption does not apply to evictions for a lease violation unless the tenant used repair-and-deduct.

For a fixed-term lease, a new rule binds the tenant only as the lease provides; for a tenancy at will, a new rule can be imposed by ending the tenancy on 30 days' notice and offering new terms.

title: Smoke Drift Between Units
bodyText: Maine has no statute on lease clauses waiving tenant claims over smoke drifting from other units. Several rules frame the question. Your smoking policy must be disclosed in writing before the lease or deposit and acknowledged by the tenant, but a tenant may not sue you solely because another tenant broke the smoking policy, or solely because you failed to give the disclosure. A lease may not absolve you of liability for your own or your agent's negligence. Maine's public-places smoking ban covers enclosed areas into which the public is invited or allowed, not private residences. Maine's workplace smoking law requires employers to adopt a written policy banning indoor smoking in any structurally enclosed location where employees perform services, and the definition does not exclude residential buildings; whether a common hallway where your staff work is covered was not resolved. Banning smoking in common areas, and stating that in the smoking policy, avoids the question.

title: No Snow Removal Statute
bodyText:
Maine has no statute that says whether a landlord or a tenant must clear snow and ice at a rental property, so the lease decides.

The library's snow removal clause, which has a tenant clear only the walks, parking and access areas the tenant uses and not areas shared with other residents, can be used in Maine.

Three Maine rules limit what the lease can do.
- Your duty to keep the unit, including its common areas, fit for human habitation cannot be shifted to a tenant except by a written agreement for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration, so keep shared areas and exits your responsibility.
- A lease term excusing you from liability for your own or your agent's negligence, for example for an icy common walkway, is unenforceable and an unfair trade practice.
- And towns may adopt ordinances requiring the owner, occupant or agent in charge of property next to a public sidewalk to clear snow and ice from it, and ordinances requiring roof guards against falling snow and ice, so check the local ordinance and say in the lease who handles the public sidewalk.

title: No Tenant Display Rights Statute
bodyText: Maine has no statute giving tenants a right to display a flag, political sign or banner at a rental, and none stopping a landlord from restricting such displays or requiring a landlord to consent before a sign is posted (a condominium association may not bar a unit owner's election signs from 6 weeks before to one week after an election, but that protects owners, not tenants). Your lease or rules may therefore set reasonable, neutral display rules, such as where flags and signs may go and how they are attached, applied the same way to everyone. Apply them evenly: a rule enforced only against displays tied to a tenant's religion, national origin or other protected characteristic can be housing discrimination under the Maine Human Rights Act. One related Maine rule does limit leases. A contract or similar agreement made after September 30, 2009 may not stop a renter from using a solar clothes-drying device, such as a clothesline or drying rack, on the rented residential property, though it may impose restrictions needed for safety, to protect the building from damage, or for historic or aesthetic values when a comparable alternative is available, and may bar devices on property owned in common with others or on condominium common elements. Cable and antenna access has its own rules (see the telecom access row).

title: Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: Maine has no landlord-tenant statute on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells, so the lease may set reasonable rules, for example requiring your consent before anything is attached to the building, limiting cameras to the tenant's own unit and entry, and requiring repair of mounting holes at move-out. General Maine laws apply to everyone, including you and your tenants. It is a crime to install or use, without consent, a device for observing, photographing or recording in a private place where a person can reasonably expect to be safe from surveillance, such as a bathroom, or to aim a device from outside at sounds or images in such a place that would not ordinarily be visible or audible outside it. Recording other people's private conversations with a device, when the recorder is not a party to them, can be an illegal interception, which matters for doorbell cameras that record audio. A separate 2025-amended law bars placing an unattended recording camera outside on another person's private property without the landowner's written consent and lets the landowner remove it; whether it reaches a tenant's camera on the rented premises was not resolved, so address exterior and common-area cameras in the lease. The same privacy laws bar you from placing cameras inside a tenant's unit.

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Maine has no statute on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in rentals, so the lease may allow, prohibit or condition them. If you allow one, Maine's money rules limit what you can collect. Any extra deposit for a waterbed, whatever you call it, is a security deposit: its primary function is to secure the tenant's performance, so it counts toward the cap of 2 months' rent for all deposits and must be returned or itemized on the usual schedule (within the time in a written lease, not over 30 days, or 21 days for a tenancy at will). These deposit rules do not apply to a unit in a building of 5 or fewer units where you live in one. At move-in you may not collect more than the first full month's rent, the security deposit and any properly disclosed mandatory recurring fee, so a separate waterbed fee due at signing is not allowed. A requirement that the tenant carry insurance covering water damage, and a promise to pay for damage the tenant causes, are ordinary lease terms that no Maine statute regulates.

title: No Association Disclosure to Tenants
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring a lease of a condominium or other association unit to disclose the association's obligations, budget or governing documents to the tenant. The Maine Condominium Act's resale disclosure, in which a selling owner furnishes the declaration, bylaws, rules and a certificate on assessments, fees and pending suits, runs only to a purchaser, and the Act's definition of purchaser excludes anyone acquiring a leasehold interest of less than 20 years, so an ordinary residential tenant is not owed it. Because your tenant must still live within the association's rules, give the tenant a copy of the declaration's use and occupancy restrictions and the current rules and regulations before signing, and say in the lease which association charges, if any, the tenant will pay. Any association-related charge the tenant pays you on a recurring basis must also appear in the signed total price disclosure.

title: Condominium Rental Restrictions
bodyText: If your rental is a condominium unit, the association's governing documents can limit how you rent it, and Maine law adds little on top. The declaration must state any restrictions on use, occupancy and alienation of units, and the association may adopt rules, regulate the common elements, charge for use of common elements and, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, levy reasonable fines for violations of the declaration, bylaws and rules. Fines and late charges are assessed against you as unit owner and become a lien on the unit, collectible like assessments. Maine has no statute capping association lease-approval fees, regulating an association-held tenant deposit, letting an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments, or limiting what tenant information an association may require. An amendment that changes the uses to which a unit is restricted needs unanimous owner consent, but whether a new leasing restriction counts as such a change was not resolved. Check the declaration, bylaws and rules before you sign a lease, and make the lease consistent with them.

title: Association Rules and Tenants
bodyText:
When you rent out a condominium unit, the association's declaration, bylaws and rules bind you as owner, and under Maine's Condominium Act the association may impose late charges on assessments and, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, levy reasonable fines against you, and holds a lien on your unit for them.

For condominiums still governed by Maine's older Unit Ownership Act, the statute itself makes tenants of unit owners subject to the declaration and bylaws. For other condominiums, the tenant's duty to follow association rules comes from your lease, so the library's association compliance clause does the work, and it should be paired with a copy of the rules given to the tenant before signing.

Maine has no statute on passing association fines to a tenant; a lease term making the tenant reimburse fines caused by the tenant's own violations is an ordinary contract term, but it is not rent, so it cannot support a 7-day notice for nonpayment of rent. Maine has no statute letting an association collect rent directly from your tenant.

Satellite dishes and antennas installed by a service operator in a building with 2 or more apartments are governed by Maine's tenant cable and antenna access law.

title: Bed Bug Law: Coverage and Retaliation
bodyText:
Two points about Maine's bed bug law are easy to miss.

First, it has no small-landlord or single-family exemption: the disclosure, inspection and treatment duties apply to every landlord of a dwelling unit, including an owner who lives in the building and a landlord renting a single house, unlike some other Maine rules that exempt owner-occupied buildings of 5 or fewer units. The pre-rental disclosure covers adjacent units currently infested or being treated, and, on request, the last date the unit and adjacent units were inspected and found free of bed bugs.

Second, the law protects tenants who use it. If a tenant asserted rights under the bed bug law within 6 months before you start an eviction, and before being served with the eviction notice, the court presumes the eviction is retaliatory; you can rebut that presumption, and it does not apply to an eviction for nonpayment of rent or for substantial damage to the premises. Document the reason for any notice you give to a tenant who has recently reported bed bugs.

Your other duties, the tenant's duties and the penalties are summarized in the bed bug duties row.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to disclose a certificate of occupancy to a tenant or attach one to the lease. The certificate still matters before you rent. In a municipality of more than 2,000 inhabitants, a building may not be occupied until the building official has given a certificate of occupancy after the required inspections, and in such a municipality that has adopted or enforces the Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code, a certificate showing compliance with that code. An owner who lets a building be occupied without the certificate is penalized under the state's land use enforcement law, unless an appeal later finds the building complied. So for new construction, conversions or other work that requires a certificate, make sure it has been issued before a tenant moves in; local ordinances may add their own occupancy permit or rental certification requirements.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall to a tenant. Two general rules still apply. If drywall or any other building material creates a condition that endangers or materially impairs the health or safety of tenants, it can breach the implied warranty that the unit is fit for human habitation, which no lease can waive except by a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration. And if you rent under a lease with an option to purchase a property of 1 to 4 units, Maine's seller disclosure law applies to that transaction, and its property disclosure statement must list any known defect, meaning a known condition that significantly affects value, significantly impairs the health or safety of future occupants, or significantly shortens the premises' normal life.

title: No Flood Disclosure for Leases
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant whether a rental is in a flood zone or has flooded before, and no state form, rider or tenant termination right tied to flood risk. Maine's flood disclosure applies to sales. For residential property of 1 to 4 units, the seller's property disclosure statement must say whether the property is in a FEMA-mapped special flood hazard area, with the flood zone and a copy of the map panel, and whether the property flooded, had flood damage, flood insurance claims or flood-recovery aid during the seller's ownership. That statement is required for a lease with an option to purchase, so if you give a tenant a purchase option you must provide it. For an ordinary lease, flood history still matters: offering a unit where a leak or flooding outside the tenant's control has led to mold growth breaches the warranty of habitability, and while flooding or other unavoidable casualty makes the unit unfit you cannot recover rent for that period. Telling prospective tenants about known flood risk is good practice.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to tell a prospective or current tenant that the property is in foreclosure or that your mortgage is in default, and no form or lease statement for it. Maine puts the notice duty on the foreclosing lender instead. In a power-of-sale foreclosure, the lender must give a copy of the foreclosure notice to any residential tenant it knows or should know of, and cannot evict the tenant except through an eviction case begun at least 21 days after that notice. After a judicial foreclosure judgment, the lender must give tenants a copy of the judgment and written notice of all later proceedings, and may evict only through an eviction case after that notice and after the redemption period ends. Your part is to give the lender your tenants' names, addresses and other contact information when it asks. Although no statute requires it, telling an applicant about a pending foreclosure before signing avoids a later claim that you hid a material fact.

title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: Maine has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so it has no notice telling a tenant whether the unit is covered by one, and nothing of that kind belongs in a Maine lease. A tenancy at will can be ended by either party on at least 30 days' written notice without stating a reason, and a fixed-term lease ends under its own terms. Every termination notice must tell the tenant of the right to contest the termination in court, and you must attach the judicial branch's form notice to any notice to terminate. Some limits work like cause rules: an eviction begun within 6 months after a tenant asserted certain statutory rights, complained to a code enforcement body or to you about required repairs, filed a fair housing complaint, or told you the tenant or the tenant's child is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking is presumed retaliatory unless it rests on a 7-day ground or a lease violation; no eviction may proceed in retaliation for membership in a tenants' organization; and a bona fide tenant of a building in foreclosure may be removed only as the federal foreclosure tenant law allows. Portland and South Portland have local rent ordinances; check them.

title: Environmental Covenants and Tenants
bodyText: Maine's statutes do not require a landlord to put a recorded environmental use restriction into a residential lease or to give tenants a contamination disclosure, but a cleanup covenant on your property can still reach your tenants. Under Maine's Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, a covenant approved by the environmental agency for a contaminated site runs with the land, binds later owners and occupants, and must be given, in the manner the agency requires, to each person in possession of the property. A covenant may itself require notice when a specified interest in the property is transferred, which could include a lease. The environmental agency has no posted rule implementing the Act, so the notice method depends on the covenant itself; check the registry of deeds for any environmental covenant on the property and follow its notice terms. If a covenant limits use, for example banning a private well, gardening or digging, write those limits into the lease so tenants know them. For a lease with an option to purchase a 1-to-4 unit property, the seller disclosure statement must also list known hazardous materials such as asbestos, lead paint, radon, underground oil tanks and methamphetamine. The environmental agency's rule list was searched at sync and has no rule on covenants.

title: No Code Order Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to tell a prospective tenant about outstanding code inspection reports, violation notices or condemnation orders on the property. Several rules make hiding them risky. You may not knowingly rent a dwelling that the state health department has posted and ordered cleared of lead-based substances, unless the department grants a waiver. A town may, after notice and hearing, adjudge a building a nuisance or dangerous, for example structurally unsafe, unsanitary, a fire hazard or unsuitable for its use, and record an order for its disposal. A tenant can sue, or defend a rent case, when a condition makes the unit unfit for human habitation and you fail to fix it after notice, and a tenant's good-faith complaint to a code enforcement body within 6 months before an eviction raises a presumption of retaliation. And misleading a prospective tenant about the unit's condition can be an unfair trade practice. If an order affects the unit, the practical course is to disclose it in writing before signing and not to rent the unit until it is lifted.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to show proof of insurance to tenants or a town, or to register rentals with the state. Some Maine towns run local rental registration or licensing programs that may ask about insurance, so check the municipality. Insurance does come up indirectly. If you treat bed bugs, you must use a certified pest control agent that carries current liability insurance. And Maine's surety bond option for tenants is not insurance for the tenant: a surety bond a tenant buys instead of a deposit protects you against loss, you may offer but not require it, and the bond and any deposit together may not exceed 2 months' rent. Carrying adequate property and liability coverage, and deciding whether to require renter's insurance in the lease, are business choices Maine law leaves to you. A lease term excusing you from liability for your own negligence is unenforceable, so insurance, not the lease, is where you manage that risk.

title: Maine Lead Notices
bodyText:
Maine requires no state lead notice, certificate or information packet at lease signing, and none at renewal; the state lease-stage lead disclosure was repealed in 2011, so the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for pre-1978 housing (the library's lead disclosure clause) is the notice to give.

Maine's own lead notice duty comes during the tenancy. Before you, or anyone you hire, carry out repair, renovation or remodeling that may disturb painted surfaces in a pre-1978 residential building with rented units, you must give at least 30 days' notice of the work and the risk of an environmental lead hazard by posting a sign on the building's exterior entry doors and sending notice by certified mail to every unit. A shorter period is allowed only if one adult tenant in each unit signs a written waiver and acknowledgment in the statutory 12-point bold form, with the sign still posted.

Emergency repairs are exempt. Each violation can bring a civil fine of up to $500. When the state health department finds a lead hazard, it posts its own notice, which you must leave in place.

title: Lead Hazard Orders and Relocation
bodyText:
Maine's Lead Poisoning Control Act adds duties that start when the state health department finds a lead hazard.

The department may inspect a dwelling on reasonable grounds, at an owner's or a child-occupant's request, or after a reported lead poisoning, and when a case of lead poisoning or lead-based substances is found it must inspect every unit in the building within 30 days (owner-occupied single-family homes excepted). If it finds an environmental lead hazard, it posts notice, tells all occupants, orders you to remove, replace or securely and permanently cover the lead within 30 days (extensions possible) and may order interim controls.

Until the work is done you must move tenants to a lead-safe substitute unit, paying moving costs and any extra occupancy charges, unless the department waives this. You may not evict a family with children because unsuspected lead is discovered, and you may not knowingly rent a posted unit until it is cleared.

Lead abatement must be done by licensed or certified people, and owners of pre-1978 rentals may do essential maintenance practices under environmental rules. Maine gives no liability shield for following maintenance standards, and violations are a Class E crime plus administrative penalties up to $500 a day.

title: Voluntary Lead-Safe Registry
bodyText: Maine has no lead-safe certificate that must be obtained for a rental or attached to a lease. Instead, the state health department keeps a voluntary registry of leased residential dwellings built before 1978 that their owners designate as lead-safe. Joining is up to you: you apply with a report from a licensed lead inspector showing the dwelling was tested for lead-based paint and lead-contaminated dust, or from a lead dust sampling technician showing it was tested for lead-contaminated dust, and the report must show the dwelling meets the department's standards. Lead-safe means the dwelling does not contain lead at a level or in a condition that is an environmental lead hazard. Registry listing does not replace the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet for pre-1978 housing, Maine's 30-day notice before renovation work, or your duties if the department later finds a hazard. If you are listed, you may mention it in the lease or advertising, but keep the testing report on file.

title: Energy Efficiency Disclosure
bodyText: Maine has no meter conservation charge or similar energy-efficiency surcharge on a utility account that a landlord must disclose to new tenants or offset against rent; residential PACE financing is a mortgage-type assessment on the owner's property with no tenant notice rule. What Maine does require is an energy efficiency disclosure. If you rent a unit that will be a tenant's primary residence and the tenant will pay for an energy supply, you must give the residential energy efficiency disclosure statement prepared by Efficiency Maine Trust and the Maine State Housing Authority before the tenant signs or pays a deposit, sign it, get the tenant's signature and keep it for 3 years; you must also give it to anyone who asks in person. Instead, you may list each prior energy supplier in the application with the statutory sentence telling the applicant of the right to a 12-month consumption and cost history, which electric and gas utilities must provide free on request. Starting January 1, 2030, a tenant who did not receive a signed statement may end the lease on 30 days' written notice, and you may not keep any fee or deposit for that termination except as the deposit law allows.

title: No Electric Submetering Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute that authorizes or regulates landlord submetering of electricity to residential tenants, and none prescribing a submetering disclosure, form or notice at lease signing. Maine's utility law expressly allows electric submetering only at campgrounds, where the charge is capped at the owner's own per-kilowatt-hour cost and the submeter user is not a customer of the utility, and at electric vehicle charging stations. Whether a landlord who submeters a building would be treated as reselling electricity was not resolved, so get advice before setting it up; the usual Maine approach is a separate utility meter and account for each unit. If you do bill a tenant for electricity, it is a utility service cost, not rent: it must appear in the signed total price disclosure whenever one is required, and it cannot support a 7-day notice for unpaid rent. A tenant who will pay for electricity is also entitled to the energy efficiency disclosure statement before signing.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Maine has no required utility disclosure that must be attached to a lease when you apportion shared-meter costs, no water submeter certificate, and no notice of energy-improvement charges on a tenant's utility tariff. The disclosures Maine does require reach the same ground. Before signing, give a signed total price disclosure listing rent, any mandatory or optional recurring fee, any utility service costs the tenant will pay and any other cost under the lease, whenever the tenant pays a recurring fee; if you cannot get the utility costs, you may give a completed energy efficiency disclosure statement instead. Give a tenant who will pay for an energy supply the energy efficiency disclosure statement in any case. If a tenant's utility would be paying for heat, electricity or another utility serving common areas or other units, you need a written agreement for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration approximating the cost, or you owe actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus fees. Any utility account in your name is your responsibility.

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to disclose to a tenant that a rental was used to make methamphetamine, no cleanup or decontamination standard for former drug labs, no ban on re-occupancy, and no duty for a landlord to report a suspected lab to police within a set time. Maine's methamphetamine disclosure applies to sales: for 1 to 4 unit residential property, the seller's property disclosure statement must report the presence or prior removal of methamphetamine, and that statement is required for a lease with an option to purchase. For an ordinary lease, other rules still matter. A unit contaminated by drug manufacturing can breach the warranty that it is fit for human habitation. A building where an owner or occupant trafficked or furnished scheduled drugs on 2 or more occasions within 3 years can be declared a common nuisance, with an injunction that runs against the building, and keeping a declared nuisance is a strict-liability crime. And a tenant who violates the law regarding the tenancy can be given a 7-day termination notice. Treat a suspected former lab as a habitability problem: have it assessed and cleaned by qualified professionals before re-renting, and disclose what you know.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a military installation, airport or air base, or within a noise, clear or accident potential zone, and no tenant termination right tied to such a location. No Maine law creates a military impact district with lease disclosures. If a property is near an active airfield or training area, telling prospective tenants about noise and flight activity before signing is good practice and helps avoid a later claim that you hid a material fact, since misleading a consumer is an unfair trade practice in Maine. Local zoning or airport overlay ordinances may impose their own requirements; check the municipality.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Maine has no lease disclosure for a former military ordnance or munitions site near the property, for a pending application to demolish the unit, or for gas or electric service that runs through a tenant's meter to serve other areas. The related rules Maine does have: if a tenant's utility pays for heat, electricity or another utility serving common areas or other units, you must have a written agreement with the tenant for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration approximating that cost, or you owe actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees; a court presumes you knew a tenant was paying for common-area service. Demolition does not change how you end a tenancy: a tenancy at will still needs at least 30 days' written notice with the court's form notice, and a fixed-term lease runs to its end unless its own terms allow earlier termination. Condominium conversions have separate notice rules.

title: Mold and Habitability
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring a written mold disclosure to tenants, but since 2025 it has a mold rule that works like one. It is a breach of the implied warranty of fitness for human habitation to offer for rent a dwelling unit where a leaking event, such as flooding or a failure of a roof, window, door, plumbing, foundation or appliance, or chronic moisture or humidity conditions outside the tenant's control, has led to the growth of mold, bacteria or other biological organisms. The rule applies when you offer the unit, so inspect for leaks and moisture-driven mold and fix them before renting, not just after a complaint. During the tenancy, the usual habitability remedies apply once the tenant gives written notice of a condition that endangers or materially impairs health or safety and you unreasonably fail to repair it, including a court complaint, a reduced-rent defense in a nonpayment case and, for small repairs, repair-and-deduct. You can address mold caused by the tenant's own conduct in the lease, but a clause shifting all mold risk to the tenant cannot waive the warranty. Towns may adopt stricter mold standards by ordinance.

title: Owner and Agent Identity
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant, at the start of a tenancy, the name and address of the owner or of a property manager or agent. Maine handles identity another way: anyone authorized to sign a residential lease or tenancy at will agreement for the owner is treated as the owner's agent for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. So if a manager signs your leases, a tenant can serve court papers and notices on that manager. Two disclosures do involve identity. When your interest in the property ends, for example by sale, whoever holds the security deposits must transfer them to the new owner, with an accounting, and mail each tenant notice of the transfer and the new owner's name and address, or return the deposits. And on a tenant's request you must disclose the name of the bank and the account number where the deposit is held. Maine has no rule that a missing identity disclosure bars an eviction. Naming the owner, any manager and a notice address in the lease is still good practice.

title: Pesticide Application Notice
bodyText: Maine's statutes leave pesticide notice to the Board of Pesticides Control, whose rules apply to rented residential buildings. Before an indoor application in a rented unit that its residents did not request, a Board-approved written notice must be given to those residents at least 24 hours and no more than 7 days ahead; for common areas the notice is posted for the same window and left up at least 48 hours afterward. The applicator is responsible but may have the landlord or building manager deliver or post the notice, and whoever does so is responsible for it. Residents may ask for the product name, EPA registration number, timing, location and re-entry interval. Baits, gels, pastes and crack-and-crevice treatments placed out of residents' reach, and treatments a tenant arranges for their own unit, are exempt from notice. A treatment may not be applied in a tenant's unit over the tenant's objection unless a public health or code enforcement official finds an immediate need, and the rule also requires that alternative control measures be tried and documented as failing before an application. For outdoor applications, a tenant may ask to be notified of spraying within 500 feet, and treated turf, ornamental and general pest-control areas must be posted. For bed bugs, Maine law is specific: treatment must be done by a certified commercial pesticide applicator carrying current liability insurance, and before entering to inspect or treat you must give the tenant reasonable notice, presumed to be 24 hours, stating the reasons for and scope of the entry; the tenant must then allow access and follow reasonable preparation measures. For other pests, the general entry rules apply: reasonable notice and entry at reasonable times except in an emergency. The Board of Pesticides Control rules (chs. 26 and 28) were read at sync.

title: Private Well Water Testing
bodyText: If a private drinking water well supplies water to your tenants, Maine requires you to test it and share the results. Beginning January 1, 2022 and every 5 years after, you must have each such well tested, through a certified or accredited laboratory, for arsenic and the other contaminants and properties on the state health department's uniform testing recommendation, which by statute includes bacteria, nitrates, nitrites, lead, uranium, manganese, fluoride, radon and, since 2026, PFAS. Within 10 days after you are notified of the results, give them to each tenant served by the well, and give any new tenant the most recent results. A 2026 law also requires every landlord of a residential building served by a private well to test the well water for PFAS no later than January 1, 2027, using a certified or accredited laboratory and the most recent EPA-approved method. Keep lab reports and proof of delivery, and give the most recent results before a new tenant signs; the library's Maine disclosure acknowledgment has a checkbox for this. If results show a problem, a contaminated water supply may also raise habitability issues.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warning for rental housing has no Maine counterpart. Maine has no statute requiring a landlord to post or give tenants a general warning about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and no list of such chemicals tied to rentals. Maine's chemical-safety laws aimed at products, such as its program for chemicals of high concern in children's products, regulate manufacturers and distributors, not landlords. The specific hazard disclosures Maine does require of landlords are separate and do apply: radon test results and the state radon notice before signing, the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing and Maine's 30-day notice before renovation work that may disturb lead paint, private well test results, and the bed bug disclosure. Asbestos, mold and meth have no lease disclosure rule in Maine but can affect habitability.

title: No Property Tax Share Statement
bodyText: Maine has no law requiring you to give tenants an annual statement of the share of their rent that goes to property taxes, or to state it in the lease or at each rent change. The figure Maine uses for renters is set by tax law instead: for the state's refundable property tax fairness credit, a renter's rent constituting property taxes is 15% of the gross rent actually paid during the year for the right to occupy the home, and gross rent excludes charges for utilities, services, furniture, furnishings or appliances you supply as part of the rental, whether or not the lease lists them separately. If you and the tenant did not deal at arm's length and the rent looks excessive, the assessor may adjust it. Because tenants claim this credit from their own records, a lease or rent ledger that separates base rent from utility and furnishing charges, and year-end receipts on request, help them. For cash payments you must already give receipts unless you live in a building of 5 or fewer units. The old rule splitting property taxes between landlord and tenant absent an agreement is covered separately.

title: Radon Testing and Notice
bodyText: Maine requires radon testing and a written radon notice for residential rentals. Every residential building had to be tested for radon in the air by March 1, 2014, and, unless a mitigation system has been installed, again every 10 years when a tenant asks; a building that starts operation later must be tested within 12 months after tenants first occupy it. Tests are done by a state-registered tester, or by you under department rules in simpler buildings. Before a tenant signs or pays a deposit, and within 30 days after you get new results for existing tenants, give the written notice on the state health department's form: the date and result of the most recent test, whether mitigation was done, the tenant's right to test, and the risks of radon. Report results to the department within 30 days. If a test shows 4.0 picocuries per liter or more, either you or the tenant may end the tenancy on at least 30 days' notice, and you cannot keep the deposit for that termination beyond what the deposit law allows.
