Failing to give the notice, or falsifying results, breaches the warranty of habitability and carries a fine up to $250 per violation. The duty covers the building, not just ground-floor units. Short-term-only buildings are exempt.

title: Disclosures Due Before Signing
No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Maine has no statewide sanitary or housing code variance procedure for rentals and no rule that a variance must be given to tenants or attached to the rental agreement. Local housing or building codes may have their own variance processes; if a town grants one for your property, giving tenants a copy is sensible. What Maine law does allow is a written agreement in which the tenant accepts specified conditions that may violate the warranty of fitness for human habitation in return for a stated rent reduction or other specified fair consideration; that agreement binds both of you, while any other lease waiver of your duty to keep the premises free of conditions that endanger or materially impair health or safety, or to meet the standards of any duly adopted ordinance or regulation, is void. The library's accepted-conditions clause is the Maine vehicle for that agreement, and a heat level below 68°F needs its own separate signed document.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to tell tenants or applicants that a registered sex offender lives in the building or nearby, and no statute protecting you from liability for not telling them. Maine's sex offender registry is maintained by the state, and public notification about released registrants is done by the Department of Corrections and law enforcement agencies, which notify the members of the public they consider appropriate. If a tenant or applicant asks, you may point them to the state's public registry. Be careful about what you say about a particular person: Maine's 2025 tenant privacy law makes it unlawful to disclose a tenant's or applicant's personal information without consent with intent to harass, intimidate or push the person out without legitimate business purpose, with damages of at least $1,000.

title: Sex Offender Residency Rules
bodyText: Maine puts no duty on a landlord about where registered sex offenders may live. There is no state proximity rule you must enforce, no crime of renting to two registered offenders who live together, and no lease statement that shields you from a local fine. The State occupies the field: a town may not regulate people convicted of sex offenses except by a residency ordinance limited to people convicted of Class A, B or C sex offenses against children under 14. Such an ordinance may bar residence only within up to 750 feet of a school or a public park, athletic field or recreational facility mainly used by children, may not reach someone who lived there before the ordinance, and may not be based on registration status; it restricts the offender's residence, not your leasing. Criminal history is not a protected class under the Maine Human Rights Act, so you may consider it under a consistent written screening policy, using no more than one paid background, credit or other screening check per applicant in 12 months, with a complete copy given to the applicant.

title: No General Lease Font Rule
bodyText: Maine has no general font-size or first-page placement rule for residential leases or lease disclosures, and no special occupancy disclosure for single-family homes. A few specific documents carry their own format rules. An agreement to provide heat below 68°F must be a separate written document, apart from the lease, clear and conspicuous, readable in plain English, in at least 12-point type and signed by both parties. A tenant's waiver of the 30-day notice before renovation work in pre-1978 housing must be in plain language, immediately precede the tenant's signature and be printed in at least 12-point boldface type in the statutory form. If a tenant buys a surety bond instead of paying a deposit, the surety's disclosure must show the word nonrefundable conspicuously in at least 16-point bold type on its first page and again just above the tenant's signature line. The total price disclosure must be plain and readily understandable by the general public. Otherwise, write the lease clearly, since a confusing term can be read against you and a misleading one can be an unfair trade practice.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants about public shoreline or beach access rights, public easements across the property, or shoreland zoning matters. Maine's shoreland disclosure applies to sales: for 1 to 4 unit residential property, the seller's property disclosure statement must give details of any shoreland zoning notice of violation, pending enforcement action, litigation, court judgment or settlement or consent agreement, and, for septic systems in shoreland zones, the shoreland septic disclosures; it must also describe the means of access to the property and who maintains any private access road. That statement is required for a lease with an option to purchase. For an ordinary lease, describe in the lease what waterfront, dock, beach or road access the tenant may use and any limits imposed by easements, association rules or shoreland permits, so the tenant is not misled about what is included.

title: Public Assistance and Vouchers
bodyText: Maine law makes it unlawful housing discrimination for anyone furnishing rental premises to refuse to rent to, or impose different terms of tenancy on, a person who receives federal, state or local public assistance, including medical assistance and housing subsidies such as a housing voucher, primarily because the person is a recipient. So you may not advertise no vouchers, turn an applicant away for having one, or charge a voucher holder a higher deposit or different rent. You may still apply neutral criteria that are consistent with business necessity and not based on receipt of assistance, applied the same way to every applicant. There is no separate statement you must put in the lease. The exemptions differ from the duty. The Human Rights Act does not apply to renting one unit of a 2-family dwelling where the owner lives in the other, or up to 4 rooms in a one-family home the owner occupies, and that exemption covers this public-assistance rule; but the ban on discriminatory advertising still applies to those owners. Violations can bring an order to rent, civil penal damages up to $20,000 for a first order, and actual and punitive damages. Whether a landlord must join a voucher program's contract terms turns on case law.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant whether the building has a sprinkler system, when it was last inspected, or that it lacks one, and no required sign or lease notice for unsprinklered buildings. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a separate question governed by the state fire code rules and local codes, covered in the sprinkler duty row. If the building does have a sprinkler system, the lease may tell tenants not to hang items from sprinkler heads, block them or tamper with fire protection equipment, and you should keep inspection records.

title: Sprinkler Requirements
bodyText: Maine's statutes and fire rules contain no general duty to retrofit sprinklers into existing apartment buildings. For new construction, the building code removes the model code's sprinkler requirement for one- and two-family dwellings, including additions and alterations to unsprinklered buildings, and the State Fire Marshal's rules likewise do not adopt the Life Safety Code's sprinkler section for one- and two-family dwellings; but new apartment buildings governed by the commercial building code keep its sprinkler requirement, with the lighter NFPA 13R system permitted up to four stories. Any required system must be approved by the State Fire Marshal. The statutes themselves require complete automatic sprinkler systems in new hotels of 2 or more stories and in high-rise commercial buildings 75 feet or taller built after January 1, 1992; a hotel includes an apartment hotel or other building with more than 15 sleeping rooms for hire, so rooming-house style rentals can be caught. An accessory dwelling unit does not need sprinklers unless it is within or attached to a structure with more than 2 dwelling units, or is in a mixed-use or nonresidential building, or the adopted fire codes otherwise require them. Violating a fire safety rule is a strict-liability Class E crime. A 2026 law (2025 Me. Laws ch. 657) directed the State Fire Marshal to study the cost of sprinkler requirements for residential buildings of 3 or more units, so check current rules before building, converting or adding units. The State Fire Marshal's and building code rules were read at sync.

title: Fire Code for Rentals
bodyText: Maine sets fire safety standards for rental buildings through rules adopted by the Commissioner of Public Safety, which govern safety to life from fire in or around all buildings, and through the Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code for construction. The State Fire Marshal's rules adopt the 2018 editions of the NFPA 101 Life Safety Code (with Maine amendments) and the NFPA 1 Fire Code, the 2019 NFPA 72 fire alarm code, and the 2016 NFPA 13, 13R and 13D sprinkler standards. The Life Safety Code's own text sets the requirements for apartment buildings, lodging or rooming houses and one- and two-family dwellings, so check it, and any local fire code, for your building type. Unvented fuel-fired heaters may not be used in a bedroom or bathroom; boarding care facilities and children's homes with 17 or more beds must meet the Life Safety Code. Violating a fire safety rule is a strict-liability Class E crime, so it does not matter whether you knew of the violation. Some fire duties are in the statutes themselves: working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and fuel gas detectors where required, approved smoke detectors listed by Underwriters Laboratories or Factory Mutual, and sprinklers in hotels (including apartment hotels) with more than 15 sleeping rooms and 2 or more stories, and in commercial high-rises, built after January 1, 1992. A 2026 law (2025 Me. Laws ch. 657) directed the State Fire Marshal to adopt the 2025 edition of the national fire alarm code; the posted rule still adopts the 2019 edition. Maine's statutes, 2025-2026 session laws, constitution, civil procedure rules and seven agency rules were searched, and the State Fire Marshal's rules were read at sync; the NFPA code texts, case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Stigmatized Property Rule
bodyText: Maine has no stigmatized-property statute. No Maine law says whether you must, or need not, tell a prospective tenant that a death, homicide, suicide or other crime occurred in the unit, that it is reputed to be haunted, or that a prior occupant had an illness such as HIV. The general rules govern instead. Misrepresenting a material fact, or answering a direct question falsely, can be an unfair or deceptive trade practice. The Maine Human Rights Act bars inquiries and statements about a person's physical or mental disability in connection with renting, which counsels against volunteering a past occupant's medical condition. And Maine's 2025 tenant privacy law limits disclosing a tenant's personal information, including health conditions and status as a crime victim, when done to harass or push someone out without a legitimate business purpose. A sensible policy is to answer direct questions truthfully without naming people or revealing private information.

title: No Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Maine has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that you must give tenants or attach to a lease, and no rule that a tenant cannot sue until it is provided. Three state documents come close. Since December 1, 2025 the Attorney General must post, and update every odd-numbered year, a model residential lease that complies with current law and includes any required disclosures and attachments; using it is not required but it is a useful benchmark. When you serve a notice to terminate a tenancy, you must attach the judicial branch's form notice posted on its website. And the summons and complaint in an eviction must carry the judicial branch's one- to two-page plain-language form describing the court process, the consequences of not appearing, rental assistance, legal and housing counseling resources and mediation, with a mediation request form. The library's Maine termination and eviction rows cover those notices.

title: No Truth in Renting Law
bodyText: Maine has no Truth in Renting Act, no state truth-in-renting booklet to give or post, and no required statement in a lease that the agreement must comply with landlord-tenant law. Maine reaches the same goals through other rules. Requiring a tenant to sign a lease term that waives a right under Maine's landlord-tenant chapters is an unfair trade practice, specific terms such as exculpation for your negligence, tenant payment of your legal fees, liens on tenant property and acknowledgments that the lease is fair are unenforceable, and a tenant can sue under the Unfair Trade Practices Act for actual damages, restitution and mandatory attorney's fees. Required pre-signing disclosures are listed in the disclosures row, and the Attorney General's model lease shows what a compliant Maine lease looks like.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Because Maine has no statewide rent cap, just-cause eviction law or general tenant purchase right, there is nothing for a property to be exempt from at the state level, and no notice or lease statement telling tenants that a property is exempt. Some Maine rules have their own exemptions that you apply without any notice: the 75-day notice for rent increases of 10% or more does not apply to deed-restricted affordable housing or subsidized housing; deposit, cash-receipt and repair-and-deduct rules do not apply to a unit in a building of 5 or fewer units where you live; and the Human Rights Act does not apply to renting one unit of an owner-occupied 2-family home or up to 4 rooms in your own home, except its advertising ban. Local rent ordinances in Portland and South Portland have their own exemptions and may require exemption claims or filings; check them.

title: No Rent Cap or Just Cause Notice
bodyText: Maine has no statewide tenant protection act capping rent increases or requiring just cause, so there is no statutory notice telling tenants that such limits apply, and no general right for tenants to buy or receive an offer on a rental you plan to sell. What Maine has instead: at least 45 days' written notice of any rent or mandatory recurring fee increase, and 75 days for increases totaling 10% or more within 12 months (with exceptions for deed-restricted affordable and subsidized housing); no rent increase while the unit violates the warranty of habitability, unless the tenant caused it; and a presumption of retaliation for evictions after protected tenant activity. A 2025 law directed the state policy office to post a model rent stabilization ordinance for towns, and Portland and South Portland have local rent ordinances with their own notice rules, so check local law. Tenant purchase rights arise only in narrow settings, such as condominium conversions and lots leased for camps in unorganized territory.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Maine requires towns to allow accessory dwelling units, and the rules reach rentals. Where residential uses are permitted, a municipality must allow at least one ADU on a lot whose principal structure is a single-family home or a 2-unit or 3-unit residential structure, whether built within an existing dwelling, attached to it or as a new structure on the lot. Under 2025 amendments, a town must allow an ADU to be built or occupied even if the lot owner does not live on the lot, so owner-occupancy requirements are barred and an ADU may be rented. One ADU per lot is exempt from density calculations, may not face added parking requirements beyond those for the single-family home, must be allowed on a nonconforming lot if it does not increase the nonconformity, and must be at least 190 square feet. Before occupancy you must verify adequate water and wastewater service. An ADU needs sprinklers only if it is within or attached to a structure with more than 2 dwelling units or fire codes otherwise require them. Exceptions include certain Lewiston-Auburn drinking water watersheds and optional town exemptions for coastal barriers, special flood hazard areas and sand dunes; shoreland zoning still applies. Once rented, an ADU is a dwelling unit subject to all landlord-tenant rules.

title: No Single-Family Zone Rental Limit
bodyText: Maine has no statute limiting the renting of homes in single-family zones to owners who live on the lot. State housing law runs the other way. In any area where residential uses are allowed, towns must permit at least 3 dwelling units per lot, including accessory dwelling units, and at least 4 per lot in a designated growth area or where public water and sewer serve the lot, and must allow an accessory dwelling unit to be built or occupied even if the lot owner does not live there. Towns may still regulate short-term rental units offered through transient rental platforms, may set dimensional and other limits the statute allows, and must design their ordinances to affirmatively further fair housing. Two different versions of the units-per-lot rule were enacted in 2025 and the Revisor marks the subsection as a conflict; both require at least 3 units, and 4 in growth or sewered areas, but differ in wording, so check the current text and your town's ordinance.

title: Detector Tampering Charges
bodyText: Maine has no statute authorizing, setting or capping a lease fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke, carbon monoxide or fuel gas detector. What Maine does provide: the tenant must keep detectors working, keeping them connected and keeping charged batteries in them, testing them periodically and not disabling them; and no one may knowingly interfere with or make inoperative a required smoke or carbon monoxide detector, a civil violation with a fine of up to $500 per violation payable in a court case, not to you. A lease may make the tenant pay your actual, reasonable cost to repair, replace or reconnect a detector the tenant disabled, and that cost can be charged against the deposit as tenant-caused damage. Maine law treats charges that reimburse reasonable costs or deter lease violations as separate from rent, so such a charge cannot support a 7-day notice for unpaid rent. A large fixed tampering fee is not authorized by any statute and could be challenged as an unenforceable penalty. Keep the fee tied to actual cost and document the tampering.

title: Asbestos Work in Rentals
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to disclose asbestos to tenants, inspect a rental for asbestos, or give a tenant notice before asbestos work. Maine's asbestos law regulates the work itself: no person, owner or operator may carry out asbestos abatement, meaning removal, demolition, enclosure, repair, encapsulation, handling or disposal of more than 3 square or linear feet of material containing at least 1% asbestos, unless licensed or certified, and the Department of Environmental Protection must be notified in writing before work begins, generally 10 calendar days ahead by mail or 5 working days by delivery. The rule binds any person and any owner or operator, defined as a person who owns, leases, operates, controls or supervises an asbestos abatement activity within a building, so a landlord renovating a rental must use licensed asbestos professionals for jobs above that threshold. For a lease with an option to purchase a 1-to-4 unit property, the seller disclosure statement must report the presence or prior removal of asbestos. Damaged asbestos-containing material that endangers tenants' health can breach the warranty of habitability.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, porches or other exterior elevated elements on rental buildings, and no statewide inspection schedule, engineer certification or report to tenants or the town. The general duties still cover them. Your implied warranty of habitability extends to common areas of the building, and you may not maintain or permit any condition on the premises that endangers or materially impairs tenants' health or safety; a rotted deck or loose railing can be such a condition. A lease term excusing you from liability for your own negligence, for example for a balcony collapse, is unenforceable. Local building or housing codes and state fire safety rules may impose maintenance, egress or inspection requirements, so check them, and inspect and document exterior structures regularly, especially before each new tenancy and after winter.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Not Waivable
bodyText: In Maine neither the casualty rule nor the duty to mitigate can be contracted around in a residential lease. Casualty: while the premises are destroyed or damaged by fire or other unavoidable casualty so that they are unfit for use or habitation, you cannot sue for rent, or for damages for breach of the lease's conditions, for that period. The statute saves an agreement contained in a lease only for buildings used primarily for nonresidential purposes and for leases securing Maine Guaranty Authority obligations, so a residential lease clause keeping rent running after a fire is not enforceable (the statute's separate mention of a written instrument to pay the rent is unsettled; do not rely on one for a residential tenancy). Mitigation: if a tenant leaves early and stops paying, or is removed for breach, your recovery is reduced by the net rent you could obtain by reasonable efforts to re-rent, unless you expressly agreed to accept a surrender and end the tenant's liability. Both rules sit in Maine's forcible entry and detainer chapter, and requiring a tenant to sign a lease term that waives a right in that chapter is an unfair trade practice. Write casualty and early-termination clauses to work with these rules, not against them.

title: Children as Occupants
bodyText: Maine has no rule that a lease must address occupancy by children, list children as occupants, or contain any statement about them. The Maine Human Rights Act makes familial status a protected class, so you may not refuse to rent, set different terms, advertise a preference, ask about familial status or evict because a household includes children under 18, someone who is pregnant or someone securing custody. Reasonable local, state or federal limits on the maximum number of occupants still apply, and housing that qualifies as housing for older persons is exempt from the familial status rules. You may list all occupants, including children, in the lease for occupancy-limit and emergency purposes, as long as the same rule applies to everyone. Lead rules give families with young children added protection: you may not evict a family with children because unsuspected lead is discovered, and must relocate them while lead hazards ordered abated are fixed. Maine's older separate statute on discrimination against families with children was repealed when the protection moved into the Human Rights Act. The owner-occupied 2-family and rooms exemption applies to the familial status rules except the advertising ban.

title: Terms a Maine Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: Maine bans specific lease terms and makes using them costly. Requiring a tenant to sign a term that waives any tenant right in Maine's eviction, rental property or security deposit chapters is an unfair trade practice unless the law specifically allows that waiver. These lease or rule terms are unenforceable and also unfair trade practices: excusing you from liability for your or your agent's negligence; making the tenant pay your legal fees to enforce the lease (except prevailing-party fees after a contested hearing for wanton disregard of the lease); requiring a lien on the tenant's property; requiring the tenant to acknowledge the lease or rules are fair and reasonable; charging a fee or penalty for ending the tenancy, other than reasonable re-renting costs when the tenant broke the lease's notice terms, unpaid rent or reasonable repair costs for tenant damage; and requiring optional or mandatory recurring fees that violate the disclosure rules. A lease is unenforceable if you lack the tenant's signed total price disclosure when one is required. Other sections separately void waivers of habitability, repair-and-deduct, common-area utility, entry, rent-increase notice and deposit rights, bar firearm bans in certain subsidized units and assistance-animal fees, and cap late fees, deposits and move-in money. Saving words such as to the extent permitted by law do not cure a banned term.

title: No Exculpation for Negligence
bodyText: A Maine residential lease or rule may not excuse you from liability for your own negligence or your agent's. Such a term is unenforceable, and requiring a tenant to accept it is an unfair trade practice, so wording like to the fullest extent permitted by law does not save it. Maine's statute names exculpation for negligence; it does not separately mention indemnity or hold-harmless clauses, but a clause making the tenant cover your own negligence has the same effect and carries the same risk. A clause making the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, household or guests cause is ordinary and lawful. Two statutes limit your liability directly, without any lease term: when a tenant makes repairs under Maine's repair-and-deduct law, you are free from liability for injury caused by those repairs; and in certain federally subsidized apartments where you must allow tenants' lawful firearms, you are not liable for firearm incidents except for willful, reckless or grossly negligent conduct. Carry insurance rather than relying on exculpatory wording.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Maine has no statute or court rule that names confession-of-judgment clauses in residential leases, and Maine's court rules contain no confessed-ejectment procedure. Such a clause would not work in Maine anyway. A landlord may recover possession only through the court's forcible entry and detainer process, with the statutory notices, the court form notices and a hearing; evicting a tenant any other way is an illegal eviction. Requiring a tenant to sign a lease term that waives rights in Maine's eviction chapter is an unfair trade practice, and a clause authorizing judgment against the tenant without notice and hearing would have that effect. Maine's consumer credit law expressly voids authorizations to confess judgment in consumer credit transactions and bars lessors in those transactions from taking them, which shows the state's policy, though that law covers credit and leases of goods rather than apartments. Do not include a confession-of-judgment or cognovit clause.

title: No Jury Waiver in Residential Leases
bodyText: A Maine residential lease should not contain a jury-trial waiver. Maine's Constitution guarantees a jury in civil suits and controversies concerning property, except where it was not historically practiced, and Maine's eviction statute gives either party the right to appeal an eviction judgment to the Superior Court for a trial de novo on any issue triable by right by a jury. That appeal right sits in Maine's forcible entry and detainer chapter, and requiring a tenant to sign a lease term that has the effect of waiving a right in that chapter is an unfair trade practice. The Legislature expressly allowed jury waivers in commercial leases between landlords and for-profit business tenants, and made no such allowance for residential leases. A tenant suing under the Unfair Trade Practices Act has a right to a jury in Superior Court, and a consumer's waiver of that Act is void. A party can still lose the jury appeal by not filing the required demand and affidavits under the court rule, but that is a procedural default, not a lease waiver. The reading rests on the statutes' text.

title: Penalties for Using Banned Terms
bodyText: In Maine, using a banned lease term is itself unlawful, not just unenforceable. Requiring a tenant to accept a lease term that waives a right under Maine's landlord-tenant chapters is an unfair and deceptive trade practice, and the specifically listed terms, such as negligence exculpation, tenant payment of your legal fees, liens, fairness acknowledgments, termination fees and improper recurring fees, are declared both unenforceable and violations of the Unfair Trade Practices Act. A tenant who loses money or property as a result may sue for actual damages, restitution and an injunction, and if a violation is found the court must award the tenant reasonable attorney's fees and costs, whatever the amount in controversy; the tenant must first send a written demand at least 30 days before suing, and your written settlement offer can cut off later fees if the judgment is not more favorable. The Attorney General may seek an injunction and, for intentional unfair or deceptive conduct, civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation. Maine has no separate multiple-of-rent penalty, and no rule that knowing use is required. Saving clauses do not help. Review your lease against Maine's lists before using it.

title: Eviction Penalty Clauses
bodyText: Maine has no statute that names a lease clause imposing a penalty because of an eviction notice or eviction case, but its rules leave little room for one. A lease may not make the tenant pay your legal fees for enforcing the lease, except prevailing-party fees after a contested hearing in cases of wanton disregard of the lease. A lease may not charge any fee or penalty for the act of ending the tenancy, except reasonable costs of re-renting when the tenant broke the lease's notice terms, unpaid rent, and reasonable repair costs for tenant damage. Late fees are capped at 4% of a month's rent. What the tenant may owe in an eviction is set by statute: to reinstate a tenancy at will after a 7-day rent notice expires, the tenant pays all arrears, rent due to the date of payment and the filing and service fees you actually paid, and a court may award costs. A fixed eviction fee, notice fee or penalty in the lease is risky; using a banned term is an unfair trade practice.

title: Rights a Maine Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Maine has a general non-waiver rule for its landlord-tenant law and many specific ones. Generally, requiring a tenant to sign a lease or tenancy at will agreement containing any term that has the effect of waiving a tenant right in Maine's eviction chapter, rental property chapter or security deposit chapter is an unfair trade practice, unless the law specifically allows the tenant to waive that right in negotiations with you. Specific sections add that waivers are void: the warranty of habitability and your duty to keep premises free of dangerous conditions and the repair-and-deduct remedy (except a written agreement accepting specified conditions for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration), the rent-reduction defense, common-area utility protections, entry and lock rules, rent and fee increase notice, the bar on increases during habitability violations, and every deposit protection. The 30-day notice ending a tenancy at will may be waived only in writing when the notice is given, and abandoned-property rights only after or upon vacating. A consumer's waiver of the Unfair Trade Practices Act is void. The few allowed agreements are narrow and must be specific, so draft them as separate, signed documents.

title: Severability and Void Terms
bodyText:
The library's severability clause works in Maine for most banned terms, with one major exception. Maine's statutes generally make an offending term, not the whole lease, unenforceable or void: the listed unfair terms are each declared unenforceable, and waivers of habitability, entry, deposit and other rights are void, leaving the rest of the lease in place.

But Maine also has a whole-lease rule: a lease or tenancy at will agreement is unenforceable if you do not receive a signed copy of the total price disclosure when one is required, that is, whenever the tenant pays any mandatory or optional recurring fee. A severability clause cannot rescue a lease from that rule, so get the signed disclosure before the tenant signs.

Severability also does not undo the consequences of having used a banned term: requiring a tenant to accept one is itself an unfair trade practice, so remove banned terms rather than relying on severance.

title: No Lease Unconscionability Statute
bodyText: Maine has no statute declaring residential lease terms void for unconscionability. Maine's unconscionability statutes cover sales and leases of goods under the Uniform Commercial Code, consumer credit transactions, condominium sales and some other consumer contracts, not apartment leases; whether a court would refuse to enforce an unconscionable residential lease term as a matter of common law was not determined, because Maine case law was not searched. Maine instead uses specific bans: lease terms that waive tenant rights or appear on the statutory list are unenforceable and unfair trade practices, and a lease may not even require the tenant to acknowledge that the lease and rules are fair and reasonable. Maine has no statute declaring any particular lease clause, such as a default for misrepresenting an animal, fully enforceable; misrepresenting an animal as a service or assistance animal is separately addressed in Maine's service animal law. Write terms that are fair on their face and within the statutory limits.

title: Unfair Trade Practices Act and Leases
bodyText: Maine's Unfair Trade Practices Act reaches residential leasing. It declares unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, and trade and commerce include the offering and sale of any property, real, personal or mixed. A tenant who leases property primarily for personal, family or household purposes and loses money or property because of an unfair or deceptive practice may sue for actual damages, restitution and an injunction; the tenant must first mail or deliver a written demand at least 30 days before suing, and if a violation is found the court must award the tenant reasonable attorney's fees and costs. A consumer cannot waive the Act. Maine's landlord-tenant statutes also declare specific practices, such as requiring a tenant to waive statutory rights or using listed lease terms, to be violations. The Act exempts activity that a state or federal regulator specifically authorizes, if you show you are regulated and the activity is authorized. Maine's Act does not list leaving blank spaces at signing or failing to give a copy at signing as specific violations, though misleading conduct can still be unfair or deceptive; give each tenant a completed, signed copy.

title: No General Plain-Language Rule
bodyText: Maine has no general plain-language law for residential leases. Plain-language requirements apply to particular documents: the total price disclosure must be plain and readily understandable by the general public; an agreement for heat below 68°F must be a separate document readable in plain English in at least 12-point type; a tenant's waiver of the 30-day lead renovation notice must be in plain language in 12-point bold type in the statutory form; and the court's form notice served with an eviction summons must be in plain, readily understandable language. The Attorney General's model residential lease, posted since December 2025, is a useful example of compliant, readable terms. Because confusing or misleading wording can still support an unfair or deceptive trade practice claim, write leases in short, clear sentences and define key terms.

title: What a Maine Lease Must Say
bodyText: Maine has no single list of terms a residential lease must contain, and an oral tenancy is allowed. Particular rules depend on what the lease says or require something in writing. To charge a late fee, you must give written notice when the agreement is made that a penalty of up to 4% of a month's rent may be charged. For a written lease, the deposit must be returned within the time the agreement states, not over 30 days. A written lease without its own termination or notice terms for material breach lets either side use the statutory 7-day procedures. Your smoking policy may be stated in the lease. Prevailing-party attorney's fees are allowed only if the lease limits them to wanton disregard after a contested hearing. The lease may permit you to dispose of abandoned property without liability if you follow the statutory notices. An agreement for heat below 68°F must be a separate signed document apart from the lease; agreements accepting specified habitability conditions or common-area utility costs must be in writing with stated consideration. Before signing you owe several disclosures, and in an eviction you must file a copy of any written lease with the complaint. The Attorney General's model lease shows a complete Maine lease.

title: Maine Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Maine sets these money limits for residential rentals, whatever the lease says. Security deposit: no more than 2 months' rent, and a surety bond plus any deposit may not exceed 2 months' rent together; deposits must be returned or itemized within the lease's stated time, not over 30 days, or 21 days for a tenancy at will, with double damages for wrongful retention. Move-in: no more than the first full month's rent, the deposit and any properly disclosed mandatory recurring fee. Application: no application or review fee, only the actual cost of one background, credit or other screening check per applicant in 12 months. Late fee: only for rent unpaid 15 days after the due date, only if disclosed in writing at signing, and no more than 4% of one month's rent. Rent and mandatory fee increases: at least 45 days' written notice, 75 days if increases reach 10% within 12 months. Bed bug preparation help: repayable over no more than 6 months unless you agree to longer. Returned checks: no statutory cap on a lease fee; a court may add a civil penalty up to $150 after the statutory 10-day notice. Deposit, receipt and repair-and-deduct rules do not apply to owner-occupied buildings of 5 or fewer units.

title: Passing Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Maine has no general statute barring you from passing governmental fines on to tenants, or limiting pass-through to fines the tenant caused. A lease may make the tenant reimburse fines that result from the tenant's own violations, such as a parking, trash or noise ordinance fine charged to you because of the tenant's conduct. Such a reimbursement is a charge, not rent, so it cannot support a 7-day notice for unpaid rent, and a recurring charge must appear in the total price disclosure. Fines for your own obligations, such as code violations, missing smoke detectors or lead hazards, are yours. One statute is explicit: a person held liable to a utility for wrongfully obtained or diverted utility service, including the civil penalty of up to $3,000 per violation, may not pass that cost on to tenants who received the diverted service because of that person's actions. And requiring a tenant to waive a statutory right through a fee clause is an unfair trade practice. Local ordinances may assign some fines directly to occupants.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Maine has no statute giving every tenant a non-waivable right to call police or emergency services, and none voiding lease terms or nuisance rules that penalize such calls in general. Victims get specific protection: a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may not be evicted because of incidents of actual or threatened violence at the premises, or because the victim reported such incidents to any agency, where that would otherwise be treated as a nuisance, damage or a lease violation. An eviction begun within 6 months after a tenant, before being served with an eviction notice, notified you that the tenant or the tenant's minor child is a victim, or reported a landlord's sexual harassment to law enforcement, is presumed retaliatory unless it rests on a 7-day ground or a lease violation and the tenant has not used the repair-and-deduct remedy. Your tenant-privacy duties under a 2026 law (2025 Me. Laws ch. 767) still allow disclosing tenant information to law enforcement in exigent circumstances or to prevent or prosecute a crime. Do not draft lease terms that count calls for help against a tenant; they risk retaliation, fair housing and unfair-practice claims.

title: Fair Housing in Maine
bodyText: The Maine Human Rights Act protects more people than federal law. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, steer, advertise a preference, make inquiries or evict because of race, color, sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, physical or mental disability, religion, ancestry, national origin, familial status, or because a person sought and received a protection order; and you may not refuse to rent to or set different terms for someone primarily because the person receives public assistance, including housing subsidies. Disability rules require reasonable accommodations and modifications and allow assistance animals without fees or deposits. You may apply criteria consistent with business necessity that are not based on a protected trait. The exemptions are narrow: renting one unit of a 2-family home where you live in the other, or up to 4 rooms in your own home, is outside the Act, but the advertising ban still applies; religious-membership housing and qualifying housing for older persons have limited exemptions. Retaliation and coercion are unlawful, and your own sexual harassment of a tenant is separately prohibited. Complaints go to the Human Rights Commission within 300 days or to court within 2 years; remedies include orders to rent, civil penal damages up to $20,000 for a first order, and actual and punitive damages.

title: Tenant Screening Rules
bodyText: Maine regulates tenant screening through several separate rules rather than one act. Fees: you may not charge to apply or review an application, only the actual cost of one background, credit or other screening check per applicant in 12 months, after telling the applicant you must give a complete copy of the results, which you then provide. Fair housing: criteria must not turn on a protected class or primarily on receipt of public assistance, and you may not ask about disability except permitted neutral questions, such as ability to meet tenancy requirements or current illegal drug use. Credit and background reports are subject to Maine's Fair Credit Reporting Act; you may require an applicant's social security number for a background check you conduct; if an applicant's report is frozen and not unlocked for you, you may treat the application as incomplete; medical debt may not appear on reports. Business screening services may disseminate only complete, current criminal records. A person whose eligible conviction has been sealed may lawfully decline to disclose it. Maine has no conditional-offer or look-back rule for criminal history, no rule limiting income tests to the tenant's share of rent, and no statutory shield for renting to people with records; use written, consistent criteria tied to business necessity.

title: Immigration Status and Tenants
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring or forbidding a landlord to ask about immigration status, no immigrant tenant protection act, and no law making it unlawful to rent to someone unlawfully present. Immigration status is not a protected class under the Maine Human Rights Act, but national origin and ancestry are, so questions or policies about citizenship or status that single out applicants by national origin, or that are applied unevenly, risk housing discrimination claims. Maine's 2025 tenant privacy law treats citizenship, immigration status and alien registration numbers as personal information that you, your agent and anyone acting for you may not disclose without consent, with intent to harass, intimidate or force a person out outside the court process and without a legitimate business purpose; the tenant may recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus an injunction and fees after a contested hearing, and the conduct can support a harassment protection order. Disclosures in response to subpoenas or to law enforcement in exigent circumstances are allowed. If you verify identity, accept a range of documents and apply the same rule to every applicant.

title: Protected-Class Inquiries
bodyText: Maine bans protected-class questions separately from the ban on discrimination itself. Anyone with the right to rent or manage housing, or their agent, may not make any written or oral inquiry about a prospective tenant's or occupant's race or color, sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, physical or mental disability, religion, ancestry, national origin, familial status, or past actions seeking and receiving a protection order. Real estate brokers and agents may not make any written or oral inquiry or record about those traits for applicants or intended occupants. The Human Rights Commission's housing rule adds that you may not ask whether an applicant or anyone associated with the applicant has a disability or about its nature or severity, but may ask every applicant the same neutral questions about ability to meet tenancy requirements, eligibility for disability-based housing or priorities, current illegal use of controlled substances, and convictions for illegal drug manufacture or distribution. Application forms and screening scripts count. The owner-occupied 2-family and rooms exemption covers these inquiry rules for owners, but not for brokers or advertising. Maine's tenant privacy law separately limits disclosing such information.

title: Victim Information Confidentiality
bodyText: Maine has no statute specifically requiring you to keep confidential the documents or information a tenant gives you to use Maine's domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking protections, such as a protection order, police report or advocate's statement used for early termination, lock changes or eviction defenses. Two rules still apply. Maine's 2025 tenant privacy law treats a person's status as a crime victim, along with contact details and other personal information, as protected: you, your agent and anyone acting for you may not disclose it without the tenant's consent, with intent to harass or intimidate or to push the person out outside the court process and without a legitimate business purpose; damages are actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus an injunction and fees after a contested hearing. And a victim enrolled in the Secretary of State's Address Confidentiality Program has a designated substitute address that state and local agencies and courts must use. Retaliation against a tenant who tells you of victim status is presumed in some evictions. Good practice is to keep victim documentation in a separate file, share it only as needed, and never with the alleged perpetrator.

title: Tenant Information Privacy
bodyText: Since 2026 Maine limits what you may reveal about tenants and applicants. You, your agent and anyone acting at your direction may not disclose a known or prospective tenant's or occupant's personal information without that person's express consent, when doing so with intent to harass, intimidate or otherwise cause the person to leave outside the court eviction process and without a legitimate business purpose. Personal information means identifying details such as name, address, phone or email; racial or ethnic origin, religion, health, sexual activity, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, citizenship or immigration status; social security, driver's license or state ID numbers; billing, financial or payment information; and status as a crime victim. Disclosures are allowed in response to valid discovery, subpoenas or judicial warrants, to Maine law enforcement in exigent circumstances or to prevent or prosecute a crime, as reasonably necessary to sell or refinance the property or for affordable housing program funds, and to respond to code enforcement or fire officials. The tenant may recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, an injunction and, after a contested hearing, attorney's fees, and the conduct can support a protection-from-harassment order. Keep tenant files secure and share only for business needs.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Maine protects tenants who organize, mainly through its eviction law. No writ of possession may issue if the tenant proves the eviction was started in retaliation for the tenant's membership in an organization concerned with landlord-tenant relationships. Separately, an eviction begun within 6 months after a tenant asserted certain statutory rights, complained in good faith to a code enforcement body or in writing to you about required repairs, or filed a fair housing complaint before the eviction notice is presumed retaliatory, unless it rests on a 7-day ground or a lease violation and the tenant has not used the repair-and-deduct remedy; joint complaints by organized tenants fall within these protections. For low-income rental housing with affordability restrictions or financial assistance, an owner who plans to sell, prepay or otherwise end those restrictions must give notice to the tenants and to any tenant organization for the property, at least 90 days before contracting. Maine has no statute guaranteeing tenants meeting space in common areas, the right to distribute flyers door to door, or recognition of a tenant union for bargaining, and none voiding a neutral lease rule on common-area use, though a rule aimed at organizing could be evidence of retaliation.

title: No Foreign Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Maine has no law restricting foreign adversaries, foreign governments or nonresident aliens from owning or leasing real estate, and no lease-duration carve-out of the kind some states adopted. Maine's statute on aliens runs the other way: an alien may take, hold, convey and devise real estate or any interest in it, and earlier conveyances to or by aliens are valid. A residential tenancy is an interest in real estate, so neither a foreign landlord nor a foreign-national tenant faces a state-law bar. Maine's separate definition of foreign adversary appears in a state technology procurement law, not in property law. Federal rules, such as sanctions, foreign-investment review and tax withholding on payments to foreign owners, can still matter for foreign-owned rentals. In screening tenants, do not treat citizenship or national origin as a disqualifier: national origin and ancestry are protected under the Maine Human Rights Act.

title: Pool Fencing and Safety
bodyText: If your rental property has an outdoor swimming pool, Maine requires a fence around it. A swimming pool for this rule is any outdoor in-ground or above-ground receptacle designed for water 24 inches deep or more; the fence or wall must be at least 4 feet high, built to keep children out, with openings no larger than 4 square inches (or vertical gaps no wider than 4 inches), and every gate or door through it must be able to be securely fastened whenever not in use. A house or accessory building may form part of the enclosure, and portable above-ground pools with sidewalls at least 24 inches high are exempt. Failing to comply within 30 days after written notice of a violation is a civil violation with fines up to $500 per day. Towns may adopt stricter or looser pool enclosure ordinances. A pool or spa used only by your apartment tenants or condominium residents and their guests is a residential pool, outside the state's public pool plan review, operation and supervision rules; Maine requires no lifeguard even at public pools, and no pool safety notice at lease signing. Pool rules in the lease, and liability insurance, are your main tools.

title: No Key Control Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring a written key-control policy, restricting staff access to master keys, or requiring background checks of employees who can enter tenants' units, whatever the size of the complex. The rules that do apply: you may enter a unit only with reasonable notice, presumed to be 24 hours, at reasonable times, and for the purposes the law allows, except in an emergency; unlawful or harassing entry costs actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, and fees after a contested hearing, and the tenant's entry protections cannot be waived. A tenant who changes a lock must give you a duplicate key within 48 hours, or within 72 hours if the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Possessing a master key designed to fit more than one lock with intent to commit a crime is a burglary-tools offense. A written key log, limited master-key access, prompt rekeying after keys are lost or staff leave, and screening of staff are sensible practices that support your duty of reasonable care.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring landlords to install steam radiator covers, on request or otherwise, and no mandatory lease rider about radiators. Radiators and other heating equipment still fall under your general duties. If you are obligated to provide heat, the heating facilities must be able to keep the unit at least 68°F at the statutory measuring points and must be operated to protect the building from freezing, and you may not maintain or permit any condition that endangers or materially impairs tenants' health or safety; an exposed, dangerously hot radiator in a child's room could qualify, especially after the tenant gives written notice. Local housing codes may set specific standards. Installing covers where young children live, and addressing heating equipment in the lease and move-in inspection, is sensible practice.

title: No Water Heater Setting Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring you to set a unit's water heater to a maximum temperature before each new tenant moves in, in the landlord-tenant law or in any energy or building statute in the searched corpus. Hot water still matters. A water heater that endangers or materially impairs tenants' health or safety, including scalding temperatures or a unit with no hot water where you supply it, can breach the warranty of habitability and your duty not to permit dangerous conditions. Where a water heater serves common areas or other units but runs on one tenant's utility, you need a written agreement with that tenant for a stated rent reduction or other fair consideration approximating the cost; water heaters used in common are listed among common areas. Repairs to plumbing equipment under repair-and-deduct must be done by a licensed professional. Plumbing and building codes adopted by agencies or towns may set temperature standards. Setting tank thermostats to a safe level at turnover is good practice.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring window guards or window stops in rentals where young children live, and no required lease notice about them. The general rules still apply: you may not maintain or permit any condition that endangers or materially impairs tenants' health or safety, and a broken window, sash or lock reported in writing can trigger the habitability and repair-and-deduct remedies. Local housing codes may require screens, guards or fall protection, so check the municipality. If a family with young children lives above the ground floor, consider offering window stops or guards that still allow emergency escape, since bedroom windows often serve as required exits under fire codes.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Maine has no statute on a subsidized tenant's refusal of a housing program inspection, and none letting you refuse a voucher tenancy, or end one, because of the program's inspection requirements. Refusing to rent to, or setting different terms for, someone primarily because the person receives public assistance, including a housing subsidy, is unlawful housing discrimination, subject to the owner-occupied 2-family and rooms exemption. A subsidized tenant, like any tenant, may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry, on reasonable notice, to inspect or to show the unit to workers or contractors, and an inspection under a program contract can be arranged on that basis; repeated unreasonable refusal can be a lease violation, and a tenant at will can be given 30 days' notice. A tenant's good-faith complaint to a code enforcement body within 6 months before an eviction raises a presumption of retaliation. Program rules under your housing assistance contract may add obligations. Whether refusing to participate in a voucher program's terms is lawful turns on case law.

title: Veterans Housing Incentives
bodyText: Maine has no tax credit for landlords who rent to veterans, but it funds programs that can pay landlords. Under the Veterans' Housing Provider Incentive Program created in 2026, the Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services awards grants to tax-exempt organizations whose core program supports permanent housing for veterans, and those organizations may use the money for housing provider incentives, risk mitigation payments and past rental debt payments for veterans experiencing homelessness. Separately, the Veterans' Homelessness Prevention Partnership Fund may make disbursements to organizations, businesses, landlords or other entities to prevent homelessness among veterans. Funding is limited and depends on appropriations and grants, so contact the bureau or a participating veterans' housing organization. Public housing authorities must give veterans and their families admission preferences in the order the statute sets. Military and veteran status is not a protected class under the Maine Human Rights Act, but a sign-on incentive program does not change your fair housing duties to other applicants.

title: Licensing for Property Managers and Leasing Agents
bodyText: Maine requires a license to engage in real estate brokerage, and its licensing law defines real estate to include all estates and lesser interests in land, which can include a lease. But the law defines brokerage as services for another, for pay, calculated to result in the transfer of an interest in real estate, and its list of brokerage activities mentions only selling, buying, exchanging, options and finding buyers; it never mentions renting, leasing or property management. So whether a paid third-party manager or leasing agent who finds tenants and signs leases for an owner needs a license was not resolved here: the Real Estate Commission's rules do not address rentals, leasing or property management. Some points are clear. An owner or lessor, and the owner's regular employees acting as part of their usual duties, are outside brokerage. Unlicensed brokerage brings a forfeiture of up to $2,000 per violation plus the compensation received, and an unlicensed person cannot sue to collect a brokerage fee. Whoever is authorized to sign your leases is your agent for service of process and notices, and the limit on money due at move-in binds your agent or broker too. Before you hire, or work as, a paid manager or leasing agent for someone else's property, check with the Real Estate Commission. Maine's statutes, 2025-2026 session laws, constitution, civil procedure rules and seven agency rules were searched, and the Real Estate Commission's rules were read at sync; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Recovery Residences
bodyText: If you own or operate a recovery residence, meaning shared, alcohol- and drug-free peer-support housing for people recovering from substance use disorder, several Maine rules differ from ordinary renting. Certification is voluntary, but since July 1, 2022 a residence must be certified under the state's criteria to receive state agency contracts or housing assistance from the state, MaineHousing or a municipality. A town may not deny general assistance just because someone lives in a recovery residence, may pay housing help for an uncertified residence for only one 30-day period, and on request pays a certified residence's operator directly. A certified residence must have a written discharge and transfer policy approved by a recognized credentialing entity; with one, it may immediately discharge or transfer a resident, despite the eviction statute, when needed for the resident's welfare, when the resident's needs cannot be met, or when others' health and safety are at risk, and the owner, operator or police may order a resident who refuses to leave off the premises. Without certification and an approved policy, use the ordinary notice and court eviction process. A qualifying certified residence (no more than 2 residents per bedroom, a full bathroom for every 6 residents, family-home detector rules) is treated as a residence for a family under the fire and building codes, though one in a multiunit apartment building must meet all state and local code requirements for that type of building.

title: Renting to a Minor
bodyText: A lease signed only by someone under 18 is risky to enforce in Maine. No action may be maintained on a contract made by a minor unless the minor, or someone lawfully authorized, ratified it in writing after turning 18, except for necessaries or real estate the minor received title to and keeps the benefit of. Whether a minor's apartment lease, or the rent owed under it, counts as a necessary is a question for the courts, and Maine case law was not searched. A separate provision gives a minor 16 or older full legal capacity to make contracts for the purpose of furthering higher education, which may reach a student's housing, though no statute says so expressly. Practical steps: rent to a minor only with a parent, guardian or other adult signing as co-tenant or guarantor, and keep the written guaranty; or ask whether the minor has a court order of emancipation, which the District Court may grant to a juvenile 16 or older. Apply the same screening rules to everyone and do not use age as a pretext for refusing families with children. If you later need to evict, name the adult tenants and "all other occupants" so the judgment reaches everyone in the unit.

title: Heating Fuel in the Tank
bodyText:
Maine has no statute on heating oil, kerosene or propane left in a tank when a tenancy starts or ends, so settle it in the lease: who buys fuel, whether the tank must be left at the same level, and how any credit or charge is figured.

Maine rules still shape the deal. At the start of a tenancy you may require no more than the first full month's rent, the security deposit and properly disclosed mandatory recurring fees, so do not require the tenant to pay you for the fuel already in the tank as a move-in charge. Fuel is energy delivered for the unit, which Maine treats as a utility service cost, not rent: if you must give a total price disclosure, list the tenant's fuel costs and any fuel reimbursement the lease requires, and do not use a 7-day nonpayment-of-rent notice for an unpaid fuel charge.

If the lease makes you responsible for heat, keep enough fuel to meet the heat standard; otherwise a tenant may buy fuel and deduct it under the repair-and-deduct rule (not available in an owner-occupied building of 5 or fewer units). A mobile home park operator may not require residents to buy fuel oil or bottled gas from a particular dealer unless it runs a central distribution system.

title: Renting Rooms and Lodging Houses
bodyText: Renting rooms is usually still a tenancy in Maine. The landlord-tenant law covers dwelling units, which include buildings and other structures rented for human habitation, so a roomer who lives in a room as a home, with no fixed-term written lease, is ordinarily a tenant at will entitled to written notice and the court eviction process. A separate innkeeper law treats hotels and lodging houses differently. A lodging house is a house where lodgings are rented, but not one renting to fewer than 5 lodgers (relatives within the second degree do not count), and a guest of a hotel or lodging house is not a tenant under the landlord-tenant laws. A lodging house must keep a register of every guest, with room number and date, and a record of departures, kept for 2 years; willful violation is a crime. Towns may require lodging houses to be licensed. The state health department's lodging license covers only stays of fewer than 183 days a year and excludes landlord-tenant rentals. Whether a long-term roomer in a house with 5 or more lodgers is a guest or a tenant is not settled by statute, so use the eviction process to remove anyone who lives there as a home. Renting up to 4 rooms in your own one-family home is outside most of the Human Rights Act; short stays may owe lodging tax.

title: Wood Stoves, Chimneys and Fuel-Burning Equipment
bodyText: Maine's landlord-tenant statutes do not say who cleans the chimney or supplies firewood for a wood, pellet or other solid-fuel stove or fireplace in a rental, so put those duties in the lease. Other Maine law still applies. Anyone who installs or services solid-fuel burning equipment, including pellet-fired central heating, or oil, propane or natural gas burning equipment must be licensed by the state fuel board; freestanding solid-fuel fireplace stoves, room heaters and cookstoves not attached to a central heating system are excepted, and the do-it-yourself exception covers only a single-family home the installer lives in, not your rental. No one may, for pay, build, install or maintain a vent or solid-fuel appliance except under the state's rules, and a paid chimney or fireplace installer must first give a written disclosure that the work meets NFPA 211. The state rules may not bar a stove from sharing a flue with another oil or solid-fuel appliance if, among other conditions, the chimney is lined and intact and a carbon monoxide detector is installed near a bedroom. Towns may adopt stricter rules. If the lease makes you responsible for heat, the 68°F standard applies, and you may not keep any condition that endangers or materially impairs tenants' health or safety; a tenant using repair-and-deduct must use a licensed professional for oil burner work.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Maine Leases: Why the Library Does Not Offer One
bodyText: Maine's arbitration act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, and a party's right to a lawyer cannot be waived in advance (14 M.R.S. §§ 5927, 5932). Maine's rental law points the other way for residential leases, though. Requiring a tenant to sign a lease term that has the effect of waiving any tenant right in Maine's eviction, rental property or security deposit chapters is an unfair trade practice (14 M.R.S. § 6030(1)). Those chapters give tenants rights they enforce in court. For example, a tenant may file a habitability complaint in the District Court or Superior Court, and any other waiver of those rights is void (§ 6021(3), (5)). The Legislature allowed lease arbitration and jury waivers only in commercial leases (§ 6017(4), (5)). A violation exposes you to the tenant's damages and mandatory attorney's fees, and to Attorney General civil penalties of up to $10,000 per intentional violation (5 M.R.S. §§ 209, 213). Federal arbitration law may override some of these limits, but because Maine attaches penalties to the lease term itself, the library does not offer an arbitration clause for Maine.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Maine follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (11 M.R.S. § 3-1311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (11 M.R.S. § 1-1308(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Maine's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (14 M.R.S. chs. 709, 710, 710-A and 710-C searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Maine's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages: Six Years
bodyText: Maine's landlord-tenant chapters set no special deadline for a landlord's suit against a former tenant, so the general limitation statute applies. Civil actions, including a suit for unpaid rent, lease charges or damage to the unit, must be commenced within 6 years after the cause of action accrues (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 752). Personal actions on contracts under seal may be brought within 20 years (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 751), but whether a residential lease counts as under seal is case law, so treat 6 years as your deadline. A promise to pay or acknowledgment of the debt restarts the clock only if it is express, in writing and signed by the tenant; a promise by one co-tenant does not bind the others (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 860). A part payment keeps whatever effect it has under the case law, but a note of the payment written by you is not enough proof of it (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 863). Time while the former tenant is absent from and residing outside Maine is not counted (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 866). For a periodic tenancy, count the 6 years separately for each unpaid installment from the date it fell due.

title: Showing Notice Cannot Be Waived in Maine
bodyText: A Maine tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, mortgagees or tenants (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6025(1)). Except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, you must give reasonable notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times; 24 hours is presumed reasonable in the absence of evidence to the contrary (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6025(2)). Any agreement by a tenant to waive any of these rights is against public policy and void (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6025(4)). So a lease term or separate signed addendum shortening or waiving notice for showings is void, and Maine has no exception for buyers or for a signed separate document. Entering in violation of the section, in an unreasonable manner, or by repeated harassing demands lets the tenant recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, an injunction and, after a contested hearing, attorney's fees (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6025(3)). Give at least 24 hours' notice for every showing; if a tenant agrees to a particular shorter-notice visit, confirm that tenant's agreement in writing for that visit.

title: No Carpet Cleaning Rule; Cleaning and Normal Wear and Tear
bodyText: Maine has no statute on carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing lets you require professional carpet cleaning as a matter of law, nothing conditions such a requirement on the carpets having been professionally cleaned before the tenancy, and there is no age or depreciation test for carpet or paint. The deposit law's general rules decide what you may charge. You may not keep any part of the deposit to pay for normal wear and tear (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6033(1)). Normal wear and tear is the deterioration that occurs from the intended use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, the household or their guests (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6031(1)). If the unit was rented in a habitable condition, normal wear and tear does not include what you must spend to return it to a habitable condition, which may include cleaning costs, unless that need was caused by you, by events beyond the tenant's control or by someone outside the tenant's household and guests (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6031(1)). Any lease provision waiving the deposit chapter's protections is void (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6036). Cautious course: charge for carpet cleaning only when the carpet is dirtier or more damaged than ordinary use would leave it, record its condition with photos at move-in and move-out, and list the cost in the written itemized statement.

title: Recording a Maine Lease Is Optional
bodyText: Maine has no lease registry and does not require you to record a residential lease. Recording matters for long leases: a lease for more than 2 years or for an indefinite term is effective only against you, your heirs and devisees and people with actual notice of it unless it is acknowledged and recorded in the registry of deeds for the county where the land lies (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 33, § 201). Between you and the tenant an unrecorded lease still binds. Instead of the whole lease, you may record a memorandum of lease executed and acknowledged by one of the lessors that names all parties, describes the property, states the date and term and describes any renewal, extension, purchase-option or transfer provisions; it need not describe the rent, and once recorded the lease is treated as recorded for all purposes (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 33, § 201). Nothing in Maine's landlord-tenant chapters turns on whether a lease was recorded. Record a memorandum if the term runs past 2 years, the lease has no fixed end, or the tenant has a purchase option it needs protected against a later buyer or lender.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Maine)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Maine property law does not use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise here. The closest Maine interest is a life estate, for example a surviving spouse who holds a home for life while the children own the remainder. Maine law says that when a tenant for life conveys a greater estate than he or she can lawfully convey, the conveyance passes only the estate the life tenant has and does not cause a forfeiture (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 33, § 157). So a lease signed by a life tenant generally cannot bind the remainder owners beyond the life estate; what happens to the tenant when the life estate ends is case law. The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder owners sign the lease or agree in writing that it continues if your life estate ends first.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property in Maine
bodyText: Maine's criminal trespass law lets you keep a non-tenant out of parking lots, hallways and other common areas. A person who knows he or she is not licensed or privileged to do so commits criminal trespass by remaining in any place in defiance of a lawful order to leave, or entering any place in defiance of a lawful order not to enter, personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 402(1)(D)-(E)). Entering a place the person may lawfully be excluded from that is posted, fenced or otherwise enclosed to exclude intruders is also criminal trespass (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 402(1)(C)). These are Class E crimes; entering a dwelling place without license or privilege is a Class D crime (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 402(1)(A)). So give the person a written no-trespass notice in person, keep a dated copy and a witness, and tell the police. A tenant's guest in the tenant's own unit is there with the tenant's permission, so deal with a problem guest through the lease and, if needed, the 7-day termination notice for a guest's violence or threats (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6002(1)(E)), not by a trespass order alone.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText: Maine has no statute requiring an employer-landlord to give a housed employee a signed disclosure of the conditions for occupying and vacating, or to offer a rental agreement when the job ends. Employee housing is covered by the ordinary eviction process: forcible entry and detainer may be brought against a tenant where the occupancy of the premises is incidental to the employment of a tenant (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6001(1)). The statute does not set a separate notice period for that case, so the cautious course is to end the occupancy with the notice the tenancy otherwise requires (for a tenancy at will, the 30-day notice, or the 7-day notice for its listed causes) before filing (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6002). Put the housing terms, including what happens when the job ends, in a written lease or employment agreement, and never remove an employee by lockout or utility shutoff.

title: Renting to Students in Maine
bodyText: Maine has no student-housing regime: no licence to rent to students, no required student-housing clause, and no special rent, deposit or termination rule for a student tenant. Maine's landlord-tenant chapters also have no exclusion for school dormitories or fraternity houses; they reach any dwelling unit rented for human habitation (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6021(1)(A)), and the hotel and lodging-house rules are the main carve-out. A student renting a private apartment or house is an ordinary tenant, and you must use the ordinary notice and eviction process. Whether a college's own residence hall is a tenancy is outside this library.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: Maine has no statute deciding whether you or your tenant holds the hunting and fishing rights on rented land or farmland, so the lease decides.
