Two Maine rules turn on the owner rather than the tenant, which is worth knowing before you rent a home with land. No one may discharge a firearm within 100 yards of a building or residential dwelling without the permission of the owner or, in the owner's absence, of an adult occupant of that building or dwelling authorized to act on behalf of the owner (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 12, § 11209(1)(A)); so a tenant can give that permission only if you authorize it. Posting signs or paint marks against trespass mean access is prohibited without permission of the landowner or the landowner's agent (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 402(4)). If you want to keep the hunting, fishing and trapping rights or let others use them, say so in the lease and describe where and when; if you want the tenant to hunt or to give permission near the home, grant it in writing with any limits.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: Maine has no building energy benchmarking law and no statute that lets a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. The one Maine rule on landlords and tenants' utility accounts points the other way: when a landlord and the electric utility agree that service in a tenant's name will transfer to the landlord instead of being disconnected, the utility may not disclose to the landlord any personal or confidential information about the tenant or the tenant's account except upon the tenant's consent, beyond the fact of the transfer and what it needs to keep service on (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 35-A, § 704(1-A)). Compilations that do not disclose a customer's identity are not confidential (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 35-A, § 704(5)(C)). If you need a tenant's usage data, for an efficiency program, a lender or a sale, get a separate written authorization from the tenant in the form the utility requires; a lease clause records the tenant's agreement but does not oblige the utility to release anything.

title: No Rights Guide Delivery Duty
bodyText: Maine does not require you to give a residential tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights, before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one. No Maine statute directs a state agency to prepare such a guide for tenants or requires a lease to carry a summary of the landlord-tenant laws, and the Maine Human Rights Act sets no brochure or poster duty for rentals. Maine instead requires specific notices, such as the statement in every notice to terminate a tenancy at will that the tenant has the right to contest the termination in court (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6002). You may hand tenants a plain-language guide if you like, but it is not a legal requirement.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Maine Lease
bodyText: No Maine statute requires a residential lease to state that the property is inside a special district, such as a water, sewer or village corporation district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges, rules or plans. We found no statute that passes district taxes or charges to a tenant; they reach the tenant only if the lease shifts them. If you want the tenant to pay a district charge, say so plainly in the lease as an amount the tenant agrees to pay; nothing does it automatically. A mandatory recurring fee that is not rent can be raised only on the same written notice as rent (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14, § 6015), so build any pass-through in at the start rather than adding it later.

title: Leasing Tribal Trust Land and Indian Territory in Maine
bodyText: Maine has no territorial-style communal land, but its Indian claims settlement law restricts leases of some tribal land. That law defines a 'transfer' of land to include a lease (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 30, § 6203(13)). Any transfer of Houlton Band Trust Land is void from the start, except for takings for public use, transfers of individual use assignments between members of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, transfers authorized by the federal settlement act, and transfers under a special act of Congress (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 30, § 6205-A(3)). Within the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot Indian territories, the tribes exercise governmental powers, including enacting ordinances (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 30, § 6206(1)), and land within those territories that is held in trust is governed by federal law as well. So if the property is on tribal trust land or in Indian territory, do not rely on this library's lease or on Maine's landlord-tenant chapters alone: confirm with the tribe and the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs what approval a lease needs before the tenant moves in or pays rent. Ordinary Maine land that is not tribal land needs no government approval to lease.
